proj_ezpAp1POh20dBnYpx0BjhU35.description:
This project will be implemented at Farm of the Future, a member of the Ecosystem Restoration Communities movement. 
Through the establishment of agroforestry systems, this project will prove to local communities’ members and local authorities that there are eco-friendly and economically viable alternatives to the monoculture plantation model. 
First, a pilot agroforestry system will be planted at Farm of the Future. About 2,000 trees will be planted on a plot of 1ha. This area will function as a demonstration site. 
After the establishment of this demonstration site, at least three local smallholder farmers will establish agroforestry systems on their land and become in turn examples for the broader community. 
This project has also an important educational goal: each tree planted will directly finance an agroforestry training program that will educate and empower at least 120 high school students per year and will ensure the long-term sustainability of the project. 
The ‘Rural and Natural’ cooperative is the organization responsible for implementing the agroforestry project and the educational training. The cooperative was established in 2020 by Farm of the Future in cooperation with the local community.
Farm of the Future, has a holistic vision for the development of the region of Caseara based on 7 dimensions: agroforestry and regenerative farming; entrepreneurship; education; eco-tourism; rewilding and ecosystem restoration; renewable energies; spirituality.
This specific project will focus mainly on the following three dimensions:
- Agroforestry, with the creation of agroforestry systems,
- Education, in cooperation with the ‘Escola Foresta’ (forest school) to train local youth in agroforestry techniques,
- Entrepreneurship, with the development of a cooperative mode that will improve local communities’ livelihoods and enhance food security.

proj_ZCspL8JYmUu0OXcx6O73I1j0.description:
ITPA was born in 1998, from the initiative of environmentalists committed to guaranteeing the protection of one of the last and most conserved fragments of Atlantic Forest, in Rio de Janeiro, the Tinguá Biological Reserve.
We are currently the largest environmental organization based in the state of Rio, where we maintain dozens of work fronts, with more than 70 employees, and we have already planted 3.5 million trees. We are involved in forest restoration actions, creation and implementation of natural reserves, natural tourism, among others.
The ITPA focuses on the bioregion called the Tinguá Bocaina Biodiversity Corridor. This is the most critical fragmentation region of the largest Atlantic Forest continuum in the country and comprises the main springs that supply water to the metropolitan region of Rio de Janeiro (about 10 million inhabitants).
ITPA maintains many areas in the process of forest restoration, with more than 3.5 million native trees in partnership with almost 100 rural landowners, through voluntary area assignment contracts and payment contracts for environmental services. It also maintains the largest brigade for preventing and fighting forest fires, with very satisfactory results for natural regeneration.
At the same time, we develop environmental education projects with schools in order to raise awareness and directly involve young people in the regeneration process of the Atlantic Forest.
It should be noted that ITPA has a headquarters with all the infrastructure for educational and forest restoration actions, integrated with a Private Reserve of Natural Heritage and with buildings built in an ecological way.
proj_ZCspL8JYmUu0OXcx6O73I1j0.longTermPlan: The long-term objective of the ITPA is to plant 15 million trees, aiming to reconnect the forest fragments of the Tinguá - Bocaina corridor and consolidate the recovery of degraded areas within areas protected by law (Conservation Units and Private Reserves of Natural Heritage).
proj_ZCspL8JYmUu0OXcx6O73I1j0.mainChallenge: The biggest challenge to carry out this project is to raise the necessary resources for forest restoration.

properties.name: Graham Bell
properties.description: The area to be reforested is around the Tinguá Biological Reserve and within the Tinguá - Bocaina Biological Corridor. This region has been deforested in the last 300 years by intensive coffee production, followed by extensive cattle ranching and the use of constant burning. This whole process has generated soil degradation, scarcity of water resources and enormous loss of biodiversity. The area has a high rate of biological diversity and a large number of endemic species, comprises the Hydrographic Basin of the Guandu River, whose waters supply and generate energy for approximately ten million people in the Metropolitan Region of the State of Rio de Janeiro. Although essential for the maintenance of life and environmental services, the site constantly suffers from increased forest degradation. Forest restoration in this area is of fundamental importance for the metropolitan region of Rio de Janeiro, for the Atlantic Forest and for the entire planet.

proj_nXBzA2sbX2tm1D75p7bfJ81Z.description:
Plant-for-Ghana is a hybrid restoration agroforestry project initiated by Plant-for-the-Planet Ghana - a national affiliate of Plant-for-the-Planet Foundation. Sustainable reforestation is the way we can restore the lost forest in the Northern Savannah Ecological Zone of Ghana and reach the overarching goal of planting 10 million trees. 
This hybrid project combines two different approaches: planting of native species and planting of agroforestry species in mixed stands. Planting high-diversity tree mixes in deforested areas not only ensures that forest restorations are resilient to the ongoing threats of climate change but also is proven to produce multi-functional forests and productive forest stands. Moreover, mixing both native tree species that will not be harvested and agroforestry species ensures that local communities can benefit from the fruit produced by subset of productive tree species that are planted (e.g., Mango, Cashew). 
Plant-for-Ghana plans to restore 10 million trees in Ghana by 2030. This year we will be planting over 16,000 native and agroforestry trees, considering the hybrid approach of this project, which employs 20 planters, 4 nursery staff, one forester, four plantation staff and two administrative staff. The next year we aim to plant over 200,000 trees on site and greatly increase the number of people involved in this project. All plantings will be made at densities that are representative of the natural density of trees in this savannah zone.  
The species we are planting this year include Kyaya ivorensis (African Mahogany), Senna siamea (caesalpinioideae subfamily), Anacardium occidentale (Cashew tree) and Pakia biglobosa (Legume family). The number of species will be increased to a minimum of 10 species planted per hectare within the next year. 
The adoption of an agroforestry approach can be likened to the proverbial use of a single hit to kill multiple flies as it has proven to be able to solve many problems at a go. This approach is adopted having in mind the community where the project is located, which would create sustainable food production to safeguard food security, landscape management and biodiversity protection.
The entire project creates green jobs in rural areas and, at the same time, raises awareness of the importance of tree biodiversity among the local people. It further creates additional carbon sinks and creates sustainable sources of income for many families in said zone. 
The project also has additional impact on:  
•	Partnering with universities to provide students with field experience and help come out with more improved and fast-growing species. 
•	Increased habitat for many animal species. 
•	Fighting the desertification of the Northern Savanna Ecological Zone of Ghana. 
•	Creating a role model project for neighbouring countries. 
•	Beekeeping for women and youth.

properties.description:
Plant-for-Ghana is a pioneer reforestation project by Plant-for-the-Planet Ghana - a national affiliate of Plant-for-the-Planet Foundation in Germany. The Yucatan Reforestation project in Mexico, with its valuable experience, serves here as a lesson learned project. Sustainable reforestation is the way we can restore the lost forest in Ghana and reach the overarching goal to plant a trillion trees. 
This project creates green jobs in rural areas and at the same time raises awareness on biodiversity among the local people. This project will further create additional carbon sinks and also create sustainable sources of income for many families in said zone. 
There are additional benefits to this project. 
· It serves as a study or research ground for the partner universities to provide students with field experience and also help come out with more improved and fast-growing species. 
· It serves as a habitat for many animal species. 
· It closes the gap in the desertification of the northern savanna ecological zone of Ghana. 
· It shall serve as a role model project for neighboring countries. 
. Beekeeping for women and youth.
In Ghana, desertification and climate change are critical issues as they seriously threaten over 84,000 km (square) or 35 % of the total land area of Ghana, displaces most of the people in these areas and threatens farming activities as a result of drought and floods which affects food security in these areas. 
Plant-for-Ghana plans to restore 10 million local tree species in the Northern Savannah Ecological Zone of Ghana, which is managed by the Plant-for-the-Planet Ghana. 
We are currently raising funds for the start of the project. A payment to the organization will be made as soon as the country is contractually secured. Until then, the Plant-for-the-Planet Foundation will hold your donations in trust. 
You are making a right decision by supporting Plant-for-Ghana with your donations! We only achieve the 10,000,000 goal with your support!. 
Thank you very much for your support! You are a change maker!

proj_wMNVTLkRIZ4TcV8oi26wlRwN.description:
The site was a forest before. It was cut down by the state. Now the local communities (ethnic minority Thai and Muong) replant, together with TROFACO. 
TROFACO is a Denmark-based non-profit climate action enterprise planting trees together with organized communities. TROFACO was started by development professionals with decades of experience in community development and agroforestry. In Son La Vietnam we work with the Vietnamese NGO Centre for Rural Economy and Development (CRED). The community group decides which species of trees to plant and crops to grow with the trees. As they make the decisions, they are invested in it, and therefore take particular care of the trees. The project is based on a contract with the community, co-signed by local authorities and by CRED. CRED staff visits the site frequently to talk with the community and check on the trees. TROFACO will visit at least once per year and take documentation pictures. These pictures will be uploaded to our database (trees.trofaco.org) with GPS coordinates and timestamps. 
To boost local development and commitment to the trees, 30% percent of the amount donated to this project (as for all TROFACO plantings) will be set aside in a legally separate fund. As we see the trees are doing well, the fund will distribute the funds to the forest group over the next 20 years. So, we are proud to provide real benefits to the community and surviving trees for the climate and our globe.

proj_vH52lGTvcjbCGKG4dINKsXJU.description:
KardiaNuts was established in 2018 through the vision of its founder for an empowered rural Colombia, with established networks for future growth, reduction of poverty and inequality, and preservation of the environment. KardiaNuts intends to achieve this vision through the development of a cashew-based agroforestry system that will generate inclusive and sustainable growth in an isolated region in Colombia. 

This project addresses development and environmental challenges in Vichada, Colombia. The population is one of the poorest in the country - the department’s multidimensional poverty index is 80% higher than national average. Smallholder producers participate in environmentally unfriendly slash-and-burn activities, unsustainable cattle raising, short-cycle less profitable crops and/or illegal activities. 

This initiative will regenerate the depleted soil in the region to support the production of subsistence crops and generate a flow of revenue through the production of cashew.

Auch im Jahr 2022 führen wir unsere Baumpflanz-Kooperation mit ISCOT in der Region Madi Opei im Norden Ugandas fort. Nachdem in den beiden letzten Jahren insgesamt mehr als 60.000 Setzlinge an Dorfgemeinschaften, Farmer und Schulen der Region verteilt worden sind, haben wir bei unseren vor-Ort-Partnern Jimmy und Joel bereits weitere 20.000 Bäume beauftragt. Diese werden in der Baumschule herangezogen um im April und Mai, mit Beginn der Regenzeit, verteilt. Hintergründe zu den Aktivitäten in den vergangenen beiden Jahren findet ihr auf den Projektseiten auf unserer Homepage.
Alle ab Juni 2022 eingehenden Spenden dienen der Finanzierung der Pflanzaktivitäten in der nächsten langen Regenzeit 2023, unser Ziel dafür sind wieder mind. 40.000 Setzlinge!

proj_1fYkuEszMqU7ryjrlEhqpkdA.description:
In response to the large-scale loss of mangroves in Mozambique, Eden Reforestation Projects initiated the Maputo Bay Reforestation Initiative with a vision to bring back the vitality of the forests that fringe the rivers and coastline of Maputo Bay in southern Mozambique. The project supports local communities to plant and manage mangrove forests, offers long-term employment and livelihood improvements to local communities while protecting the important biodiversity that relies on mangrove forests to survive. The program began in October 2018 with two planting sites near Maputo and has now expanded to many planting sites in Maputo Bay. The benefits of the work include helping protect coastal communities from environmental disasters, improving fisheries, removing carbon from the atmosphere, and increasing biodiversity while also addressing the urgent need for poverty alleviation and women's empowerment.

Djabissa Site Description


The Djabissa mangrove reforestation project is located south of Maputo, Mozambique, along a large channel that leads to the Maputo Bay. Before starting the project, the mangrove forests found in this area were severely impacted by deforestation and forest degradation from charcoal production and wood collection for cooking, construction, and other purposes. Eden now partners with the local community to reforest this massive mangrove estuary.

proj_EnErCebV90R97Uv2WbGVhB15.description:
Whitebark pine are a keystone and foundational species for high-elevation ecosystems in the western US, and their seeds are a food source for over 110 wildlife species including the threatened grizzly bear. in December 2022 they were listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act.

With Salesforce’s support, we helped to plant the next generation of whitebark pine in two high-priority restoration areas identified in the National Whitebark Pine Conservation Plan.

One is in northern Montana on the Flathead National Forest, which has already lost nearly all of its whitebark due to early outbreaks of white pine blister rust. This area is decades ahead of other areas in planning, and has identified sites that are suitable and stable for whitebark over the long term, where we can grow “founder stands” to restart the population. The seedlings we plant will be able to withstand future outbreaks of blister rust due to having special genetic resistance. 

The other sites are in Oregon, in the Cascades, where the disease outbreak is in earlier stages – one is the City of Bend, Oregon’s municipal (drinking water) watershed and the other is at the top of Paulina Peak, a site with high recreation use.

proj_z4VFz8QZq2suDRaydA14xYsO.description:
Our Girls Education program is focused on reimagining a system where less than 1% of girls move on to secondary school from primary.  We are centered on changing persistent attitudes towards girl’s education and the cultural and customary traditions that keep girls from attending and excelling in school. We work together with parents, caretakers, schools and government officials to create this change. The program provides academic mentorship, textbooks and supplies, life skills and sanitary pads to 2,500 girls across Northern Uganda. Girls education is considered one of the most cost-effective and cheapest ways to reduce emissions. The faster female education can be scaled up, the greater impact it will have on the environmental, workforce, health indicators and population growth. 

It is poverty that keeps girls from completing primary and continuing to secondary school. As we provide families with trees every year they keep their daughters in school they will have a sustainable income that can enable them to pay for school fees. Our program provides seedlings, trainings and technical support. By supporting this program you help girls access the fundamental right of education and help the planet at the same time!

proj_pHGBl9lG3B1jqg7wiRrZZjtm.description:
The Atlantic Forest and Caatinga biomes, located in Northeastern Brazil, shelter several rare and endangered species, also providing essential resources for vulnerable populations living in this region. Their few forest remnants are under severe threats due to deforestation and unsustainable use of natural resources. We urge to draw attention to Northeastern biomes and communities, so neglected in the environmental and social agendas, by restoring key forest areas and promoting long-term change.

The ReNordestando Campaign will plant 200,000 seedlings on priority areas for native species' protection, allied to ecosystem services improvement. This will secure water and food for local communities under a sustainable perspective in both biomes, while controlling harsh ongoing climate change effects in the region, as desertification and heat islands. We will also prioritize local suppliers for the provision of inputs and services for activities, moving the regional restoration productive chain forward.

This initiative will enable the restoration of 120 hectares of native forests in the Northeast of Brazil, potentially increasing habitat amount, connectivity, and quality for over 500 currently endangered species of fauna and flora; providing co-benefits for over 200 local families with access to more abundant, sustainable natural resources in climate-resilient landscapes; and also promoting socio-economic change for at least 50 people directly involved in the restoration productive chain.

CEPAN is not tax-deductible and cannot issue donation receipts!

proj_qTsc3O3rTVZdaCc0K4NY8zj5.degradationCause: The native forest is disappearing to plant eucalyptus, mainly for cellulose production. They are much more likely to catch fire than native trees. Wildfires are becoming more frequent. We are working to regenerate land lost to wildfires and also plant native tree species.
proj_qTsc3O3rTVZdaCc0K4NY8zj5.description: Wildfires are a major threat to ecosystems. Wildfires are increasing their number every year and their catastrophic consequences. We are working to restore degraded land due to wildfires and also plant trees to prevent future wildfires in certain areas. In this part of Spain, the substitution of the native forest for eucalyptus has increased drastically the number of wildfires.  While eucalyptus is a very flammable tree that catches fire very easily and produces a lot of bark debris that propagates the fire with the wind the native forest composed mainly of oaks and chesnuts is much harder to catch fire and acts as fire cutters when a fire starts in a eucalyptus area. Therefore we are also planting these trees around eucalyptus areas to stop fires.
proj_qTsc3O3rTVZdaCc0K4NY8zj5.longTermPlan: Regenerate the forest cover lost due to wildfires and gradually recover the native forest. The community plays a crucial role in the project, we work with local schools to promote environmental awareness. Wildfire prevention, and participation of the community in the chestnut recollection.
proj_qTsc3O3rTVZdaCc0K4NY8zj5.mainChallenge: The main challenge is the increasing amount of eucalyptus plantations and wildfires. Also, rain frequency is decreasing each year.

proj_odXvr2kA7N5JCEfvcJ2AcJsw.degradationCause: The original rainforest was destroyed for agricultural purposes using Tavy (slash and burn agriculture). Tavy is used principally to grow staple crops like cassava and rice, but unfortunately the burning is often followed by an invasion of non-native species, which compete with trees.
proj_odXvr2kA7N5JCEfvcJ2AcJsw.description: Green Again Madagascar seeks to restore damaged rainforest reserves in Madagascar. True ecological restoration is more than simply planting trees, rather it involves a long-term commitment to assisting the recovery of an ecosystem. Ambodijirofo is one site where GreenAgain Madagascar has trained and employed several members of the community to plant native trees locally on privately owned land.  The original forest on this land was destroyed many years ago and the community is gaining collective interest in restoring it. The staff are now independently constructing a nursery of native trees and office for data analysis.
proj_odXvr2kA7N5JCEfvcJ2AcJsw.longTermPlan: They’ll continue to grow and share their knowledge with locals. Interested landowners seek their help for reforestation on their land. They will construct a data center to record the number of trees planted and measurements to calculate ecological statistics specific to the ecology of this region.
proj_odXvr2kA7N5JCEfvcJ2AcJsw.mainChallenge: Invasive species outcompete the natives and strip the soil of nutrients. These non-Malagasy trees grow fast and decompose slowly which alters the soil and leaves it unfavorable to native species. Their dried leaves cover forest floors, encouraging fires to spread rapidly across the land.

proj_8QBjwKnIx2icquPX6J1y0dbx.description:
Our campaign goal is to plant a minimum of 100,000 trees in Ireland and 1,000,000 trees in Africa in 2020. We pledge that for every single native tree planted through our campaign in Ireland, we will plant a minimum of ten trees in Africa. This initiative will support the vital food and farming needs of Africa’s rural poor, while contributing to the wider global effort to absorb carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
The aim of the campaign is to amplify the efforts of people living in Ireland, and to create a global partnership in the fight against climate change. Climate justice is the challenge that defines this generation and we invite you to play your part.

proj_eKBbIt7Bzavu9o7xzCAqjS2t.description: The forests in Mexico, the country's most populous state, are increasingly threatened by the destruction of large areas of forest through deforestation, forest fires and overgrazing. Poor management of natural resources is exacerbating the situation. Often the soil quality has already deteriorated to such an extent that natural regeneration of the forests is no longer realistic. Sustainable reforestation is the last option here to prevent further erosion by renewing the protective vegetation and increasing soil fertility. In this way, the remaining forests and their resources can be saved for the future. With this goal in mind, Plant-for-the-Planet Mexico AC and PROBOSQUE, an organization affiliated with the Mexican Ministry of the Environment, have agreed to work together in the state of México (capital Toluca). The special feature of this project is that the reforestation comprises a total of 197 sub-areas of different sizes, all of which are managed in small, mostly rural structures. Of these, 92 are jointly managed ejidos, while the remaining areas are distributed among small farmers and cooperatives. All restored sites have been declared protected areas. When selecting the newly planted trees, care was taken to select a mixture of native tree species suitable for this part of the country. These include various species of pine, agave, a type of mimosa and Mexican cypress. They integrate perfectly into the existing forests and thus help to preserve the local biodiversity of secondary plants and animals. If this project cannot be realized due to circumstances related to the climate crisis, we will inform you and allocate the money to another project managed by Plant-for-the-Planet, preferably in the same country and of the same quality.

proj_9P7TiyLqmuJ5592hAfxA8t3R.description:
This restauration project is critical to the communities and forests surrounding Santa Rita Tlahuapan.  In the ejido of Tlahuapan the people depend on their environment for much of their livelihood.  Their land is under stress from climate change, increases in population and increased number of bark beetles.  This project will restore many hectares of natural forests which will provide habitat for many animals, ensure that underground water reserves continue to be replenished, minimize soil erosion and control harmful insects.  
This area is also home to several precious lightning bug sanctuaries.  A significant decrease in their population has been observed and the trees we plant will provide restauration of the forests where they live.  It is critical to the ejido that their habitats are maintained as they are an important source of tourism.
   
The project involves and aids significantly the people of Santa Rita Tlahuapan.  It includes an education program that will help give them tools and understanding so they can live more sustainably and successfully with their environment.
The high-altitude region of Santa Rita Tlahuapan is situated in the mountains between Mexico City and the city of Puebla near the active volcano Popocatepetl.  It is a beautiful, natural area that is home to many animals.  We are dedicated to conserving all of the fauna and flora of this beautiful region.

proj_4lodDjNp2pmmw8rXpej7m4yM.description:
This project was started aiming to make a green environment by planting various species of trees which are locally fit and suitable. This land is Nepal Sanskrit University Manpur Dang and local a group of people has taken 41 hectares of land in the lease for 20 years for purpose of making a green environment for fighting climate change and taking benefit from the fruit-based trees. There are many trees already available like around  2500  trees of mango, and 700 trees of Indian rosewood though around 400 plants trees of Indian bay leaf and teak were planted by a group of people last year.
This project's main objective is to make a green environment and to develop an Agrotourism or Agroforestry model in the coming future so a group of people has been working accordingly.  Another benefit of this project is to other adjoining communities people are also eager to the plantation in community and private land as a restoration model so they are asking for us to nominal support for the plantation program in new areas of the same location. 

  Our project also contributes to mitigating global warming and reducing greenhouse gases in the atmosphere by developing a greener environment. Local people can be using the timber from the plant after 20 years based on the using policy of restoration projects and they need to replant tree 3 instead of the loss of 1 tree modality as well as they can take benefit from fruit-based trees regularly.
The project will help the community to mitigate climate change effects and potential disasters as well such as soil degradation, heavy rainfall flood, drought, etc. Another major effect is other adjoining communities people can be practices such kinds of reforestation project activities because everyone has been highly affected by climate change and its related disasters. This project could be able to improve the living condition of local people by generating forest-based economic activities.

proj_MLzN8V4ArH9u41W8wa42UN2X.description:
Since 2019, American Forests has worked closely with the state of Rhode Island, municipalities and local nonprofits to develop and deploy a suite of climate and health tools that optimize urban forests for climate and health outcomes. As part of this pilot project, American Forests developed the first Tree Equity Score Analyzer (TESA), a state-of-the-art interactive map-based tool that can be used to plan tree planting projects at the parcel level and quantifies the specific local benefits to planting trees in that area.  

In 2021 and 2022, American Forests’ grassroots partner, Groundwork Rhode Island, will be the first to use TESA to decide where to plant 140 trees in high-need areas – many on residential properties - in the cities of Pawtucket and Central Falls. Both cities have some of the highest rates of impervious surfaces in the state and suffer disproportionately from heat islands. Groundwork Rhode Island has strategically focused their planting efforts in private properties in an effort to positively impact Tree Equity Scores and where survival rates are highest. Funding from Salesforce will allow Groundwork RI to work in partnership with the Pawtucket and Central Falls Health Equity Zone to expand their successful tree giveaway program “Trees4Us” to homeowners, tenants and businesses in high priority areas.
proj_MLzN8V4ArH9u41W8wa42UN2X.longTermPlan: Will have more details as work gets under way.
proj_MLzN8V4ArH9u41W8wa42UN2X.mainChallenge: Pawtucket and Central Falls have high concentrations of impervious surface which has intensified the urban heat island effect and contributed poorer health outcomes. Many of the areas with the highest climate health risks are lower income, communities of color, and have a low Tree Equity Score.

metadata.motivation: Sites are selected based on their tree equity score, which determines sites most in need of additional canopy. The lower the score, the higher the need. Scores are calculated based on a series of data including existing tree canopy, population density, income, employment, surface temperature, race, age, and health.

The Kigezi region which is located in south western region is one of the areas  in Uganda most affected by soil erosion. This happens very fast due to the hilly landscape of the region and  uncontrolled deforestation in the past

After doing our needs assessment, we realized, that we first have to create awareness to the local communities and regional stakeholders. Especially, we had to start planting immediately.

We have 30 volunteers in our field, we facilitate them with hoes, boots, rain coats, and meals since we plant the whole day. And we also need fuel / gas to facilitate our truck that transports seedlings from one nursery bed to another.

proj_9ShooMmxbB3thnsKZ1rSAXEw.description:
The Konso are a tribe in South-West Ethiopia. Their lifestyle and the agroforestry that they have practiced for centuries, with its impressive terraced fields, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. They can plant, cultivate and refine trees like no other group in Ethiopia and are role-models and experts for rural community-led forestry management. The Konso people depend on agroforestry and they need the ecosystem services of forested land to survive in a semi-arid environment.
With the existing five nurseries KDA would have the capabilities to supply more than a million seedlings per year. These can be planted on lands held by a cooperative of young people (with a 99 year lease). Furthermore, this youth group can acquire and develop the expertise through training with the Konso Development Association (KDA). The youth groups will be encouraged to start own multipurpose tree nurseries to maintain their plantation and to start a nursery business for additional income generation.
The Konso Development Association (KDA) is a non-political, non-religious and non-profit making local NGO (Non-Governmental Organization). KDA was founded in 1993 as a response to the natural and socio-economic problems at the root of the region’s pervasive poverty. KDA is a community-based development organization that facilitates work to sustainably improve the living conditions of the people in the region.
The Konso Development Association (KDA) is a partner of Plant-for-the-Planet. As part of the pioneer collaboration project “Plant-for-Ethiopia”, since 2019 they are working together to develop a sustainable forestry management system as well as a vocational training programme for youth.

visit: https://konsoda.weebly.com for details

KDA is not tax deductible and cannot issue donation receipts!

Giant dipterocarp forest extends from the tropical to the subtropical regions in South-east Asia. These forests, which are the most extensive forest types within the tropics, are greatly endangered and the least protected. More than half of the large trees observed in Southeast Asia rainforest belong to dipterocarp family accounting for the overwhelming majority of the tree biomass. Our project focused on restoring and protecting the giant dipterocarp forest in southern Philippines.

Endangered Species International is tax deductible in France, Philippines, Republic of Congo and the US!

proj_V5C6dsdL5aytR1xlOYw1b6US.description:
Bolivia is the poorest country in South America. The smallholder farmers in the Andes suffer under conditions of erosion, poor soil quality and climate change. There are, however, good methods to improve conditions with agroforestry, tree planting and water reservoirs.

Paraíso Verde, which includes Camp Chocaya along with a host of other farms, focuses on agroforestry: mixed planting of fruit trees, deciduous trees and vegetables with the aim of improving the income position of farmers. Other goals are also important, such as improving soil quality and water supply. The deciduous trees function here as green fertilizers to improve the soil quality. The fruit trees (mostly apple trees) produce fruits and thus increase farmers’ income. Our approach can help farmers triple their income.

This project thus contributes in various ways to the quality of life and income of the farmers involved and to improved environmental conditions.

proj_azZNfJrlQapnOY0WmNIjpkYw.description:
STRENGTHENING WOMEN TO PLANT FRUIT TREES FOR SUSTAINABLE LIVELIHOOD
The livelihoods of NYAKABINGO and KABUGHABUGHA communities are deeply dependent on farming and other land use, which provide incomes and food. According to our needs assessment 65% of these community residents are mostly small land holdings of between1-5 acres or less. Fruits for sustainable Livelihoods will work for vulnerable families who are most at risk from poverty and malnutrition.
Planting fruit trees is a popular way that local farmers can improve the productivity of their land. Through this project, we plan to establish two tree nurseries and train participants to graft and handle their own high-quality fruit trees. These can then be sold for a profit or planted to enhance their own farms. The project will focus on various fruit crops like mango, avocado, jackfruit, citrus, orange and paw paw which have high nutritional value and sell for a good price in local markets.
By helping farmers plant fruit trees on their land, we are helping farmers get alternative sources of income mostly marketing fruits thus reducing their reliance on natural forests, protecting them from overexploitation combined with the advantages of agroforestry; this is a positive step for both people and ecosystems living around Mt Rwenzori Forest National Park.
WHY BUILD A NURSERY BED
A nursery bed in the community will assume stewardship or ownership to the community we are serving. This will attract more community members to get involved in the tree-planting project because they will assume a sense of belonging to the project.
Producing seedlings is in the long-run cheaper and so cost effective than buying seedlings from other nursery beds – the main challenge so far. By training community members skills and knowledge will be gained e.g. to build an own nursery bed. The community will be much involved in all stages of the project and create employment opportunities like the full time nursery bed attendant and this will stimulate a sense of belonging to inspire most community members to join
In future it is planned to re -green and restore the degraded landscapes of NYAKABINGO AND KABUGHABUGHA rural communities that are severely affected by Climate Change. In this project, we will plant 500,000 fruit trees until 2030 that is when availed with necessary resources to establish a large tree nursery. Currently we start with a nursery bed costing USD $4564 for which we request climate change champions to help us mobilize and channel to this project in Uganda, East Africa.

proj_fkIuSjSlNyhAa5x0YJ36hp8v.description:
The Taita hills are the northernmost end of the Eastern Arc, a chain of ancient mountains running from S.E Kenya to S Tanzania. The Hills have a unique, highly threatened forest biota and are the highest-ranking conservation priority in Kenya. Deforestation is estimated at 98% and currently, only 12 highly fragmented forests remain with a combined total area of 500Ha only. The extreme levels of habitat loss, reduced forest connectivity and high levels of forest disturbance are causing severe threats to the Taita Hills' unique biodiversity.   
Since 2014, in collaboration with other partners, we have focused our conservation efforts in protecting and restoring the cloud forest as well as enhancing ecological connectivity for these threatened endemic species. The science-driven multi-tactic approach involves Planting of indigenous tree species on degraded public land, eradication of invasive/exotic species and replacing with indigenous species, Land purchase on critical sites to protect species and connect habitats, policy and advocacy, Awareness and conducting research that guide on proper conservation approach.
With full involvement of the local community and the local government, we have identified 32 patches of degraded public land (c.380Ha) that range from 3-20ha and well distributed within the Taita Hills which form our target restoration areas. Through our restoration pilot project, we have formulated a practical approach that will see virtually all the identified 32 patches restored with natural vegetation in a span of 18 years. We are currently  restoring 20 hectares located in 3 strategic sites. 
If the restoration of all the targeted sites is achieved together with the targeted land purchase, we shall achieve a 100% increase of the existing natural forest. this will significantly increase habitats and highly enhance forest connectivity thus solving the conservation puzzle of threatened species of both flora and fauna. Our restoration work will also contribute towards everting climate change and in ensuring increased water supply that will benefit local communities among other benefits.

proj_WZkyugryh35sMmZMmXCwq7YY.description: In 2015, we discovered that one of the most biodiverse areas, the Calakmul Biosphere Reserve in Mexico, was facing a significant environmental challenge: vast areas of medium semi-evergreen forest and seasonally flooded lowland forest had been deforested for cattle ranching and forestry exploitation. In response, we set out to restore biological interactions, ecological processes, and biogeochemical cycles by rehabilitating the affected areas. Today, a dedicated team of 36 people at Plant-for-the-Planet A.C. is working to restore these ecosystems, planting up to 9,000 trees in a single day. We focus on 17 native tree species from the Yucatan Peninsula, ensuring they are given the conditions to adapt successfully to their new environment. Plant-for-the-Planet doesn’t work alone. We collaborate with local farmers, government agencies such as the Ministry of Environment, Biodiversity, Climate Change, and Energy of the state of Campeche, as well as initiatives like “Production for Wellbeing” and “Sowing Life” in the states of Campeche, Yucatan, and Quintana Roo. These programs aim to combine the conservation of natural resources with their sustainable use. Our actions are part of a larger goal: to plant 100 million trees by 2030. For more information, visit: a.plant-for-the-planet.org/yucatan/

proj_Nu3mkdz0pFf9Tnqc2Vm1y5xh.description:
The Planet cooler restorers projects aims to restore the landscape in Njoro Sub County through planting of 3 million trees by the year 2030. The project will mainly plant fruite and  indigenous tree species. This will enhance the tree cover in the target area by 30%. The trees will be planted through an agro forestry approach in private farms within the location. To enable this, the planet coolers restorers’ project will produce tree seedlings at its nursery site at Gachuhi center. These seedlings will then be issued to farmers to plant on their farms. Proper preparation of the planting areas will have to be done before the seedlings are issued to ensure that issued seedlings are actually planted properly. Farmers will be assisted with the site preparation work. Also, the farmers will be sensitized and capacity built to improve their knowledge and skills on agro forestry and restoration in general. 
The project area was chosen because of the wanton degradation that has occurred over the years. This degradation has had negative effects on the community’s livelihoods making them very vulnerable, especially to the impacts of climate change. This has mainly manifested through soil degradation leading to sharp drops in agricultural production and which had multiplier negative effects on the area socioeconomic wellbeing. The degradation also had many negative ecological impacts including reduction in stream flows of rivers such as River Nderit, River Naishi, and River Njoro. These rivers were important sources of water to the community. The rivers also feed the Nakuru National park, which has an alkaline lake. They are thus the source of Fresh drinking water to the wildlife in the national park. The area is thus also the catchment area for Lake Nakuru which is a very important biodiversity hotspot that is particularly highly famous for the large populations of flamingos that it supports. 
The project thus aims to restore the local forest landscape through agro forestry for improvement of biodiversity, ecosystem services and building of community resilience to climate change. This will be achieved through agro forestry tree planting, sensitization and capacity building, and livelihoods improvement through restoration work. Besides, the project will improve support community based natural resources management strategies, improve food security, engage in advocacy for landscape restoration, improve environmental governance, create job and business opportunities through agroforestry, improve water quality and availability for human and wildlife use among other benefits.

proj_6d2N1mW91SVeAEIm74AxAkIT.description:
The Sundarbans are threatened by various challenges, namely, population pressure, spatial transformation, excessive resource extraction, salinization, sea-level rise, and climate change, thus, making it difficult for it to survive even till 2100 (WWF Report, 2017). The project aims to address some of these issues. The tiger forms a very important part of both the ecology and economy of the Sundarbans, providing great economic returns. D. Balasubramanian mentions in his writing, the various functions of a tiger reserve that contributes to ecology, the economy as well as culture and planting the trees contribute to the habitat conservation of the tiger thus contributing to the tiger and other wildlife conservation in the long run. (Balasubramanian, 2017).
Thus, the plantation of mangroves around villages at the Periphery of the Sundarbans National Park directly impacts rural livelihoods by creating jobs in nursery and planting activities, improve fisheries catch, provide flowers, fruit, fodder and fuel to rural communities and wildlife, generate oxygen, reduce carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, fight climate change, and benefit endemic wildlife including the endangered Tiger. Reforestation thus provides ample livelihood opportunities for the people in the buffer area, preventing them from venturing into the forest and minimising chances of conflict and empowerment of the dwellers as a result.

A study developed by American Forests and Texas Trees Foundation showed that optimizing tree canopy, along with other surface cooling measures in greater Dallas would reduce heat-related deaths by 22 percent. 

The city of Dallas has identified several high-impact neighborhoods with low Tree Equity Scores and severe urban heat islands. Funding is needed to help Dallas continue planting shade-providing trees in vulnerable communities.
proj_b0QCfioZWIMpoR0Xe0uI3Ncl.longTermPlan: Irrigation system will be installed to provide consistent watering for a minimum of two years and City of Dallas maintenance staff will steward long term in each of the parks that receive additional tree canopy cover.
proj_b0QCfioZWIMpoR0Xe0uI3Ncl.mainChallenge: Summer temperatures are predicted to average 10 degrees hotter by the end of the century in Dallas. Increasing tree canopy in particularly vulnerable communities could reduce heat related deaths by 22%, making tree planting in urban areas more urgent than ever.

metadata.motivation: Sites were selected based on fitting one of the following criteria: 1. Less than 20% tree canopy cover (40% recommended) 2. People in poverty over 65% 3. Minority population above 85%. These metrics can be found using American Forests' Tree Equity Score.

proj_htWDArPM6UNr45urYfaiHiyO.degradationCause: The original rainforest was destroyed for agricultural purposes using Tavy (slash and burn agriculture). Tavy is used principally to grow staple crops like cassava and rice, but unfortunately the burning is often followed by an invasion of non-native species, which compete with trees.
proj_htWDArPM6UNr45urYfaiHiyO.description:
GreenAgain Madagascar works alongside rural communities to conduct ecological experiments that are finding successful methods to restoring damaged rainforest reserves in eastern Madagascar. True ecological restoration is more than simply planting trees, rather it involves a long-term commitment to assisting the recovery of an ecosystem. 
Amarotandrazana is one village where GreenAgain Madagascar has trained and employed several members of the community to maintain a nursery of locally sourced native species and plant trees on privately owned land according to conditions of scientific experiments.  Degradation of the original forest on this land began many years ago and the community is gaining collective interest in its restoration. Skilled staff are learning the steps to independently operate the nursery and office for data analysis.
proj_htWDArPM6UNr45urYfaiHiyO.longTermPlan: To grow their team, expand the nursery, and construct an office to operate independently in their data collection and ecological analyses for reforestation specific to this microclimate. Our local team is a resource for interested landowners to seek help for reforestation on their damaged land.
proj_htWDArPM6UNr45urYfaiHiyO.mainChallenge: An invasive fern, Dicranopteris linearis, and other non-native trees are fast growing with leaves that take a long time to decompose, altering the soil composition so it's unfavorable for native species.  Dried leaves of these invasive trees encourage fires to spread rapidly across the land.

metadata.motivation: For generations, the area has been damaged by fires due to slash and burn agriculture. From that participation, they have the skills and knowledge to open a nursery and be a resource locally.

proj_fsj4WiG71hgjnSKe0PqBdthJ.degradationCause: Die Teefabriken verbrauchen enorme Mengen an Brennholz, das sie von Gemeindemitgliedern kaufen, um Tee zu kochen. Das Abbrennen von Holzkohle und die Holzernte sind weitere einkommensschaffende Tätigkeiten für die Bauern, die zu einer Verschlechterung der Umwelt führen. Hinzu kommt, dass die Initiative zum Pflanzen von Bäumen gering ist.
proj_fsj4WiG71hgjnSKe0PqBdthJ.description: Agroforestry efforts directly contribute towards achieving two fundamental goals: improve the livelihoods of vulnerable communities while restoring the environment. According to their size of land, smallholder farmers receive different beneficial tree species such as  indigenous, native and fruit trees that will provide firewood, fodder for livestock, increase income to rural farmers through sale of fruits, support nitrogen fixation in the soil, improve soil fertility and improve biodiversity of the area. At the same time, these trees regenerate the soil that leads to increased productivity and attracts rain. Nevertheless, we do not only deliver trees to farmers: we also work with them closely, providing training on how to take care of them, the importance of trees, and climate change. This way, sustainability of the efforts is supported, as communities raise their levels of awareness and contribute to protecting the environment. In addition, after a few months after planting,we carry out field visit to planting sites to  monitor the trees, assessing their survival rate and appearance and offer technical advice to farmers on maintenance of the trees planted.
proj_fsj4WiG71hgjnSKe0PqBdthJ.longTermPlan: Bei der Pflanzung von Bäumen arbeiten wir eng mit den Gemeinden zusammen, um das Bewusstsein zu schärfen. Wenn sie verstehen, wie wichtig der Schutz der Umwelt für ihr Leben und für künftige Generationen ist, können sie sich Gehör verschaffen, schädliche Aktivitäten stoppen und Forderungen stellen, wenn andere sie durchführen.
proj_fsj4WiG71hgjnSKe0PqBdthJ.mainChallenge: Der Mangel an finanziellen Mitteln ist das größte Hindernis. Auch das Wetter stellt eine Herausforderung dar, da es sich um eine halbtrockene Region handelt und die Aktivitäten die Umwelt ständig schädigen.

metadata.motivation: Being a semi-arid area, significantly affected by high rate of deforestation the soil suffered serious degradation and massive erosion and rains are scarce.On the other hand, there is Low tree cover in the area and extreme hot weather, loss of important tree species in the area that supports biodiversity and ecosystem function of the area.
metadata.longTermPlan: While planting trees, we work closely with communities to raise awareness. If they understand the importance of environmental conservation for their lives and for the future generations, they will be able to spread the voice, stop degrading activities and raise demands when others perform these.
metadata.mainChallenge: Lack of funding is the main constrain. Also, the weather is a challenge for being a semi-arid region and continuous harmful activities for the environment.
metadata.degradationCause: In the past years Tea factories consumed enormous amounts of firewood to cure tea, buying it from community members and this contributed to high rate of deforestation in the area. Charcoal burning and timber harvesting were  other source of  income generation activities for the farmer therefore this  lead to environmental degradation. Prolonged drought and famine, exponential growth in population also resulted to degradation as more land were demarcated and cleared for agricultural purposes.

proj_fsj4WiG71hgjnSKe0PqBdthJ.motivation: Da es sich um ein halbtrockenes Gebiet handelt, das in hohem Maße von der Abholzung betroffen ist, sind die Böden stark geschädigt und leiden unter massiver Erosion, und es regnet nur selten, außerdem ist der Baumbestand in dem Gebiet gering und es herrscht extrem heißes Wetter, und es gehen wichtige Baumarten verloren, die die biologische Vielfalt und die Ökosystemfunktion des Gebiets unterstützen.
proj_fsj4WiG71hgjnSKe0PqBdthJ.name: Agroforestry for rural livelihoods improvements in Kenya

proj_jr3mFYM4PeaIaLBfGlJPuCKd.description:
Through this project, Salesforce is helping us to restore longleaf pine forests in Alabama to improve wildlife habitat, support watershed health, and improve recreational experience for visitors. Salesforce will help us plant 11,000 trees, which is just a portion of the 1000-acre project.

Longleaf pine ecosystems are one of the most biologically diverse in the U.S., home to several ESA listed species, including the red-cockaded woodpecker and gopher tortoise, and more than 900 different species of plants. Longleaf and shortleaf pines once dominated the southern U.S. landscape, but today exist on less than five and fifty percent of their historic ranges, respectively. Shortleaf pine is an essential habitat element in mixed-forest types and is important for wildlife habitat, local cultural ties, and water quality. Due to the species’ ecological significance, longleaf and shortleaf pine reforestation receives broad support, as these projects fit into large multi-state, multi-agency efforts to restore the pine ecosystems across the Southeast.

This project will also provide long-lasting carbon benefits, as longleaf pine is the longest living southern pine species, and both longleaf and shortleaf pine are highly resistant to disturbances associated with climate change including fire, drought, insects and disease. 

This project is part of the 50 Million for Our Forests Campaign, which was publicly launched on Earth Day 2018, with a goal to raise funds to plant 50 million native trees on our National Forests by Earth Day 2023. Every dollar donated is matched with two dollars from the U.S. Government. Through our tree-planting program, we plant native trees in priority areas in need of reforestation as a result of natural disturbance, i.e. wildfire (80%), landslides, hurricanes, wind storms. Over one million acres of our National Forests are in need of reforestation. Our goal is to have all projects completed by 2025.
We work with the U.S. Forest Service to plant trees. Trees we plant are sourced from six Forest Service tree nurseries where native tree seedlings are grown for planting on National Forests. These trees are grown from locally sourced seeds, and the nurseries serve as research centers for the agency to develop disease-resistant strains of trees.  
Seedlings are planted only when conditions are optimal, using the best available science, and monitored post planting, ensuring the highest possible survival rate.

proj_oJ5njoUbjrxOjZjyMnl8ysbc.description: Established in 2007 and based on over 20 years of research, the Inga Foundation led by Honduran foresters/agronomists pioneers the revolutionary agricultural system of Inga Alley Cropping to address environmental devastation and food insecurity. Since 2012, the Inga Foundation’s simple agroforestry system of Inga Alley Cropping has planted over 5 million trees and dramatically transformed the lives of over 450 subsistence farming families with more than 2700 participating.The ability of the resilient Inga tree to anchor, enrich, and regenerate depleted soil provides food security with 100% success for families with 2 year-old alleys. These fast-growing, native Inga species which fix nitrogen in the soil  provide organic cash crops as well as significantly reduce global carbon emissions, protect wildlife and marine habitats, preserve water sources and yield a year’s worth of firewood. The basic grains/cash crops are grown without herbicides, pesticides, chemical fertilizers, or heavy equipment.  Inga seedlings are planted in rows on steep, degraded slopes and require no technology or heavy equipment. A crop is planted when the seedlings are planted and it is harvested (a small side-dressing of mineral rock phosphate is needed and the only other inexpensive supplements used are K-mag and lime). After 18-24 months, the trees are pruned, with the branches supplying a year's worth of firewood and the leaves a soil-protecting mulch. Crops are again planted between the rows and shaded as the resilient trees regrow. After the crops have matured, they are harvested and the cycle repeats. The Inga alleys survive 7 months of drought, providing a crop without a drop, and stop erosion and mudslides--while positively addressing 12 of the 17 United Nations SDGs with NO NEGATIVE IMPACT whatsoever on the remaining 6.This low-input, debt-free, and bottom-up program is available now and gives families the means to achieve “land for life,” farming their plots with truly sustainable agricultural practices. Inga Alley Cropping is not just an alternative to the cutting/ burning of tropical rainforests, it is an integrated solution to stopping it altogether.

proj_XjyrwvTHqZJ9vC9cquEPdXwQ.description:
Idesam’s Carbon Neutral Program (PCN) was created in 2010 to connect large urban centres to forests, enabling people, companies and initiatives to take responsibility for the impacts they generate on the planet, offsetting their greenhouse gases (GHG) emissions. The compensation is made through the recovery of degraded areas in the Uatumã’s Reserve located in the state of Amazonas.
Our planting model – called the Agroforestry System (SAF) – is a form of land use that combines tree species (fruit and/or timber) and agricultural crops: these two elements interact ecologically and complement each other, optimizing the farmer’s produce, the diversification of production and the more efficient use of natural resources.

This form of work generates not only environmental but also socioeconomic benefits, since it guarantees food security and income generation for the families involved in the program, promoting socioeconomical development while reducing the pressure on deforestation for land conversion.  

Therefore, in addition to being an important tool for the recovery of unproductive areas, our planting model plays an important role on climate regulation as planted trees capture carbon from the atmosphere mitigating the effects of climate change, and regulate much of the rainfall production. Moreover, Agroforestry Systems present themselves as an important strategy for local social development, as they value traditional knowledge using native species of nutritional, economic and social value to the local community, such as the cará, cassava and açaí for food, rosewood and andiroba for the production of oils used in cosmetics, as well as species of wood use such as Ipê and Cumaru. 

Combining the planting of trees with sustainable production, our Project achieves: restoration, climate regulation, deforestation mitigation and socioeconomic development.

The work methodology of the PCN has already been recognized by several initiatives and is now part of the Bank of Social Technologies of Banco do Brasil Foundation (FBB).

Idesam is not tax deductible

proj_6PKQjUdikQOPG0MwjlLwCFiF.description:
This project is part of the Reforestation Campaign which has been promoted by the Jovel Valley Watershed Committee (CCVJ) and has been going on for 15 years. The campaign is launched every year at the beginning of the rainy season in May/June and concludes in September.  Our proposal is to design and revegetate the territory considering the various ecological niches to imitate the resilience of the ecosystems. We aim to restore ecological capacities such as biodiversity, water filtration and storage, carbon capture, and living soil.

We understand that reforestation involves more than just planting trees. That is why we not only give plants to those who request and have space for reforestation, but we also consider socio-cultural, ecological, economic, and spiritual aspects to make decisions together with the people and make proposals of local interest for the reforestation of the territory.

In the same way, the aim is to raise awareness and reconnect the urban population with their livelihoods and their territory. For this purpose, social reforestations are carried out, in which the general population is invited to reforest the rural environment.

proj_6ZUCxXI8jNQ6xOD6rbm4IHlD.description:
Tsarasoatra is the main office for the region and the site of GreenAgain’s EcoSchool. The EcoSchool is a unique program where crew members work and study. In the countryside of Madagascar, there are obstacles to education, and like most young people, many of the crew did not complete formal studies to earn a diploma. EcoSchool is providing an alternative for these young minds. They are learning how to plant trees, maintain the nursery, work with a team, collect data in the field, operate a GPS and measuring devices, fill data in an excel spreadsheet on a computer, and skills of construction.  
The projects they are conducting contribute to data intensive ecological experiments written by scientists who are researching reforestation techniques specific to Madagascar forests.
	The EcoSchool offers dormitories to host crew members who live far away and can also host visitors to conduct trainings at the field station. Opening our doors to exchange ideas and share knowledge is important to better our practice
proj_6ZUCxXI8jNQ6xOD6rbm4IHlD.longTermPlan: Our staff of young individuals from the villages are constantly learning and growing in their knowledge and skill set. When they have advanced in their progress, they are encouraged to build nurseries close to their home and families, thus expanding access to our reforestation methods.

proj_Cw1ZAjHXvjlC5Dfel2pWf4GX.description:
AYUDH Europe is an international youth movement, dedicated to empowering young people to contribute to a peaceful and sustainable world and become compassionate leaders with a sense of tolerance, solidarity and global responsibility.

Not tax deduction information available yet!

As such, AYUDH has been dedicated to plant over 3000 trees in the last 14 years.

In July 2018, AYUDH launched "Trees for Peace", a new tree planting campaign, celebrating the full dedication of AYUDH Europe to renew its efforts towards tree planting.

Trees for Peace is more than a tree-planting campaign, it combines concrete climate action with education for sustainable lifestyles, while fostering a community of young Europeans, dedicated to making a difference. From Lisbon to Munich to Copenhagen – across ten European countries, our youth volunteers meet to plant together.

Each Trees for Peace activity is carried out by young people (aged 15 – 30) and is combined with workshops on sustainable living. We believe that planting trees is a powerful way to bring people together, experience community, and strengthen a sense of global responsibility and leadership in young people. It can inspire youth from all backgrounds to be active citizens, bringing them together to build a more sustainable and peaceful future.

Our objectives are:

1) Through tree planting initiatives, give to youth all over Europe an important toolkit of skills and values such as planning, management, sense of active citizenship, social and ecological awareness.

2) Turning tree planting in a socially useful activity, by fostering community building and collaborating local administrations by realising cost-free green areas and community fruit orchard, supporting in particular those administrations (e.g. municipalities) which are unable to create afforestation project due lack of budget availability.

3) Create a concrete impact on environmental protection, by:
- a) Planting trees which absorb our CO2 emissions, reducing our carbon footprint;
- b) Planting native species to the European landscape, preserving the original European biodiversity and planting endangered or rare indigenous species which are threatened by human activity, pests or by alien invasive species;
- c) Creating projects of soil restoration, using tree planting as a tool to fight back soil erosion caused by natural adversities (floods, landslides, drought) and degradation by human activities.

Our goal is to plant over 1000 trees by 2021.

When the goal will be reached, the campaign will continue and a new goal will be set.

properties.description:
AYUDH Europe is an international youth movement, dedicated to empowering young people to contribute to a peaceful and sustainable world and become compassionate leaders with a sense of tolerance, solidarity and global responsibility.

Not tax deduction information available yet!

As such, AYUDH has been dedicated to plant over 3000 trees in the last 14 years.

In July 2018, AYUDH launched "Trees for Peace", a new tree planting campaign, celebrating the full dedication of AYUDH Europe to renew its efforts towards tree planting.

Trees for Peace is more than a tree-planting campaign, it combines concrete climate action with education for sustainable lifestyles, while fostering a community of young Europeans, dedicated to making a difference. From Lisbon to Munich to Copenhagen – across ten European countries, our youth volunteers meet to plant together.

Each Trees for Peace activity is carried out by young people (aged 15 – 30) and is combined with workshops on sustainable living. We believe that planting trees is a powerful way to bring people together, experience community, and strengthen a sense of global responsibility and leadership in young people. It can inspire youth from all backgrounds to be active citizens, bringing them together to build a more sustainable and peaceful future.

Our objectives are:

1) Through tree planting initiatives, give to youth all over Europe an important toolkit of skills and values such as planning, management, sense of active citizenship, social and ecological awareness.

2) Turning tree planting in a socially useful activity, by fostering community building and collaborating local administrations by realising cost-free green areas and community fruit orchard, supporting in particular those administrations (e.g. municipalities) which are unable to create afforestation project due lack of budget availability.

3) Create a concrete impact on environmental protection, by:
- a) Planting trees which absorb our CO2 emissions, reducing our carbon footprint;
- b) Planting native species to the European landscape, preserving the original European biodiversity and planting endangered or rare indigenous species which are threatened by human activity, pests or by alien invasive species;
- c) Creating projects of soil restoration, using tree planting as a tool to fight back soil erosion caused by natural adversities (floods, landslides, drought) and degradation by human activities.

Our goal is to plant over 1000 trees by 2021.

When the goal will be reached, the campaign will continue and a new goal will be set.

proj_iDdqc7AvhTPJqLSjBlOAbAuk.description:
One Tree Planted is a U.S. charity focused on global reforestation. We plant trees all around the world. Our model is simple so that anyone can get involved: 1 USD plants 1 tree.

We are working in the southwest of Western Australia, which is recognized as a top biodiversity hotspot but has been historically over-cleared.

The goals of this project are to restore habitat, conserve biodiversity, and buffer/extend important wildlife corridors in a biodiversity hotspot. Through the re-establishment of species-rich native vegetation, primarily alongside riparian areas, we will capture atmospheric carbon while supporting conservation. Working with the local community, we seek to undertake these works to preserve and restore the region's natural heritage and natural capital.

proj_M7PPbBvQKNxOI4wJcf5BZmjY.description:
Habiba Community is an innovative start-up established in 2007 in the town of Nuweiba, in the Sinai peninsula of Egypt. Habiba Community follows the model of inclusive business for a circular economy and has a tremendous impact on the social and environmental fields locally. 
For over a decade, we have encouraged the local population to be more responsible toward the environment, 

Thorugh this project, we will support the expansion of agroforestry locally by supporting local bedouin farmers in establishing new agroforestry systems and by expanding our own agroforestry operation at Habiba Regenerative Farm. 

By combining different indigenous trees, shrubs, bushes and crops, the project aims at improving the soil's nutrient cycle, building a microclimate that will attract humidity, as well as improving food security and livelihoods.

proj_ylr1kxPKCvz9O986Vd7iflu3.description:
Help us restore native forests across the Chignecto Isthmus. This internationally recognized ecosystem connects Nova Scotia to the rest of Canada, and is vital for communities, wildlife, and our shared climate – but only if we can protect it first. The vulnerability and importance of the isthmus is why we have been restoring forests in the region since 2014.

Known by the region’s original and present Indigenous communities as the Mi'kma'ki district of Siknikt, this area has served as a rich and important meeting place for the Mi’kmaq Nation for thousands of years – and has provided a vital land bridge for local communities, the region’s unique wildlife, and natural biodiversity. Unfortunately, the region faces many threats – from forest habitat fragmentation to risk of flooding exacerbated by climate change. 

With your support, Community Forests is restoring and protecting these lands by planting more than 350,000 trees across multiple forest restoration sites on the special Chignecto Isthmus. We plant a diversity of 11 native tree species like red oak, white pine, and sugar maples on properties owned by Community Forests. Our climate-adaptive forest management prioritizes ecosystem restoration and climate change resilience – and with your help we can restore diverse and healthy forests that will provide important wildlife habitat, climate benefits, and ecosystem protection for generations to come.
proj_ylr1kxPKCvz9O986Vd7iflu3.longTermPlan: The site is now owned and held in trust by Community Forests International for the purposes of permanent forest restoration, to ensure that the trees planted will never be clearcut and the restored forest will thrive for future generations.

properties.name: Brooklyn Restoration Forest
properties.description: Between 2019 to 2021, Community Forests International would like to plant 500.000 climate change adaptive native trees in New Brunswick, Canada and we need your help! This project is part of a larger effort to restore the region's special Acadian forest, which is one of the most diverse forests in Canada. It contains 32 species of trees, 226 bird species, and is home to a diversity of mammals including moose, black bear, fisher and bobcat. Unfortunately, it is considered one of the most threatened forest types in Canada. Community Forests International aims to strengthen the Acadian Forest and is targeting one of the province's most flood-prone region. Community Forests International is tax deductible in Canada!

The Mangrove Restoration Project will involve the reforestation of more than eight hectares of degraded mangrove forest on Pemba Island, Tanzania–one of the world’s most fragile regions. Mangrove forests are crucial resources for main¬taining the livelihoods of fishing communities. These vital ecosystems surround the island with a bio-shield of trees with strong interlocking roots that hold soil in place against waves and flooding and provide critical wildlife habitat.

Community Forests International is tax deductible in Canada!

proj_e4FLTe8bSU10upZtadu0PRrF.description:
After 3 years’ pilot Hara planting in coasts of Bushehr province, we are encouraging efforts of rural communities in Southern Iran for planting mangroves and artificial forestation of Hara. We started cultivation of Hara and other tropical trees in Bushehr province since 2018. Until now we planted about 60000 Hara tree in three sites. Continuing this work and increasing area of artificial forests of Hara tree and other tropical trees in Southern Iran need two main jobs. 1- production of seedlings, site detection and cultivation, 2- cultural programs for introducing the importance of this job. 
For the first purpose we established a greenhouse which is able to produce more than 5000 seedlings per month. The cost of each tree from seed collection to transferring to the selected site is 4 US dollars including: seed collection from mangrove forest: 0.5 $; Seedling preparation: 2.5 $; seedling cultivation in site: 1 $. The success rate of tree growth after 1 year in all trees sites was 98% in average. Benefits of this project: 1- Hara planting does not need watering or tree protection after forestation. 2- There is no limitation of lands regarding to non-productive sites for other industries or local communities. 3- Increase of chance of fish production for local communities. 4- Very low chance of firing and very high tolerance of heat and bad environmental condition by Hara forest.
For the second purpose we established a documentary production team which is producing short documentaries about trees. Each three months a five minutes’ film is the goal of this team. The first film named “Hara Planting for the Beauty Planet” finalized and is available from this link: https://filmfreeway.com/projects/2313314 Benefits of the second goal: 1- introducing the importance of tree planting for local communities. 2- encouraging people to join this movement. 3- documentation of planting methods for other tree planting groups .

proj_SRbh04MAV1Nb1h5Q9T24SIRh.description: Since 2005, this project has been protecting native mangrove and forest areas in East Jawa, Indonesia by shifting land from open access into the Clungup Mangrove Conservation (CMC) area, planting and conserving mangroves in partnership with local communities, educating young people, and creating livelihood alternatives to extractive industry.The CMC area is now 117 hectares and grew to include coral reefs in 2013 and native inland forests in 2018. This is the result of years of advocacy with the government resulting in the release of a Presidential Decree giving management rights to local communities.Key components of the project include: Community-led, ongoing identification and mapping of ecological destruction or disturbancesCommunity-led 24x7 patrol of the conservation areasTraining and planting using the Miyawaki-method Training and implementation of ecotourism in partnership with CMC communitiesDevelopment of community-owned mangrove and native plant nurseriesContinual planting of mangroves to reach the ideal forest cover (as listed in the Coastal Protected Forest standard)The project has a community-centered approach to conservation - collaboratively designing ecosystem stewardship alongside livelihood development. In order to ensure long-term protection of the CMC area, it is critical that local communities have opportunities to shift their livelihoods away from extractive practices like wood and coral theft and fishing by harmful means. The project trains and mobilizes community members to build a locally-driven ecotourism and conservation industry. Currently more than 100 locals are involved in ecotourism, 80% of whom were previously forest encroachers. Local ecotourism livelihoods include: providing homestays, owning and operating food stalls, guiding tours, leading cultural events, and managing and attending services like parking areas.Additional stakeholders who are engaged in this conservation and ecotourism project include the Ministry of Marine Affairs and Fisheries and the Department of Marine Affairs and Fisheries (DMAF).

metadata.benefits: Since the 50 hectares of Kakamega Forest has been designated to WWANC for protection and restoration in 2019, our focus has been on restoring the portions of forest that have been most degraded from logging and cutting for firewood. Since late 2020, 6,000 native trees have been planted, half of which are considered vulnerable or endangered. Additionally, 40 women have launched microenterprises to support Kakamega Forest protection, including clean cookstove businesses to enable communities to consume less firewood and native tree nurseries to supply reforestation efforts, homestead tree stands for firewood, and agroforestry.  Over the next year, women’s Community Forest Associations will partner with Kenya Wildlife Service and Kenya Forest Service to create community-led conservation indicators that the CFAs will monitor and report on.
metadata.motivation: The protected mangrove and coastal area is a critical nursery ground for underwater species. The area has been known to produce high quality fishery products with Tuna being its flagship commodity. After 16 years of community-led protection practices, the area has brought back ideal ecological outcomes, including the availability of suitable places for fish and shrimp to breed, a longer fishing season, and the return of mangrove land cover.The protected forest area is the source of 13 water springs that feed the village of Tambakrejo and the Sendang Biru Lake. The forest still holds a few native tree species that play a significant role in maintaining the ecosystem balance, making the area crucial for research and education.
metadata.longTermPlan: Conservation and rehabilitation of coastal and marine ecosystem in 5 years:10 ha of additional mangrove areas10 ha of additional coral reefs areas3 hectares of sea grass areasLaunch of blue carbon offsetting programIntegration of tech-based patrol systemImplementation of coastal community development programs, including:Environmental School for local childrenWaste Education that includes beach and underwater clean upSustainable mangrove management trainingCoastal conservation research program
metadata.mainChallenge: Climate change: Unpredicted tides affect newly planted mangrovesLong dry season negatively impact young mangrovesCovid-19 Pandemic: Significant reduction of income from ecotourism has resulted in a much lower conservation budgetLockdown restricting social interaction has negatively impacted the project’s ability to conduct education and planting activitiesFunding: Recent shifts in donor priorities towards COVID-19, including funds from the government, has meant less budget for conservation

WHY MAMA? 

This is a call of the smallest generation (who can't plant themselves yet) to all adults to answer for their actions! 

It depends only on us what the house in which our children live will be like. 

This is the philosophy of #Mamaplantatree:
"Let’s help our children to remove the consequences of our actions behind us."

We plant new forests beetween fields, or FILTER WOODLINEs bettween field and twons to prevent dust storms; between lakes and towns to prevent wind storms; along roads to absorb CO2 and filter gas emissions to protect alongliving areas.

This year we can reforest more 340 ha of land, more than 3 million of new trees can be planted. 

Species planted vary from region to region and for every planting site is being confirmed with local ecologist, who authorize the plants type. 

These are our first locations, where woodline is needed as a protection from dust storms (more will follow).
