proj_skIGjRcczH5EMWhYPDb2bMYX.description:
Endangered Trees is a community enterprise and agricultural cooperative in Surin / Thailand with the mission of planting endangered tree species, reforest expired rice patties and rubber tree plantations and organize tree planting events for the local population. Our aim is to mitigate global warming, bring benefits to the local population and save endangered trees from extinction.

Many rubber tree plantations that were established in the boom years (2005 to 2011) are not profitable and farmers want to cut the trees and sell the log. Perfect opportunity for our foundation to plant new trees, and turning the monoculture into a forest and diverse ecosystem. The established rubber trees provide perfect shade for the young saplings to grow. Once the new trees are three to five years old, some of the rubber trees may be cut down.

Rice paddies become expired or abandoned, when the young generation does not want to continue with the rice farming business their parents have pursued, and parents are too old to take care of the plantations. This is an opportunity for Endangered Trees to plant micro-forests, with endangered tree species, providing the young generation with an income through sustainable forestry. 

There are also many rice paddies in the area that are too wet, meaning water being stuck in the paddy for months after the rainy season, and tractors are unable to cut the rice. Those paddies are often abandoned up by farmers, as cutting by hand is arduous and unprofitable job. With this more opportunities arise for Endangered Trees to plant micro-forests on those abandoned rice paddies.

In addition, Endangered Trees foundation organizes tree planting events for the local population and plant trees on public land, around municipality lakes, with help of the mayor and the local schools. 

Endangered Trees is also involved in the primary school in Baan Cha Niang Village, organizing many projects from English teaching to tree planting projects with kids aged 5 to 12.

Each student aged 11 and 12 will godfather a tree and take care of it as part of our philanthropic mission.

In addition, for each tree that is planted by our organization, one Baht is paid into the student's piggy bank.

proj_mMa0LlRqcyizJUSnLl0JCtwf.description:
Baga Forest Reserve is among the 10 nature forest reserves located within Lushoto District Council and it is situated at Mgwashi Division within Baga ward at Baga village. This forest was burnt some years ago, and that fire was caused by human economic activities such as charcoal making and searching for fuel wood. The aim of this project is to restore the nature of Baga Nature Forest Reserve by planting a total of 980,000 indigenous trees including some indigenous tree species such as Markhamia Lutea and Albizia Albida as well as planting 2,000,000 fruit trees to community owned farms as agroforestry scheme. The Western Usambara forest reserves of Eastern Arc Mountains are under severe threat of being cleared through human activities particularly agriculture, fuel woods collection, hunting and construction activities due to poor management. The forests are managed by central government of Tanzania and serves as water catchment, soil protection, and source of timber, non-timber for millions of rural people, electricity through HEP plants and biodiversity hotspot home for hundreds of species.
This project is going to provide benefits to all citizens Living within Lushoto District, Tanzania, and the World as a whole.
Changamoto Youth Development Organization expects to plant 2,980,000 both indigenous trees at Baga Forest Reserve and 2,000,000 fruit and native trees to community owned land by December 2027 and this project aims at increasing the environment conservation know-how as it will involve a package that involves Forest Management Plan which will be reviewed to the respective Forest Management Team of Baga Village. This project will also flourish lives of citizens at Mgwashi Division by planting tees t their farms which are friendly with the crop cultivation and by doing so, the division will be turned form grey color to greenish color. Up to this moment, Changamoto Youth Development Organization has already visited Baga Nature Forest Reserve and Mgwashi Division as well and our goal is to plant 980,000 indigenous trees at this Baga Forest Reserve.

proj_va1IJrmXLMc5YDuDUiJJZ1FU.description:
One Tree Planted in Partnership with The Jane Goodall Institute implemented a project to support long-term and large-scale restoration of selected Albertine Rift forests through a public-private partnership for restoration and management. This contributes to carbon sequestration, supports ecosystem functions such as water catchment, engages local communities in sustainable practices, and maintains habitat for highly endangered species relying on the Albertine Rift for survival - including the endangered chimpanzee. 

This project is restoring a forest corridor between two remaining protected forests of Budongo and Bugoma by planting a mix of native trees to establish a conservation forest. Once established, this area will receive formal government protection. 

The project is working with local communities to ensure long-term success. The restored community forests will be buffered by a combination of community agroforestry, and plantation of selected fast-growing timber species to ensure sustainability and provide alternatives for fuel woods. Ultimately, the project is providing significant ecological, socio-economic, and cultural benefits. An exit strategy is implemented at an early stage, allowing local stakeholders to take full responsibility for the project in the long term.
proj_va1IJrmXLMc5YDuDUiJJZ1FU.longTermPlan: This project supports a long-term and large-scale restoration of the Albertine Rift forests, working in full partnership with the government and the community for a successful exit strategy built from the project outset through a consultative and participatory approach involving key stakeholders.

proj_5nEBZS0R4Zv7XLSVgC2jdlpK.description:
The ‘Green Schools’ mission is born out of a need to scale the positive impacts of the Miyawaki Method through effective, equitable and efficient use of resources. The expertise and strength of each partner is utilized symbiotically to build maximum impact through collaboration, partnerships, knowledge and credit sharing, and putting proportionate skin in the game.

The mission will create dense native Miyawaki forests across 65 sites in schools and institutions in Aurangabad (rural) to build green-lungs for the schools and villages – Harit Maharashtra Abhiyan. The uniqueness of this program comes from the democratization of knowledge about the Miyawaki Method. We’ll train a team to oversee the implementation of these forests, as well as teams for each school to implement the Miyawaki Method effectively.

This program also focuses on spreading awareness about the need for native species conservation to schools. The program is designed in a way to instill ownership of the forests and the impact that the school will make through nurturing it to maturity.
proj_5nEBZS0R4Zv7XLSVgC2jdlpK.longTermPlan: We use the Miyawaki Methodology specifically to build long-term protection into our forests. The large mix of 100% native species is nature’s inherent way of planning for resilience. The support that we grow and nurture within the community is also a critical part of the long-term strategy.

proj_9YZxwGeIkwALyW2k3MQ15Fh1.description:
Centro Ecológico Juvenil - Ökologisches Jugendzentrum Cajamarca/ Bolivien
Verein Centro Ecológico Juvenil (CEJ)

Gründung: 1990 in den Anden Boliviens von Student*innen und Dozent*innen der Pädagogischen Hochschule Sucre. 

Fläche:  Unser ökologisches Jugendzentrum besitzt 17 ha. Land. 
Katasteramt Eintrag: Centro Ecológico Juvenil (CEJ), verantwortlich: Ing. Alberto Tapia. Zusätzliche wurden vom CEJ 105 ha Bergabhänge hinzu gekauft und den jeweils erstgeborenen Töchtern der Bauernfamilien überschrieben, mit der Auflage zwanzig Jahre ihre kahlen Gebiete aufzuforsten. Somit entstand der erste zusammenhängende Wald rund um das Jugendzentrum (122 Hektar Fläche). 

Aufforstung:  Die umliegenden Bauern wurden nach und nach, von unserem Erfolg angeregt,ebenfalls tätig und bepflanzten ihre kahlen Berge. Inzwischen sind 500 Hektar bewaldet. In einem zusammenhängenden Wald wachsen nun 30m hohe Bäume. Darunter leben und wachsen im Biotop eine neue eigene Tier- und Pflanzwelt. Im Abstand von jeweils fünf bis zehn Jahren wird ein Teil des Baum Bestandes„geerntet“. Die Pflanzdichte beträgt 1-3m. 

Pflanzsaison:  ist während der Regenzeit von Dezember bis März. Etwa 80% unserer Setzlingeschaffen es die Trockenmonate zu überleben. Pflanzaktionen werden von Schüler- und Studentengruppen durchgeführt und vermehrt von den Bewohnern der Region.

Holzverwertung: die Bewohner nutzen das Holz für ihre Häuser und Möbel und erzielen Gewinne mit Brennholz- und Bretterverkauf. So haben sich die Lebensbedingungen der Familien in der Region wesentlich verbessert. 

Agraranbau:  die Felder (Kartoffel-, Mais-, Gemüseanbau) profitieren von dem Humus am Rande und auf kleinen Flächen im Wald. 

Kurse:  aus dem ganzen Land und vor allem auch aus den übervölkerten Städten lernen Besucher*innen im Zentrum praktische Umweltarbeit. Wir bieten im Zentrum Kurse zu ökologischen Themen an, wie z.B.: Imkerei, Terra Pretta, Gemüseanbau, Baumpflanzungen, Walddurchforstung, Kleintierhaltung, Fischzucht, Solarenergie, Holzverwertung, u.v.m. 

Erholung/ Quellen:  wir bieten ein wunderschönes und gesundes Erholungsgebiet für Tagesausflügler, Gruppen und Feriengäste an. Sieben unterschiedlich, mit eigenen  Materialien gebaute Häuser, beherbergen die Besucher. Ein 30 km langer Kanal nach Sucre führt Jahr für Jahr mehr sauberes Trinkwasser aus den Quellen unseres Waldes in die Stadt. 

MitarbeiterInnen: unsere vier ständige Mitarbeiter*innen und zahlreichen Ehrenamtlichen sind verantwortlich bei der Wald-und Feldwirtschaft, der Tierhaltung und sind z.T. ebenfalls Dozenten für angebotene Kurse. 

Spendenbedarf: jährlich 30.000 € für Gehälter und Pensionsansprüche, Versicherungen, Baumschulen, Saatgut, Tiernahrung, Wegebau und Transportgeräte.

Ein Baum kann bei uns mit einer Spende von 6 € finanziert werden. Einen Hektar karger Boden kann für 500 € mit 1000 Bäumen bepflanzt werden und dabei unser Waldprojekt weiterführen. 

Je mehr Spenden wir erhalten desto mehr kahle Berghänge werden mit Baumsetzlingen bepflanzt. CEJ hat seit drei Jahrzehnten wertvolle Erfahrungen gesammelt. Kommt uns besuchen und staunt über die Kraft des Waldes in den Anden, (3200m ü. d. Meeresspiegel) 

Wir sehen unseren Schwerpunkt in der Förderung von Jugendlichen damit sie eine gute berufliche Perspektive erlangen und dabei ökologische Zusammenhänge verstehen um Bolivien und unserer Erde in eine lebenswerte Zukunft für alle zu bieten.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------


Association Centro Ecológico Juvenil (CEJ) 

Founded: 1990 in the Andes of Bolivia by students and lecturers from the Sucre University of Education. 

Area: Our ecological youth center owns 17 hectares of land. Land registry entry: Centro Ecológico Juvenil (CEJ), responsible: Ing.Alberto Tapia. In addition, the CEJ bought 105 hectares of mountain slopes and assigned the first-born daughters of the farming families to reforest their bare areas for twenty years. This created the first contiguous forest around the youth center (122 hectares). 

Afforestation: The surrounding farmers, stimulated by our success, gradually became active and planted their bare mountains. There are now 500 hectares of forest. Trees 30m high now grow in a contiguous forest. A new animal and plant world of its own live and grow underneath in the biotope. Part of the tree population is "harvested" every five to ten years. The planting density is 1-3m. 

Planting season: is during the rainy season from December to March. About 80% of our seedlings manage to survive the dry months. Planting campaigns are carried out by school and student groups and increasingly by the residents of the region. 

Wood utilization: the residents use the wood for their houses and furniture and make a profit by selling firewood and boards. The living conditions of families in the region have improved significantly. 

Agricultural cultivation: the fields (potato, corn, vegetable cultivation) benefit from the humus on the edge and on small areas in the forest. 

Courses: visitors to the center learn practical environmental work from all over the country and especially from the overpopulated cities. In the center we offer courses on ecological topics, such as: beekeeping, terra pretta, growing vegetables, planting trees, forest thinning, keeping small animals, fish farming, solar energy, wood processing, and much more. 

Recreation / sources: we offer a wonderful and healthy recreation area for day-trippers, groups and holiday guests. Seven different houses built with their own materials accommodate the visitors. A 30 km long canal to Sucre brings more clean drinking water from the sources of our forest into the city year after year. 

Employees: our four permanent employees and numerous volunteers are responsible for forest and field management, animal husbandry and are in some cases also lecturers for courses offered. 

Donation requirement: € 30,000 annually for salaries and pension claims, insurance, tree nurseries, seeds, pet food, road construction and transport equipment. We can finance a tree with a donation of € 6. One hectare of barren soil can be planted with 1000 trees for € 500 and continue our forest project. The more donations we receive, the more bare mountain slopes are planted with tree saplings. CEJ has gained valuable experience over three decades. Come visit us and be amazed at the power of the forest in the Andes, (3200m above sea level)

We see our focus in the promotion of young people so that they gain good professional prospects and understand ecological relationships in order to offer Bolivia and our earth a livable future for everyone.

properties.description: The CEJ Youth Center in the village of Cajamarca near Sucre/Bolivia From 1990 until today hundreds of thousands of trees have been planted in this center in the Bolivian Andes. Also the neighboring farmers of the high valley of Cajamarca (3200 m asl) planted, according to our example, more than 400,000 trees. As a result, they have gained fertile land for growing trees. Thirty years ago there was little grass in the dry rocky soil, with which the goats and sheep nourished themselves. Now a broad forest covers the slopes. It grows: pines, eucalyptus, cedros, alamos, oaks and kewiñas. The floor is now a wet carpet. It grows edible mushrooms, moss and herbs. The bare rocky earth has become one transformed little paradise. Even springs are now bubbling out of rocks. Numerous insects and birds settle down. There are eight beehives which deliver delicious honey twice a year. The climate has also become noticeably milder. There is now more rain, which also the drinking water channels for the Nearby town Sucre fills more fertile. We have: workshops and accommodation with kitchens and bathrooms for z.b. Environmental groups, Bolivian and international volunteers, school classes, families, clubs and and also for individual hikers. You will find clean air and numerous opportunities for hiking and climbing, also beautiful forest playgrounds and educational areas. For those who want to help with forest thinning, vegetable farming and small animal breeding and educational guidance of visitors are permanent tasks. In the last 30 years, the center received no public funds. The works were through donations and above all the great commitment of Bolivian and international volunteers. We are open to friendly people of all ages from all over the world! Centro Ecológico Juvenil (CEJ) is tax deductible in Germany!

Soil fertility was impacted when nutrient-rich humus burned or was washed away by rainwater.
proj_rQyuHuoqrSJ3MSX0qXkvJjFs.description:
We will rehabilitate ex-forest-fire areas in Bawan village in Borneo. We want to support people in this village, of who about 80% work in gold mining, 15% in forest logging. We want to establish nature-based restoration as alternatives for earning money. 
Our organization is unique because we are 100% led by locals. We have worked in international organizations before. We believe we will have the highest project success because we're working from within the beneficiary communities and are socially well connected. 
We will plant local agricultural crops, forest fruits, and trees, to create biodiversity-rich systems that benefit local people, animals, and the natural ecosystem. We will focus on known vegetables for local markets, native nuts, cooking spices, and others.  
This activity will improve the income of farmers in a sustainable manner. We will reduce the area of degraded land, store Carbon, produce more Oxygen and water, and improve soil quality. In this project, we collaborate with indigenous communities, students in environmental sciences, and technical personnel from the Pandu Alam Lestari foundation.

proj_cCIrmBRdoGcUrxbbMEx2hdrU.description:
The Cool Climate (Clima Legal) is a permanent project of Apremavi. Its objective is to plant native trees to neutralize CO2 emissions, mitigating the effects of climate change and contributing to the conservation of biodiversity in the Atlantic Forest biome. It has different membership modalities for both individuals and corporations.

As well as the organization’s relevance for environmental preservation and conservation, the native seedlings that were placed in the land through the various projects developed over time also grew, in a continuous process. Among the many numbers and indicators that can be cited to represent Apremavi’s work, the impact on landscapes stands out, representing the planning of rural properties, the protection of water resources and biodiversity, and even the diversification of the source of income in the family farming.

Check out some before and after provided by Cool Climate - By Apremavi in different cities, contexts, and scales over time.

proj_08KPr5UC3XliXwWgDqNgiIHs.description:
The Milihoi / Kichwa cha Nyoka Site site is nearby Lamu Town, which is a UNESCO World Cultural Heritage site with a vibrant history. The surrounding areas, including our project site, have a history of trade with countries as far away as India, dating back to the 12th century. Historically, mangroves have been an essential part of the local economy. They were harvested for dhow construction, exported for the tanning industry, and used for building materials.
Mangrove harvesting was banned in 1997,
but harvesting continued despite the ban.
In 2019, legal harvesting was reinstated. The primary occupation in this area is fishing and small-holder agriculture. Lamu County faces several challenges, including insufficient social services, very little fresh water, underdeveloped infrastructure, and food insecurity. Eden started its project at the Kichwa cha Nyoka/Milihoi site in 2020. This site is a mosaic of heavily degraded areas that need enrichment planting and healthy mangrove forests. The deforested section is 159 hectares, and there are another 1 million hectares in need of enrichment planting and protection.

properties.name: Kichwa cha Nyoka / Milihoi
properties.description:
The Kenya mangrove reforestation program in centered in Lamu County near Lamu Town on the northeast coast of Kenya. Lamu County supports about 33,500 hectares of mangrove forest, representing about 60% of Kenya's mangroves. Historically, mangroves have been an essential part of the local economy. They were harvested for dhow construction, export for the tanning industry (ash and bark) and building materials. Mangrove harvesting was banned in 1997 but harvesting continued despite the ban. Today, the coastal communities in this area are among the poorest and most marginalized in the country. 

Lamu Town is a UNESCO World Cultural Heritage site that has an incredibly rich history. The surrounding areas (including the project site) have a history of trade with countries as far away as India, dating back to the 12th century. The local artisans still make traditional dhows by hand that are pure works of art. It truly is a unique place. 

Milihoi / Kichwa cha Nyoka Site Description

The Milihoi / Kichwa cha Nyoka planting site is a mosaic of heavily degraded areas, sites in need of enrichment planting, and healthy mangrove forests. The mangrove forests are exploited for mangrove poles and other commercial uses, leading to large-scale degradation and deforestation in some areas. 

Through the support of our sponsors and active participation from the Mpeketoni and Milihoi communities, Eden Reforestation Projects operates mangrove reforestation and forest protection project to bring back the forest's vitality in this area. The project supports local communities to plant and manage mangrove forests on community land surrounding the village, offers long-term employment to local communities and livelihood improvements while protecting the important biodiversity that relies on mangrove forests to survive.

proj_fNOcPNWMojsm9Fs7mgLTF4vV.description:
The project would target an area of 200 acres of farmlands as part of this project in Andhra Pradesh. Practices such as agroforestry and multilayer farming model are predominant forms of TOFs in agriculture ecosystems. Such interventions have high potential for enhancing the revenues of farmers from their subsistence agriculture lands in addition to carbon sequestration that increases the green cover outside the forest zones while enhancing the livelihoods of farmers. Agroforestry is viewed as one of the best tools for optimizing farm productivity, increasing smallholder incomes, and building resilience in rural communities while contributing toward increased forest and tree cover. These systems reduce the stress on natural forests for forest produce such as fruits, timber and other NTPFs. More tree cover on private lands also helps to rehabilitate and restore degraded land and allows these private lands to increase their contribution to ecosystem goods and services. For example, increased tree cover stores carbon, helps to stabilize soil, and regulates water flow, reducing the risks associated with flooding. Increased tree cover also expands habitat for pollinators needed for agricultural crops, as well as other biodiversity. Trees can help communities increase their resilience to climate change and other shocks, not just through protection from extreme events, but by diversifying economic opportunities (through provision of fruits, wood, and other tree products).

The project aims to increase tree cover outside forests by promoting multi-strata agroforestry models through community mobilization & participation for enhancing livelihoods of farmers following natural farming methods. 

To achieve the above aim the project will work on the following objectives:
Objective 1: To increase the green cover outside forest areas and improving soil biodiversity & carbon sequestration through agroforestry.
Objective 2: Enabling farmers make a transition from chemical farming to sustainable farming practices. 
Objective 3: Providing farmers with additional livelihood opportunities.

proj_erGn01OcApz6cZX16rXp5FHy.description:
Intensive clearing of subtropical northern NSW has left a fragmented forest immensely vulnerable to threats of climate change, bushfires, and invasive weed degradation. This region was once the largest area of subtropical lowland rainforest in eastern Australia and now the remnants total less than 1% of the former size, approximately only 1000 hectares made up of small fragments scattered across the region. 

Wildlife corridors are connections across the landscape that link up areas of habitat. They support natural processes that occur in a healthy environment, including the movement of species to find resources, such as food and water. Wildlife prefer to use forest to move across a landscape as crossing empty paddocks and roads can be life-threatening.

This project is assisting with the restoration of a wildlife corridor that connects habitat from the eastern Byron Bay nature reserves up into the western habitat areas of Nightcap National Park. Over 50,000 trees will be planted at this location to connect habitat and allow wildlife to move between fragmented forest.

Conserve Natural Forests (CNF) is a non-profit NGO operating primarily in Mae Hong Son and Chiang Mai Provinces of Northern Thailand. Our mission is to restore natural forest landscapes throughout Thailand to optimal structure, functionality, and resiliency in ways that protect and enhance biodiversity, self-regulate landscape ecological functions, and improve the livelihoods of local communities in the long term.

properties.name: 002 Muang Pang
properties.description: Conserve Natural Forests (CNF) is an environmental non-profit foundation focused on forest restoration and wildlife conservation in the Mae Hong Son Province of Northern Thailand. Since 2014, we have dedicated ourselves to preserving and enriching ecosystem balance and function, restoring degraded landscapes, and reintroducing endangered species to their natural habitat. Our original project site, located a few kilometres south of Pai, includes our tree nursery, demonstration forest, and organic farm. The land also functions as a semi-wild rehabilitation site for a number of endangered species, including birds, tortoises, and the Asian elephant. Our projects would not be possible without the invaluable support of the local community and Thai government, and we are thankful for their help and the help of other like-minded individuals who have facilitated our development these past years. Our reforestation projects aim to offset the effects of climate change and protect native ecosystems. This includes the preservation of local old-growth forests and restoration of nearby degraded landscapes. We also work with local communities to promote agroforestry and other sustainable farming practices through education, training, and capacity building. With the help of our friends, we work year-round throughout Mae Hong Son and Chiang Mai Provinces to rebuild the beautiful and biodiverse tropical forests of Northern Thailand. Conserve Natural Forests’ goal is to implement practical, proven methods of forest restoration in order to mitigate the damages resulting from deforestation and forest degradation. We strive for an optimal balance between widespread and effective forest restoration – measured by the conservation of biodiversity, ecological health, and carbon sequestration – in conjunction with improving the economic and environmental quality of life for the local communities within our engaged region. CNF aims to be an ambassador for forest restoration, sustainable land practices and wildlife conservation in Northern Thailand. We use the Framework Species Method to guide us in our reforestation projects. We plant between 25 and 40 native species on our restoration sites depending on a variety of factors, including altitude, average temperature, soil quality, and the species composition of the surrounding ecosystem. Each tree we plant provides a specific service in the forest: Some trees fix nitrogen in the soil or retain moisture during the dry season. Fast-growing pioneer trees flourish in the sunlight and shade out weeds while climax trees grow slower but live longer. We also plant a mix of fruiting and flowering trees to attract seed-dispersing animals and insects to our land in order to enrich biodiversity and promote healthy succession. Our restoration projects typically require 3 to 5 years of management. We use a variety of Assisted Natural Regeneration (ANR) techniques – including weeding, mulching, enrichment plantings, and natural fertilization – to maximize the success rates of our trees. After about five years, nature takes over and the forest becomes self-regulating. Birds and mammals eat the seeds and disperse them to other areas, naturally increasing the size of the forests. The results have been astounding, but there remains a great deal of work left to be done!

We use a variety of Assisted Natural Regeneration (ANR) techniques – including weeding, mulching, enrichment plantings, and natural fertilization – to maximize the success rates of our trees. After about five years, nature takes over and the forest becomes self-regulating. Birds and mammals eat the seeds and disperse them to other areas, naturally increasing the size of the forests. The results have been astounding, but there remains a great deal of work left to be done!

properties.description:
Conserve Natural Forests (CNF) is an environmental non-profit foundation focused on forest restoration and wildlife conservation in the Mae Hong Son Province of Northern Thailand. Since 2014, we have dedicated ourselves to preserving and enriching ecosystem balance and function, restoring degraded landscapes, and reintroducing endangered species to their natural habitat. Our original project site, located a few kilometres south of Pai, includes our tree nursery, demonstration forest, and organic farm. The land also functions as a semi-wild rehabilitation site for a number of endangered species, including birds, tortoises, and the Asian elephant. Our projects would not be possible without the invaluable support of the local community and Thai government, and we are thankful for their help and the help of other like-minded individuals who have facilitated our development these past years.
Our reforestation projects aim to offset the effects of climate change and protect native ecosystems. This includes the preservation of local old-growth forests and restoration of nearby degraded landscapes. We also work with local communities to promote agroforestry and other sustainable farming practices through education, training, and capacity building. With the help of our friends, we work year-round throughout Mae Hong Son and Chiang Mai Provinces to rebuild the beautiful and biodiverse tropical forests of Northern Thailand.
Conserve Natural Forests’ goal is to implement practical, proven methods of forest restoration in order to mitigate the damages resulting from deforestation and forest degradation. We strive for an optimal balance between widespread and effective forest restoration – measured by the conservation of biodiversity, ecological health, and carbon sequestration – in conjunction with improving the economic and environmental quality of life for the local communities within our engaged region. CNF aims to be an ambassador for forest restoration, sustainable land practices and wildlife conservation in Northern Thailand.
We use the Framework Species Method to guide us in our reforestation projects. We plant between 25 and 40 native species on our restoration sites depending on a variety of factors, including altitude, average temperature, soil quality, and the species composition of the surrounding ecosystem.
Each tree we plant provides a specific service in the forest: Some trees fix nitrogen in the soil or retain moisture during the dry season. Fast-growing pioneer trees flourish in the sunlight and shade out weeds while climax trees grow slower but live longer. We also plant a mix of fruiting and flowering trees to attract seed-dispersing animals and insects to our land in order to enrich biodiversity and promote healthy succession.
Our restoration projects typically require 3 to 5 years of management. We use a variety of Assisted Natural Regeneration (ANR) techniques – including weeding, mulching, enrichment plantings, and natural fertilization – to maximize the success rates of our trees. After about five years, nature takes over and the forest becomes self-regulating. Birds and mammals eat the seeds and disperse them to other areas, naturally increasing the size of the forests. The results have been astounding, but there remains a great deal of work left to be done!

proj_jdwBUX1heHgwCCZg0AEjFxrF.description:
Working with schools in Kitui County in Kenya, we engage students and teachers in learning about the environmental benefits of planting trees. The project also demonstrates best practice in tree planting, and supports parents to plant trees on their own land. The main species planted is an indigenous, fast growing and drought resistant tree called ‘Melia Volkensii’. This tree has many uses, including edible leaves used as fodder for animals, pruning branches for firewood, and as forage for bees. It can be easily integrated into crops through agroforestry farming systems. We are also planting indigenous species to provide shade, fruits and other products. 

The project aims to work with up to 20 schools to plant areas of their grounds with plantations of around 1 acre. Farming communities will also be engaged, planting trees on their land.

proj_DMq70t91f1ceWdO29Ln12nhe.degradationCause: Armenia, as a forest-poor country with only about 11% of forested area and a very disparate distribution of forests, is suffering from a lack of forest cover
proj_DMq70t91f1ceWdO29Ln12nhe.description:
The project envisages implementing a biodiverse stratified agroforestry pilot project on community-owned lands affected by deforestation, with the active involvement of the inhabitants of Lernavan village. 
Particularly for the sloping treeless area, which is degrading due to intensive grazing, restoration is essential for preventing soil erosion, contributing to water infiltration and retention, regulating of local climate, and creating green spaces. It is planned to create a biodiverse stratified agroforestry system, including broadleaved forest trees as well as fruit trees and a variety of fruit- and nut-bearing shrubs and bushes in combination with grains/legumes or fodder plants. 
Due to the existence of micro-areas with different slope conditions within the designated site, there will be different planting concepts and patterns, which reach from alley cropping with rows of trees and shrubs bordering the terraces, where different agricultural crops will be grown to pure reforestation islands and belts in the steeper areas. 
Whilst on the terraced area, although the terraces are eroding, it will mostly be possible to prepare the ground mechanically. The steepness and complexity of the terrain above the terraced area and on the adjacent protrusion make it necessary that the preparation of the ground will be carried out mainly by hand. In this area, the surface flow of water during high intensity rainfalls also causes damage to the underlying lands. In the future, the plantings will play a water-regulating role and, at the same time, will have a recreational significance. 
Members of the village will take care of the plantings and manage both the trees and shrubs, as well as the agricultural crops. This includes weeding, soil preparation, and mulching, as well as pruning of the trees and shrubs. During the first years also partial irrigation during prolonged dry periods in the growing season may be required to support the establishment of the trees and shrubs. Whilst taking care that the plants receive only the water needed in order to support the development of a strong and well-developed root system, water will be provided as long as necessary.
Former experience with reforestation in the villages of Ttujur (Aragatsotn), Chambarak (Gegharkunik), and Dzoraglugh (Aragatsotn) shows that metallic grids must fence the planted areas in order to prevent the intrusion of cattle and sheep during the grazing period, as they can easily destroy newly planted saplings and severely damage and inhibit the growth of young trees. In addition, a guard has to be appointed, who takes the responsibility of checking the fencing for damage regularly and repairing possible damages in order to guarantee that animals cannot enter the site. Currently, there is no other secure option of fully excluding animals from the planting sites. After some years, when the trees are high and robust enough, the fences will be donated to the village, and they can use them for fencing other new-planted areas. This approach will further ensure the sustainability of the project.
proj_DMq70t91f1ceWdO29Ln12nhe.longTermPlan: With the agroforestry systems generating a long-term benefit, we expect to raise interest for agroforestry among neighbouring communities and private farmers, bringing more abandoned land sustainably back into use, increasing structural diversity, (agro-)biodiversity and resilience.
proj_DMq70t91f1ceWdO29Ln12nhe.mainChallenge: Due to the fact that the area has not been covered by forest for decades and since there are no forests nearby, spontaneous, natural regeneration of a forest ecosystem is rather unlikely.

proj_veoAYffxK7lIcesYnM57qNOj.description:
Hakalau Forest National Wildlife Refuge, on Hawaii’s Big Island, is the ‘last stand’ for a number of endangered Hawaiian bird species. Recent research has documented that native birds are using planted koa forests, which American Forests helped establish in the mid-90s. Hakalau has quietly emerged as one of the best examples of successful native forest restoration in the world. Yet, Hakalau’s planting efforts have largely gone dormant in the intervening decades due to limited capacity and resources.

Long-term restoration potential exists on the refuge as over 5,000 acres of pasture are available to convert back to native forest, and an even greater area exists on the surrounding lands owned and managed by the Department of Hawaiian Home Lands, a group eager to engage with forest restoration but unable to without additional funding and support. The higher price point on this project reflects the need to increase nursery capacity and unlock greater reforestation potential throughout Hawaii.
-------------------
2022 Update: We planted the last seedlings in April 2022, capping two years of revitalizing planting efforts on Maunakea. Your support allowed us to not only expand the Kanakaleonui Bird Corridor uphill, but also to build capacity with the Mauna Kea Watershed Alliance, the Department of Hawaiian homelands, and gain strong buy-in from US Fish and Wildlife Service. These plantings require extraordinary effort and expense, including 4+ hour drives on bad roads to reach planting sites, and labor-intensive site preparation to allow seedlings to compete with invasive grasses. They are also some of the most impactful and valuable seedlings that you can hope to find. Based on past plantings, we can expect these seedlings to start providing habitat for several species of endangered birds, like the Hawaiʻi ʻākepa, ʻakiapōlāʻau, and ʻiʻiwi, by 2040.

proj_7hmwFxpNnXzlqmJoDr7KJY3V.description:
In partnership with the Florida State Forest Service, we planted containerized longleaf pine and south florida slash pine between 7/11/2022 and 7/15/2022 (Lake Wales is rather unique among longleaf sites for being suited to summer planting).  This restotation project will create a number of benefits:
- Climate: Longleaf pine and South Florida slash pine are hardy, long-lived species native to Florida. Both are adapted and highly resilient to fire, drought, insects, and wind, especially compared to the slash pine plantations that they are replacing.
- Wildlife: This planting project will benefit multiple native wildlife species by improving the structure, composition and function of the forest. This is in large part achieved by the ability of native pines to establish and sustain a healthy fire regime. Reestablishing longleaf and slash pine at this site will improve wildlife cover, nesting, and browse habitat, and enhance the stand’s ability to burn in a healthy way by providing more continuous fine fuels. Native wildlife on this tract include whitetailed deer, black bear, wild turkey, quail, Florida panther and other species. Several threatened, endangered, and keystone/foundation species present on the tract include gopher tortoise, Florida scrub jay, Florida panther, bald eagle and sand skink.
- Labor: Planting was completed by a contract crew of 12 planters for five ten-hour days.
- Water: The Lake Wales Ridge State Forest plays an integral role in protecting and improving water quality in the Kissimmee Basin, which encompasses more than two dozen lakes in the Kissimmee Chain of Lakes, including their tributary streams and associated marshes, and the Kissimmee River and floodplain.

proj_L0tlHeaKT5EoOlDlmH0wUvAv.description: Deforestation of Sundarbans mangrove forest has become a grave concern for the environment because forests are vital source of biodiversity and livelihoods but are depleting at an alarming rate.  Forests are natural carbon storage systems balancing the weather and resisting the adverse impacts of natural calamities. The Bangladesh Sundarbans is one of the world largest mangrove forest ecosystem accounts 44% forests of the country and 4% of Bangladesh landscape. The Sundarbans with an area of 10000 sq. km. shared between two neighboring countries Bangladesh (62%) and India (38%) is a mangrove ecosystem. The Sundarbans is an ideal habitat for a variety of mammals, waders and seabirds and also the nesting sites for both marine turtles (Lepidochelys olivacea) (Blower, 1985) and 3.5 million people depend on Sundarbans resources. The Sundarbans is a Wetlands of International Importance (Ramsar site) that are also an UNESCO declared World Heritage site. Illegal forest felling, wildlife hunting, habitat degradation, climate change and good governance are causes of concern. Unsustainable harvesting of Nypa fruticans (golpatta) i.e. Cutting of central leaf, honey harvesting causes deforestation and production, fish and crab harvesting using poisonous chemical violating occupational ethics by the stakeholders hamper natural regeneration of Sundarbans resources depleting production and mangrove terrestrial and aquatic ecosystem. Indiscriminate harvesting and illegal felling of tiger prawn fries from Rivers and canals dwindling the prey-predator relationship and aquatic biodiversity. High demand of shrimp larvae for shrimp farming in the Sundarbans buffer zone making the Sundarbans ecosystem degraded. There is an urgent need for forestation in the buffer zone especially the accreted land /island (char land) evolved on the River bank and is possible for plantation by NGOs/private sector thus reduce the  Sundarbans deforestation and storage carbon for future generation.

proj_itaSbQGmpsGPhXkBl9l7iJWk.description:
This Assisted Natural Regeneration (ANR) project sits within the Greater Mahale Ecosystem (GME) in Western Tanzania. It is a 4.8 million-acre landscape, primarily comprising Miombo woodland, that harbors incredibly high biodiversity, including more than 90 percent of Tanzania’s endangered chimpanzees. It is also home to some of the country’s most marginalized indigenous communities, whose members survive on less than $1 per day. 

The GME’s existence is threatened by increasing levels of environmental degradation caused mainly by human activities, and exacerbated by climate change. More than 80 percent of the people living in the GME area depend on natural resources for survival, with trees and forests being integral to the health of both the ecosystem and the people living in this area. To address environmental degradation in the GME and its socioeconomic impact on the people who live there, TNC partnered with Pathfinder International in 2012 to form the Tuungane project. The Tuungane project provides knowledge and tools designed to improve daily life and protect natural resources in a way that empowers local people to build a sustainable future of their own design.

To manage and protect their forests, local communities are currently involved in village land use planning, sustainable forest resource management, and tree planting. One critical component of sustainable reforestation not implemented to date is the natural regeneration of indigenous tree species, or ANR. ANR takes advantage of the ‘underground forests’ already in the soil; instead of planting new trees, we can regenerate existing and dormant seeds on both farms and in degraded forests, resulting in the survival of trees which have been adapted to the natural environment for millennia.

ANR involves training community members how to manage tree regrowth, which includes protection against disturbances and reducing competition from grasses and bushes that hinders growth of naturally regenerated trees. It’s an incredibly simple, yet effective, technique which was pioneered in Niger and is easily replicated. 

Our goals are to:
•	Incorporate ANR into the existing efforts of the Tuungane project, leading to the regeneration of up to 800,000 trees across ~1,000 hectares at a cost of $0.25 per tree. Additional benefits include:
o	Community: Increased resilience to climate change through increased soil fertility, shade, and water availability and more fuel, fodder, and timber for subsistence use. 
o	Environment: carbon sequestration estimated at 1.2 million tonnes of CO2 over 50 years, increased habitat for birds and insects, return of indigenous tree species, and water filtration.
(Photos © Ami Vitale | The Nature Conservancy)
proj_itaSbQGmpsGPhXkBl9l7iJWk.name: Restoration of Forest Landscapes through Assisted Natural Regeneration in Western Tanzania

proj_YPXJ9e9iiy4Ras0zknJkxyH6.description:
The Mucelia site lies on Mozambique's eastern coast in Zambezia Province. Mucelia is 13 kilometers from the small town of Macuze and 50 kilometers from the city of Quelimane. The administrative capital of the province, Quelimane, began as a Swahili trade center. The city was once part of the Kilwa Sultanate, a Medieval sultanate founded in the 10th century. At its height, the sultanate stretched across the Swahili Coast. It was ruled by several different Arab families until the Portuguese overthrew them in 1505. Vasco da Gama stopped in Quelimane in 1498 on his journey to India.

This region is heavily reliant on fishing and agriculture. The native mangrove forests provide many raw materials the local villagers need to make a living, such as wood for boats, buildings, tools, and charcoal. As a result, deforestation is widespread at this site, and the remaining mangroves struggle to regrow the forest. Dwindling forest health and forest stock exacerbates the poverty already present. Further, basic needs such as education, drinking water, and health care are difficult to come by.

We (Eden) will hire local people to reforest their region by planting mangrove trees at Mucelia while stimulating economic growth, breaking the cycle of poverty, and empowering the community.
proj_YPXJ9e9iiy4Ras0zknJkxyH6.longTermPlan: The long-term plan is to provide support to the local community to collect mangrove propagules and strategically plant 6 million trees in areas that have been heavily degraded or deforested.

Through this project marginal farmland is converted to permanent woodland by planting 14,478 trees over 9.5 hectares. proj_95TqFfC3Z5FU99HKKdNwM6TL.description:
Fundación Reforestemos is a non-profit organization that strives to be a leader in recognizing and recovering the environmental value of Chile’s ecosystems. We promote cultural change in relation to caring for the environment, recovering Chilean native forests and raising awareness about the importance of healthy, strong forests.

The initiative will contribute to the active restoration of areas degraded by bushfires in this national park that is highly visited from the citizens of Concepción. The Nonguén National Park is home to a very important watershed, since it supplies water to more than half a million people, and its ecosystem services have historically been threatened by bushfires and illegal logging. The planting of these trees will be a great contribution to the protection and restoration of new green areas available to the community, which in Chile are under the minimum recommendations of the World Health Organization.

Fundación Reforestemos is not tax deductible and can not issue donation receipts yet!

proj_Rep57jIWWazf4gHc3fLEpfvp.description:
Let’s plant trees together and spread solutions with agroforestry and permaculture leading to a positive climate impact!

In the same go we will support rural people to reach food safety, to become ecologically and economically sustainable, and to get literate in how to preserve their livelihood. 

Hence, you are definitely making a great decision to support this project!

We are at the right spot for reversing massive erosion that washes away valuable soil that is polluting the lakes at the same time. Therefore, we start from the top of the mountain with countermeasures. On 3007-meter-hight, the Arba Minch University (AMU) has got 24.6 hectares which have been deforested by the local villagers leading to depletion of humus through erosion. Now, as part of the solution a meadow orchard and an agroforest shall be planted on at least half of this area. In total 17,000 trees will help to stop the loss of humus, while absorbing a part of the overmuch CO2 out of the atmosphere (more precisely absorbing the carbon (C) and giving back the oxygen (O2)). In the orchard and agroforest, we will plant trees like apple, pear, plum and chestnut trees. Below those trees partial shade trees and lower plants like vegetables will be planted for symbiosis. With this agroforestry and permaculture concept, we also introduce Terra Preta with several benefits. It will give long lasting fertilization to the soil and will increase the growth of plants. The preserved and improved humus will capture additional CO2 and will store water, which raises the level of the ground water as well. This overall approach, will help the resilience of these trees, create biodiversity and diverse nutrition. Planting, maintaining and later sales of surplus fruits and vegetables will create long-term income for the villagers. The villagers will be trained to train others to become multipliers for this high impact approach with great leverage effect.

In the name of todays and future children, thank you very much for your support!

This project is TAX deductible in Germany.

---------------------------------
AMU EcoVillage Project develops a sustainable high-quality lifestyle for rural regions in Africa. 
It aims to build a small prototype village with modern buildings from natural materials with renewable energy, resources-oriented wastewater systems for fertilizer and soil substrate production, self-sustained and sustainable surplus farming capabilities, a preventive healthcare center, a project-based learning environment for local villagers and students, and of course to provide internet access.
Additionally, it shall act as incubator and accelerator for green inclusive business start-ups. A sustainable forestry is only the start.  
In short it supports 16 out of 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) from the United Nations (UN). 
 
Contact: project@unavision.eu

proj_85wUqdYlqzqzeh43lN6kHLse.description:
The Brazilian Atlantic Forest is one of the most biodiverse forests in the world yet only 7% of the original forest remains as small, isolated fragments. Restoring the forest is extremely vital to safeguard the remaining biodiversity and combat the progressive loss of the world’s species and for our climate as well. The high carbon sequestration potential of second-growth forests in the Latin American tropics means the Atlantic Forest is a key player in the climate change agenda. A partnership with Instituto de Pesquisas Ecológicas (IPÊ), the project aims to create forest corridors between remaining fragments, increasing tree cover and habitat connectivity for native species. The community-based nurseries, seed collection and planting activities are under the management of local people who, thanks to our project, are empowered to earn a living while restoring the forest.

WeForest is tax deductible in the Netherlands! TGE is possible in several European countries.

proj_bfAyPDJ1Ffzze5AfOccnXNIR.description:
SAFE TREE is an innovative Eco-friendly Tree planting system which creates very favorable conditions at the newly planted plants root system, by maintaining constant moisture, stable temperature, dynamic ventilation and strong fertilization, thus it provides the plant the ability to survive itself securely and grow fast indeed.

Nigeria’s Ecosystem Restoration Project in Benue State, is a tree planting project that is intended to stop desertification, create favorable conditions for agroforestry crops and forest gardens and combat soil degradation and erosion.
Desertification advancing has implications on communities living in the Benue fringes of the Arid Zone in Nigeria. Forests are often cleared for farms, and cutting down trees provide a quick source of income for those living in poverty.
Our main target is to create agroforestry crops and forest gardens. To do this the first step is to plant and grow native trees for food and substances. After that when these trees are growing the farmers can develop agricultural cultivation near and below the trees. 
In the phase of planting, we add mycorrhizae. The mycorrhizae are symbiotic monoorganisms which are attached to the roots of the plant, take from them light to live and in return they dissolve inorganic elements of the soil, create beneficial components for the plant, aiding it in absorbing them and improving also the colloidal attributes of the soil.
In this way they combat soil degradation and erosion rejuvenating the earth.
The trees to be planted would be sourced from a Nursery site to be established in Benue State 
Our planting partners/community members would harvest seeds from native trees nurture them into seedlings at local nursery and subsequently plant them. We are proposing to plant 1500 trees in the interim with a prospect of scaling it up as the project gain more traction in the area. 
At this early stage of the project, the following native tree species would be planted. These native tree species work in harmony with farmers’ bio-intensive gardens to help create a more nutrient rich soil. As the land within Makurdi zone regenerates, crop yield would increase, and farmers would be able to feed their families and sell extra products for income.
The following are the native tree plants that would be sourced from community nursery site(s):
Mahogany (Khayasenegalensis) –	400
Mango trees 			- 	300
Locust bean (Parkiabiglobosa) 	-	300
Tenera oil palm (Eleasguinensis)- 	200
Ogbono (Irvingiagabonensis)	-	200
Teak (Tectonagrandis)		-	100
Total :	              1500

proj_UJ96KUbReAlguhLLS3r9psZC.description:
Defenders of the Planet (formerly known as Rwenzori Environment Conservation Project) is a registered non-governmental and nonprofit environmental organization  founded in the year 2005 by concerned community members who saw a need to contribute to environmental conservation due to current environmental challenges such as the issue of climate change, threatened biodiversity among others.
We raise public awareness on the relevance of environmental conservation and management, we empower communities with technical expertise and trainings on environment. We conserve and restore water catchments such as rivers, lakes and wetlands. We promote tree planting and agro forestry as well as carrying out various projects in the field of climate change.

According to a baseline survey done in August, 2018 by DEPLA in communities living near Rwenzori Mountains National Park, the following environmental challenges were established;
1.	Low level of awareness on environmental education
2.	Encroachment on Mt. Rwenzori forest for charcoal burning and timber.
3.	Existence of Bare hills and soil erosion/ landslides

Over the last few years, the forest cover in Kasese has significantly reduced. Community members reported that many parts of the sub counties had extensive forest and tree cover but now most of it is gone. This has resulted in loss of biodiversity and severe land degradation due to soil erosion and loss of fertility. The local people note that many areas which used to be very fertile are now barren and the overall agricultural productivity in the area has declined dramatically which is pushing people deeper into poverty. Moreover, pressure on the remaining forests and trees is high as the proportion of people depending on them for firewood and non-timber products is quite high. 

There is high deforestation pressure for firewood, charcoal burning, brick burning among others. The community members cut trees but they don’t plant new ones which have resulted in various consequences of climate change such as unreliable and inadequate rainfall, water sources drying up, over flooding and poverty due to loss of livelihoods. In addition this has put on pressure Mt. Rwenzori Forest national park which is of global importance.

The project will be implemented in Rukoki  and Kahokya sub counties and will target communities who stay near Rwenzori forest.
The project will involve providing 2,000,000 tree seedlings to beneficiaries who stay near Rwenzori Forest. The trees to be planted will be agro forestry species, forestry species as well as some fruit trees.
Tree species to be planted will include Grevillea robusta, Maesopsis eminii, Eucalyptus grandis and Bathedavia.
Defenders of the Planet (DEPLA) will raise the seedlings in nursery beds after which they will be distributed to beneficiaries when ready for transplanting.
There will be training of beneficiaries on tree planting and environment conservation which will be carried out as radio talk shows, by visiting schools and holding community trainings at our nursery beds.
Trainings will be provided to all project beneficiaries on how to care and look after the trees, soil and water conservation measures trainings will also be provided to the beneficiaries. 

Before transplanting, the project team headed by the forestry officer will register tree beneficiaries and survey their lands to identify how many trees each beneficiary need and the species suitable for the beneficiary’s land.


Project Goal
To help communities around Mt. Rwenzori plant 2,000,000 trees seedlings so as to reduce pressure on Mt. Rwenzori forest which is of global importance.
To train over 3600 people on forestry and soil conservation measures
Project 
Outcomes
1.	Improved community environmental education and awareness.
2.	The project will reduce soil erosion, increase water table, improve soil fertility and promote agro forestry in local communities. 
3.	Forest and tree cover (with appropriate species) promoted on slopes that are vulnerable to climate-driven increases in erosion and landslide risks.

proj_6JkxhrIH6gh5UTaZYVbDD19n.description:
The region of the Pôrô located in the North zone of Ivory Coast is a region that undergoes every day the effects of climate change. The population, having little information on the behavior to adopt in the face of this global scourge accuses most often the State which, at its level is sometimes limited in its actions. It is the responsibility of NGOs to look at it and provide a lasting solution to mitigate the effects of climate change. The contribution of the NGO PAGE VERTE will be one of the biggest support that the NGOs that fight in Côte d'Ivoire in the field of the Environment try to put at the disposal of the populations. Raising the awareness of more than 3,000 people to the protection of the environment in this area and also planting 10,000 trees will be a saving action for the population as this will prevent the advance of dessert and will also produce a mild climate in reforested sites.
The general objective of the project is to develop actions aimed at Reforestation and Environmental Education in the northern area of Côte d'Ivoire, specifically in the region of Pôrô.
In other words:
·       Environmental Education in Elementary and Secondary Schools in the communities of the region of Pôrô,
·         Raising awareness among charcoal producers and farmers on slaughter illicit trees for the production of charcoal and agriculture in the pitches with slopes,
·         Construction of the plant production center and activities of reforestation in the Communities
This is, from the start of the project, to involve all the customary leaders, religious, civil, youth associations and any other group that exists in the area and is likely to be affected directly or indirectly by said project.
This involvement must be done by raising awareness in order to understand the merits of the project and to get everyone to marry him.

No tax deduction information available yet!

proj_oEAbWpTPUQObkR0jkz4g5Jep.degradationCause: The degradation of the soil and the environment in this entity is due to the practice of inadequate cultivation techniques leading not only to infertility of the soil but also to its degradation in certain places of cultivable areas due to the population explosion.
proj_oEAbWpTPUQObkR0jkz4g5Jep.description:
It has been for several years that we observe the excessive and abusive use of available land spaces by the practice of inadequate cultivation techniques leading not only to infertility of the soil but also to its degradation in certain places of cultivable spaces due to the demographic explosion justified by a high and unplanned birth rate, but also by the immigration of populations to the large centers exploring insecurity and which unfortunately ignore the practices of modern agro-forestry systems. This situation pushes the local communities of the territory of Nyiragongo to move to the Park in search of arable land in order to meet some of their basic needs.
To achieve this, the WWID / HFL organization seeks to enhance forest environments by initiating permaculture activities and protect the biodiversity of Virunga National Park.
Thus, nurseries of pre-selected agro-forestry species will be set up and popularized to the population with a view to recharging degrading areas and maintaining them on farms, which means that we will have to set up 7 nurseries of agro-forestry species but if we started from the price of seedlings we would be opposed to buying a seedling at the price of 0.8 $
In this perspective, this project is not only part of the Priority Plan of the Provincial Government of North Kivu, but also of the national sub-program for the management of protected areas.

proj_jIg2aW8I6RkLHwLcEZodh5Wq.description:
Plant-for-Ethiopia
Let’s grow the pioneer Ethiopian forestry management project!
This project has just started, and you can already be part of it. Not only does it have a wide range of benefits for the planet, but also for the region and all the people living there. You are definitely making a great decision if you choose to support it!
Plant-for-Ethiopia will develop a sustainable forestry management system as well as a vocational training programme for youth. In doing so, it provides a huge contribution to local welfare and prosperity. At the same time, the forests we create are a source of materials, food, biodiversity, and soil fertility. And, last but not least, the trees bind carbon dioxide in the long term and thus reduce the impact of global warming.
This will become a lighthouse project for other countries in the Global South!
Plant-for-Ethiopia is part of Plant-Together; a collaboration between Plant-for-the-Planet and local Tree Planting Organisations. It brings together the strategic expertise of Plant-for-the-Planet as a global mobiliser for reforestation to mitigate the climate crisis, and the hands-on competence of professional local partners from across the globe, who plant and nurture the trees. Plant-for-Ethiopia is the pioneer collaboration and first partnership.
The local Tree Planting Organisations are the Ethiopian Orthodox Church Development and Inter-Church Aid Commission (EOC-DICAC) and the Konso Development Association (KDA). Check them out on the App.
By the way… thank you so much for your support! You are incredible for helping us to do amazing work in Ethiopia.

proj_SuKA0nlGqbv4PZib0xnaoUSs.degradationCause: In the 20th century, large areas were cleared for timber and land for a rapidly growing population. Extensive destruction has been linked to 7 threats: encroachment, logging, charcoal production, clear felling, growing of marijuana, landslides, livestock grazing and fires.
proj_SuKA0nlGqbv4PZib0xnaoUSs.description: Working with schools around the Mount Kenya Forest Reserve, CHASE Africa and Mount Kenya Trust will plant woodlots on school grounds. Schools have up to 10 acres of land, and are motivated to plant trees to provide a sustainable source of firewood and timber. This helps reduce pressure on the indigenous forest which surround Mount Kenya - Africa's second highest mountain. The trees also improve biodiversity and provide shade in the playground when they are growing. Children engage in learning about the importance of trees, and the woodlots also act as demonstration sites to inspire parents to plant trees on their own land. We work with schools who are motivated to care for the trees on their land over the period of growth, which means we have excellent survival rates and can cut costs associated with fencing. We have run successful schools projects since 2016, and hope to expand this work over the coming years to support many more communities.
proj_SuKA0nlGqbv4PZib0xnaoUSs.longTermPlan: The school woodlots will be used for timber production (reducing pressure on the native forest) and also to plant native trees, encouraging their introduction around homes. The timber trees will likely be replaced once cut down.
proj_SuKA0nlGqbv4PZib0xnaoUSs.mainChallenge: The main challenge is past and ongoing degradation of the indigenous forest. By encouraging communities to plant trees on their own land, we can reduce pressure on the native forest which people rely on for their livelihoods.

proj_4jIZiMYhCLt9jDqbk5bMS7js.description:
UPDATE: As of December 5th, 2022 this project is part of "Bulindi Chimpanzee and Community Project (BCCP)" - This project aims to significantly reduce threats via restoration and conservation of chimpanzee habitat in key areas in the Hoima corridor, with development of long-term alternatives to deforestation. It directly addresses root causes: need for alternative livelihoods and wood for cooking and timber. 

Coffee is a chimp-friendly cash crop: chimps do not eat coffee (thus coffee growing will not generate ‘conflicts’); unlike common cash crops (tobacco/rice) that require virgin soil, coffee does not require that forest is cleared for planting. 

We will raise and distribute 200,000 high-quality robusta seedlings, establish coffee farmer associations (CFA), provide planting and maintenance support. The CFAs will negotiate the best price for beans once trees fruit (3–4 years). 

This planting programme complements our other project activities such as daily, long-term conservation monitoring of chimpanzees within the corridor.

The Bulindi Chimpanzee & Community Project is tax deductible in Uganda!

proj_BcDy0MniYLcV1cGSGzbvb7dR.description:
Cameroon includes circa 10% of the Congo Basin rainforest and although the country appears heavily forested,there is a continuous loss of natural forests (about 30ha/hour). Deforestation is strongly associated with timber harvesting, slash-and-burn agriculture, charcoal production and natural disasters.

In a bid to safeguard her then over 45.6% surface area forest cover (>40% today), the government of Cameroon in 1994 enacted the Forestry Law. The goal of which was to ensure sustainable management of forest and other natural resources.  One of the major innovations in the 1994 law was the concept of community forest that granted local communities access, use, management and marketing rights over substantial portion of the non-Permanent Forest Estates. As of 2011, 301 community forests had been attributed in Cameroon, accounting for 4% (1 million hectare) of the country’s forests estates. The South West Region of Cameroon accounts for 19 community forests, including the Etinde Community Forest.
The Etinde Community Forest is located in Fako Division of the South West region of Cameroon and has a total surface area of over 1000ha. It is part of a chain of protected areas within the Mt, Cameroon biodiversity hotspot and is home to forest elephants, chimpanzees, monkeys, drills amongst other amazing wildlife species. 
Unfortunately, parts of the forest has been lost to logging, agriculture and lava flowing from Mts. Cameroon and Etinde (active volcanoes). The deforestation rate is estimated at over 0.51% annually. 
As we speak, over 2/3 of all water bodies in the area have dried up leaving over 5000 people in water scarcity.
The aim of this project therefore is to plant 10,000native tree species in the deforested parts of the forest. We anticipate that the planted trees will contribute in recharging ground water & improving water tables (indicative of the return to flow of streams and rivers over time), restore wildlife habitat (thus reducing human-wildlife conflicts) and restock non-timber forest products (spices, fruits, nuts, honey, medicine etc that serve as an important source of income to the local people). Tree planting would also enhance the carbon sequestration ability of the ecosystem.

proj_jfwBmeOKamvN504VBol3ZHM2.description:
The Sacred Mountain is a 273 hectares mountain in the Andes of southern Ecuador. It spans an altitude between 1550 and 2330 m above sea level. Its natural vegetation composes of a mixture of a tropical mountain rainforest, tropical dry forest and tropical cloud forest. This requires and – at the same time – allows for a great biodiversity and it actually is located in one of the world’s most precious biodiversity hotspots!

To restore the natural ecosystem we need to work the ground before starting to plant trees. We will use water retention landscaping (also called “rainwater harvesting”) to raise the groundwater table, to prevent further erosion and to regenerate and revive the barren soil. As the mountain slope is pretty steep, these structures have to be implemented by hand – the use of heavy machines is not possible. Therefore, the cost-per-tree might be comparably high. However, it does make a lot of sense to restore natural ecosystems on steep mountainsides that are not productive and not useful for agriculture. In fact, we should mostly reserve highly productive plane landscapes for agricultural uses and focus on less productive lands for natural reforestation!

The Sacred Mountain – natural Reforestation is a well-planned thoughtful ecosystem restoration project combining the protection of threatened biodiversity and the mitigation of climate change. It serves as a wildlife reserve that helps to connect highly diverse National parks and stores great amounts of CO2 at the same time! 

With your help we can make it become reality!
Thank you very much for your donation! <3

proj_wqgGnda7Je2791h2214996tY.description: The project is geared towards the regeneration and restoration of the waste land within the water tower of Mt. Elgon. This region serves the entire region of great Lake Victoria that shares its waters into Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania and at the same time it is the source of River .Nile that runs into Red sea through Ethiopia and Egypt. We are focusing on giving the correct information, practices and training to the farmers in this region whom have been using traditionally methods for land preparation i.e. bush fallowing that has resulted into ecological disaster via erosion, bush fires and deforestation, On the other hand population explosion has resulted into great danger to the ecosystem since people have encroached the forest to get land for farming and also grazing field field. Landslides have been of great danger especially during long and heavy rains seasons. We encourage the farmers by giving them the best species that are indigenous but leguminous in nature such that they restore soil fertility while also using them for financial gain on managed harvesting program. This also help to prevent people going for timber in the forest and also other medical plant from the forest. Our team educate them on the self-sustainability of the program and also land preparation, nursery management, transplanting as well tree maintenance and management.
proj_wqgGnda7Je2791h2214996tY.longTermPlan: Protection of forest from fires, no land clearance for agriculture and habitation uses, proper monitoring of plant diseases and pest by planting indigenous trees, constant survey of the forested land to avoid encroachers, use of mobile tree app to tract our trees on real-time, fencing

proj_IayG16fWq0B5ukJE0M7fiiKn.description:
Our goal on Borneo is the large-scale reforestation of degraded former rainforest areas, in a way that doesn’t only save the environment and climate, but also create sustainable livelihoods for the local population. With the revitalization of deforested and degraded areas, the soil fertility of whole regions can be transformed and thus made usable again for humans, animals and plants.

The main cause of deforestation on Borneo is the global and local need for resources, like wood, palm oil and mineral resources such as gold. That’s why we believe that sustainable reforestation and active environmental protection can only work if the local population also benefits economically. Only if we succeed in meeting the needs of the people with our reforested areas, we can protect the remaining primeval forests of Borneo.

In order to secure the income of the local population and protect the environment, we have developed an intelligent agroforestry concept based on three pillars:

1. The planting of fast-growing trees: We use pioneer trees with high growth rates on our land, which are in demand from the timber industry at attractive market prices and are ecologically beneficial.
2. The cultivation of cash crops: fruit and vegetables, peanuts, cocoa, coffee and spices between the tree rows guarantee the population a fast and constant income. 
3. Regenerative agriculture: Through the use of special plant species and a multitude of different plant forms, soil quality and biodiversity and thus productivity are continuously improved. The replanting stops erosion, restores water and nutrient cycles and mitigates climate change, as the growing trees absorb carbon from the air.

We support farmers with seedlings, expertise and diverse training and provide them with market access for their products. In order to transform the timber and food industries towards greater sustainability, we work along the entire value chain from the planting of the trees to the end consumer.

So far we have planted over 1 Million Trees together with smallholder farmers on Borneo. While working towards this first goal we have learned a lot and optimized our practices, so we are now ready for our next ambitious goal: reforest Borneo on a larger scale and plant 100 Million Trees!

proj_N6DGzA2RkRuv6HldQGkPrPmQ.description:
AstilleroVerde’s reforestation program, TreesForSeas, envisions healthy forest systems in the Bellbird Biological Corridor of Costa Rica for an integrated, sustainable future in which communities and nature mutually thrive; mitigating the impacts of climate change to protect our planet’s diversity, functionality, and integrity for generations to come. 
The objectives of this program are: 1) plant trees for carbon sequestration and timber replacement for Ceiba Maritima, 2) restore ecological function to degraded, deforested land, in the Bellbird Biological Corridor and Gulf of Nicoya region of Costa Rica, 3) promote community resilience.

proj_U3QlC4V6MzaUYYEj73KzB7ER.description:
Intensive clearing of subtropical northern NSW has left a fragmented forest immensely vulnerable to threats of climate change, bushfires, and invasive weed degradation. This region was once the largest area of subtropical lowland rainforest in eastern Australia and now the remnants total less than 1% of the former size, approximately only 1000 hectares while still home to a rich array of species, some of which are incredibly rare in Australia.

In 2019-2020 the fragmented forest and drought allowed bushfires to burn into this subtropical region and badly affected the rainforest. Tree planting and regeneration work in this area will be focused on fire affected sites needing immediate attention for recovery, degraded forest with high invasive weed infestation, and bringing back rainforest to where it was previously cleared for agriculture. The main site we are working on is adjacent to the national park and so the rehabilitation of this site and removal of weeds is necessary to protect the national park from the weeds. This site was once beautiful rainforest and we will bring it back through this project.

proj_W3ERDYuQq7hQVQCyb9Yswrt6.description: Bäume dienen nicht nur als CO2-Speicher, sondern haben auch eine wichtige Funktion im Wasserkreislauf, da sie die Wasseraufnahmefähigkeit der Böden steigern und Verdunstung aus den oberen Bodenschichten minimieren. Die RG Rhein-Main wird in einer Pflanzaktion sobald wie die Corona-Pandemie es zulässt zusammen mit der Nachbar-RG Rhein-Neckar und dem Wasserbeschaffungsverband Riedgruppe Ost in 300 Bäume pflanzen. Die Aktion findet im Wildpark auf dem Gelände des Wasserwerks statt, direkt neben den Wildschweinen. Gepflanzt werden Roteichen und Vogelkirsche. Die Vogelkirsche dient neben der Funktion im CO2- und Wasserkreislauf als Futter für heimische Vögel und Insekten. Also heißt es: Ran an den Spaten und Lospflanzen!

proj_VeREoFRy6aF0ekx4fWqJ3mIu.description: Providing a fantastic opportunity to support the reforestation of a multi-purpose native woodland, the project will in time allow the farm to diversify its business while supporting the local environment and biodiversity.  Native silver birch will eventually be thinned and coppiced, providing a supply for fuelwood for both the farm and surrounding houses. Sycamore will be managed on a continuous cover basis, with occasional trees felled to provide a source of hardwood timber for local mills. All the other species in this woodland will help to enhance regional biodiversity and increase the connectivity of forest habitats in a highly agricultural part of Scotland. On top of this, the trees themselves will sequester close to 4,000 tonnes of CO2e during their growing lifetime. The project will be managed under the UK government's Woodland Carbon Code which ensures it is independently monitored and verified.
