proj_4urzfQ47Xwv5SlNOurnXn2hU.degradationCause: Küstenlandschaften und Mangroven sind durch schädliche Aktivitäten wie illegale Abholzung und Entwaldung, Verschmutzung durch feste und flüssige Abfälle und unnatürliche Umleitungsdämme bedroht, die zu unausgewogenen hydrologischen Verhältnissen und damit zu einer stetigen Verschlechterung des Mangrovenökosystems führen.
proj_4urzfQ47Xwv5SlNOurnXn2hU.description: Manchón Guamuchal Nature Reserve are threatened by harmful activities on coastal land such as illegal logging and deforestation in watershed regions, solid and liquid waste pollution, and unnatural diversion dams that cause unbalanced hydrological conditions leading to a consistent deterioration of the mangrove ecosystem. To overcome these challenges, this project proposes to plant and monitor the growth of 1,330,000 mangrove and broadleaf tree species to restore 1,025 hectares within the mangrove ecosystem of Guatemala over the next four years (December 2021-November 2025).
proj_4urzfQ47Xwv5SlNOurnXn2hU.longTermPlan: Da die Projektplanung gemeinsam mit den Gemeinden erfolgt, sind diese an der Arbeit beteiligt und verstehen die möglichen positiven Auswirkungen auf ihr Land. Das Projekt ist so angelegt, dass die Gemeinden geschult werden und lokale Führungspersönlichkeiten bestimmt werden, um die Langlebigkeit und die Akzeptanz der Gemeinden zu gewährleisten.
proj_4urzfQ47Xwv5SlNOurnXn2hU.mainChallenge: Das Naturreservat Manchón Guamuchal ist durch schädliche Aktivitäten an der Küste bedroht, wie z. proj_CgoJfaypzTRWeZ5bCRQZtDP9.description: This project will plant 140 urban trees at seven different elementary schools in Brownsville, Texas. Keep Brownsville Beautiful has a large number of student volunteers from their local high schools that they will engage to help plant the trees in the schools. The culminating event is scheduled to celebrate Arbor Day, during which they will also distribute seedlings to the community that can be planted at home. This project is more than just about planting the trees - it is about educating the community, specifically youth, on the importance of trees.

proj_gNHIESSoSSpiYXLvoqe5TT2y.degradationCause: The original mountain rainforest has been logged by companies for more than 30 years. The IPRA law of 1997 attributed the land to the Obu-Manuvu tribe as their traditional living places. CADT No. R11-DAV-1108-091 granted ownership of the land to the tribe in 2008.
proj_gNHIESSoSSpiYXLvoqe5TT2y.description: Since 2011, EGIP Foundation has been supporting tribal communities in the hinterlands of Davao City in agroforestry and in the reforestation and protection of their ancestral rainforests. As of December 2023 more than 36000 forest trees (especially of the endangered Dipterocarpus family), plants of non-timber-forest products (like bamboo and rattan) and local fruit trees have been planted on 12 refo sites with more than 58 has and been taken care of by the tribal communities. Additionally, more than 130 tribal forest rangers have been trained and deputized by the City of Davao and by the Department of Environment to protect the existing and the planted forests.

properties.name: Reforstation Mount Karilongan
properties.description: The first agroforestry or reforestation area in Mount Karilongan, where EGIP Foundation together with the Obu-Manuvu Community in Macatabo (Barangay Carmen, Baguio District, Davao City) planted since 2012 approx. 18.000 forest and fruit trees as well as permanent crops (mainly abaca bananas, coffee, cacao) have been planted since 2012, thus transforming the cogon grasslands left after rainforest deforestation into an area with relatively high (agro)biodiversity.

properties.name: Reforestation site Patag
properties.description: Since 2011, the Philippine NGO Eurogenerics Inc. Foundation (EGIPF) has been supporting indigenous cultural communities (ICC) in the hinterlands of Davao City with forest protection, reforestation and agroforestry within their Ancestral Domains. The ICC shall be empowered to manage their Ancestral Domain in a sustainable and environmentally friendly way protecting the environment and the Ancestral rainforest with its biodiversity while sustaining their livelihood with agroforestry products like fruit trees, banana, abaca, coffee and cacao. As of now, around 18.000 forest and fruit trees have been planted on 30 has (with around 625 trees per ha) by the tribal farmers of the ICC in Sitio Macatabo, Barangay Carmen, Baguio District, Davao City. Presently, the farmers go on collecting seeds and wildlings, raise them in the project nursery or on their own and continue planting or sell them to EGIPF or other reforestation projects. EGIPF was asked by the elders of the Obu-Manuvu tribe to continue this successful approach and planted around 2,000 forest and fruit trees on 3 has together with the communities of Likuyan, Ladi-an and Patag in Baguio and Marilog District, Davao City in 2020 and despite of the Corona Crisis. Another 92 ha within the Mount Sinaka Key Biodiversity Area are being prepared for replanting in the following years. The overall goal will be to reforest around 15.000 has (i.e. around 10 Mio. trees) together with the 15 Indigenous Communities of the Obu-Manuvu Ancestral Domain. The more donations will come in, the faster we can achieve this goal. Hence this request for donations! … and every donor gets his/her own name plate! The reforestation costs of 6 Euro per tree include 3 Euro for raising the seedlings, site preparation and planting and 3 Euro for a 3-year maintenance of the plantations by the tribal farmers. proj_ON5HC3IfetF3TO1EMWxjV6Uc.description:
Lushoto District is one of the eleven councils in Tanga Region located in northeastern Tanzania. The district has an area of 2.051 square kilometers which accounts for about 7.3 percent of Tanga region land area. It borders with Korogwe District in thesouth and Mkinga District further east, same district of Kilimanjaro Region in the northwest and the republic of Kenya in the northeast.
This project was initially started since January 2017 as CYDO organized its members to use their own funds to prepare some few tree nurseries for reforestation to planted to the 12 the burnt natural forests in Bumbuli and Lushoto councils whereby all these district councils are located within Lushoto District’s Administrative boundary. Among the 12 natural forest that are going to be planted with new indigenous trees is Magila Nature Forest Reserve, which was burnt to some of its parts due to human economic activities of making charcoal. 
We have decide to ask for funding to help to facilitate reforestation process in this natural reserve forests because the burnt forest is very important to the surrounding villagers as they were able to enjoy a nice environment, get firewood and got some water for drinking, commercial and social activities were done effectively at that time before it was burnt.
We are going to plant indigenous trees known as Albizia Gummifera with its family name known as Mimosoideae and it is known as ''Mshai'' in Swahili language. This type of indigenous tree is mostly recommended to be planted within a natural forest as it conserve moisture and support water conservation and it is preferable to be planted even nearby sources of water. This Albizia Gummifera is suitable to be planted in the  altitude of 1500-1600 m with rainfall up to 1040 mm, the conditions that are similar to what is being experienced at Usambara Mountains and in Lushoto at large. Each Kilogram of Albizia Gummifera comprises of 9,000 seeds and produces about 6,750 trees per each tree nursery.The duration needed to serve for the tree nursery takes about 4-6 months to be ready for planting procedure to start.

ENGLISH VERSION BELOW

Agroforst ist die Kombination aus Landwirtschaft und Forstwirtschaft. Gleichzeitig können ökologische Lebensmittel (Getreide, Kartoffeln, Gemüse, Obst) produziert und die Umwelt mit ihrer Flora und Fauna sowie die natürlichen Ressourcen geschützt werden. Bei dieser Landnutzungsmethode stehen Ackerkulturen zusammen mit Bäumen und Sträuchern auf derselben Fläche. Durch die Anwendung der Agroforstmethode wird der Atmosphäre viel CO2 entzogen, da die Bäume Kohlenstoff in ihren Stämmen, Ästen und Wurzeln speichern. Zudem begünstigen Bäume mit ihren tiefen Wurzeln den Wasserkreislauf und schützen die Böden vor Abschwemmung. Zudem reichern sie den Boden mit fruchtbaren Nährstoffen an, welche wiederum den Anbaukulturen zugutekommen. 

Agroforstsysteme haben über ihre Ökosystemdienstleistungen eine günstige Wirkung auf die Umwelt. Warum wendet man sie dann so selten an? Mit der grünen Revolution kamen Traktor, Kunstdünger und Insektenvertilgungsmittel. In der Folge wurden die Äcker größer und die Bodenfruchtbarkeit wurde künstlich erreicht. Die Pestizide vernichteten aber nicht nur Schädlinge, sondern auch Nützlinge und Bestäuber. Ein Großteil der Landwirtschaft erzeugt auf diese Art billige Lebensmittel. Die Folgekosten für den Verlust der Bodenfruchtbarkeit, für die Wasserverunreinigung, für die Zerstörung der Biodiversität und unsere Gesundheit erscheinen nicht in der Bilanz. Insbesondere heute ist es angesichts der Gefahr neuartiger Pandemien wichtig, neue Wege der Lebensmittelproduktion zu erforschen und einzuschlagen.
Das Agroforst-Projekt im Hochtal von Cochabamba in Bolivien untersucht, welche Baumarten und Feldfrüchte sich gegenseitig unterstützen. Die Bäume auf dem Feld (Obstgehölze, Begleitbäume mit Ammenfunktion und Edelholzbäume) sind in Reihen gepflanzt, die soweit auseinander stehen, dass dazwischen mit tierischer Zugkraft oder maschinell Ackerkulturen angelegt werden können, wie Mais, Kartoffeln, Kürbis, Bohnen und Tomaten. Die Begleitbäume schützen das artenreiche Produktionssystem vor Hitze, Trockenheit, Starkregen und Schädlingen, lockern den Boden, erhöhen die Bodenfruchtbarkeit und verbessern seine Wasserspeicherfähigkeit. Die Obstgehölze stellen eine alternative Einkommensquelle für die bäuerliche Familie dar und die Edelholzbäume sind eine Investition in die Zukunft. Das Gesamtkonzept und die Bodenverbesserung sollen auch unter Klimaveränderungen für sichere Ernteerträge sorgen, wodurch die Migration bäuerlicher Familien unterbleibt. 
Das Pflanzen der Bäume ist aufwändig. Zuerst einmal müssen die Bäume zum Überleben in dem hiesigen Höhenklima (2.600 M.ü.N.N.) einen guten Wurzelbalg haben, denn nur dieser gewährleistet, dass sie in der langen Trockenzeit genügend Wasser aufnehmen können. Zudem wird aus demselben Grund jedes Pflanzloch mit Kompost angereichert. In den ersten Jahren wird eine Bewässerung der Baumreihen unumgänglich sein. Die Obstgehölze benötigen ihren Erziehungsschnitt, die Edelhölzer müssen regelmäßig aufgeastet und die Ammenbäume heruntergeschnitten werden. All das erklärt die relativ hohen Kosten von 6,50 € pro gepflanztem Baum.
Der Projektstandort befindet sich im Tal von Cochabamba, in der Nähe des Tunari-Nationalparks, dessen Hänge im vergangenen Jahrhundert abgeholzt worden sind. Die dortigen kleinbäuerlichen Familien leben von der traditionellen Subsistenzlandwirtschaft auf kleinen Ackerflächen und etwas Vieh. Weidedruck an den Hängen hat zu Bergrutschen und Bodenerosion geführt, deshalb sind Armut und Mangelernährung verbreitet. Die Klimaveränderungen mit Wetterextremen und langen Trockenzeiten verschärfen das Problem der Bodenerosion und den Mangel von Beregnungswasser derart, dass mancherorts die landwirtschaftliche Nutzung unmöglich geworden ist. Diese prekäre Lage gefährdet auch die Umwelt und die natürlichen Ressourcen. Es ist dringend erforderlich nach einer Lösung dieser Problematik zu forschen. Die Kombination von Nutz- und Begleitpflanzen in ein und derselben Parzelle eröffnet eine Alternative. Sie bietet auch eine Reihe von Umweltdienstleistungen, die in Zeiten des Klimawechsels sehr wichtig sind. 
In Mollesnejta wird seit mehr als 20 Jahren mit Agroforst experimentiert und die Ergebnisse über NGOs mit Kleinbäuerinnen und Kleinbauern in der Region umgesetzt. Es konnte gezeigt werden, dass die Anwendung von Agroforst die lokale Biodiversität sogar an ökologisch sehr geschwächten Standorten wiederaufleben lässt, die Bodenfruchtbarkeit sich signifikant verbessert und die Bodenwasserspeicherfähigkeit zunimmt. Durch die agroforstliche Anwendung können Bauernfamilien auf vorher sehr ausgedörrten Flächen viele Produkte ohne den Einsatz von Agrochemie ernten. 
Für den Erhalt des Ökosystems der andinen Täler ist eine zügige Ausweitung der agroforstlich produzierenden Flächen wichtig, damit die Zerstörung der letzten Land- und Wasserressourcen gestoppt werden. Aufgrund der bisherigen Ergebnisse werden heimische Baumarten und von der lokalen Bevölkerung erwünschte Obstgehölze mit der traditionellen Fruchtfolge von Ackerkulturen kombiniert. Mollesnejta, mit langer Erfahrung und breitem Wissen im Bereich Agroforst, wird die Projektleitung vor Ort innehaben, so die Pflanzvorbereitung, das Auspflanzen und die Pflege der Agroforstparzellen. 

Agroforestry is one way to increase carbon stocks in the landscape while also providing local people with some immediate benefits from harvesting of crop plants. This increases the incentives for enriching the land with long-lived plants. Yet, in many situations, we still need to find out, which types of trees and agricultural crop plants can be best combined. Hence, the aim of this project is to identify which combination of trees and edible plants facilitate forest restoration while at the same time meliorating the soil in order to ensure its productivity in times of climate change to avoid migration of local farmers. 
The location of the project is on the property of the Mollesnejta research farm in a semiarid Valley of the Bolivian Andes, located nearby the Tunari National Park, which was completely deforested in the 1960s.  The farmers in the Park live on subsistence agriculture. They keep cattle and cultivate crops with traditional farming methods but the yields are low. Malnutrition and poverty are widespread. Reasons for the low yields are that deforestation and overgrazing in the past has caused extreme soil erosion and landslides. In addition, intensive agriculture and the increasing exposure to extreme weather events due to global warming make farming almost impossible in some locations. All these factors put this unique environment and all the people who depend on it in an extremely precarious situation, and there is an urgent need to find approaches to counteract this environmental crisis.
Agroforestry, the combination of trees and crops in the same area, is an effective solution to this problem because this type of land-use can provide many ecosystem services. Therefore, agroforestry is considered a promising tool for restoring landscapes in face of climate change. For more than 20 years, experiments with agroforestry have been carried out in Mollesnejta and the experiences have been passed on to NGOs and small farmers from the regions. Previous results from Mollesnejta show clearly substantial benefits for native biodiversity and that even on extremely degraded sites, the conditions of the soil have improved considerably when managing the land through agroforestry. As a result of this, agroforestry allows farmers to achieve sustainable production and hence higher income on formerly degraded sites. We will plant native trees and other edible crop species (Date Palms, Apples, Indian Figs) that are preferred by the local community. 
Planting the seedlings is complex. First of all, in order to survive in the local high altitude climate (2,600 m.a.s.l.), the trees must have a good root bellows, because only this ensures that they can absorb enough water during the long dry season. In addition, for the same reason, each planting hole is enriched with compost. In the first years, watering the rows of trees will be unavoidable. The fruit and timber trees will need regular pruning and the nurse trees will need to be cut down. All this explains the relatively high cost of 6.50 € per planted tree. Due to their established experience with agroforestry systems in the region, Mollesnejta will be responsible for the actual management of this project including all planting, site preparation and maintenance activities.

proj_e6qpdjxOeLOi6N3DjeZzXSb1.description:
The Northern east Tanzania covers an isolated major part of the Eastern Arc and coastal ecosystems where thousands of endemic species dock.  Life opportunities are limited to rainfall overdependence agriculture, fishing, Charcoal making and lumbering. The current falling agricultural produce sprang charcoal and illegal lumbering leading to extinction of hundreds of species (The IUCN global red list). Researchers conclude extreme poverty and hunger to have largely geared such destructive activities. 
The trees to be raised will be from 20 well studied indigenous species to restore lost biodiversity and stabilize species richness in scratched natural forests and rivers of Amani forest reserve, Pangani river, Zigi river and Muuzi river.

proj_qQzDtPqBg5P1YUtKMpnKSmwW.description:
The biggest lagoon in Taiwan locates in Taijiang National Park. Owing to the rather stable living environment compared to Taiwan Strait, Qigu lagoon provides the habitat for over 200 species of marine creatures and migratory birds. 3 of the species are classified as “CR“, 4 classified as “EN“, and 12 classified as “VU“ by IUCN. Rhizophora stylosa, the precoius specie of mangrove can also be seen in the area. Moreover, 60% of the population of endangered species “Black-faced spoonbill“ migrates to the Qigu lagoon and the nearby fish farming ponds in winter. Local fishermen made use of this natural resource to farm fish and oysters, giving rise to a unique aquaculture industry. 
Due to climate change and sea level rise in recent years, the barrier island of this largest lagoon in Taiwan have been disappearing rapidly. If the barrier island disappears, the lagoon ecology will collapse, and its precious and rich biodiversity will also cease to exist. Therefore, Taijiang National Park invites TOAF(our organisation) to plant trees along the shore of the barrier island. Aiming to stabilize the sandbank, fix the sand, and improve the terrain, the afforestation project includes: 1. newly planted windbreaks, 2. renewal of the existing degraded forest, 3. increase in the number and density of mangroves.

properties.name: Taijiang National Park Barrier Island
properties.description:
As an island with around 1,500 km of coastline, Taiwan needs coastal forests to preserve its environmental integrity, such as protection against damages caused by strong winds, salt spray, shifting sands, and typhoons, as well as prevention of fog.  By planting seedlings, Tse-Xin Organic Agriculture Foundation, the Forestry Bureau, and enterprises work to establish coastal forests.  

Along the coastline, it is critical to protect seedlings from strong winds with fences to ensure better survival and growth. 

By using self-watering planters, we can meet the needs of growing plants such as continuous irrigation,  moderate soil temperature, and humidity.  Therefore, seedling survival is greater than 90% and growth rate is twice those of seedlings without self-watering planters.

We renew aging forests of coastal Taiwan which are in decline by planting a variety of native species that increases biodiversity instead of exotic plant species.

Learn more by contacting Ms. Li-Yi Cheng at  ly.cheng@toaf.org.tw

Aerobic Tree Planting Empowerment Foundation, where we are dedicated to addressing the pressing challenges facing our environment today. 
We emphasise empowering young people, college students, and women in communities to spearhead the restoration of our environment through tree planting. 
Deforestation and environmental degradation profoundly impact ecosystems, food production, health, and livelihoods. In our communities, there is a need to revive the culture of tree planting to prevent severe consequences for our planet. Our foundation firmly believes that tree planting is a solution and a blueprint for addressing these pressing issues. We can lead the path towards a healthier Earth and a sustainable future by encouraging and advocating for tree-planting endeavours. 
We emphasise empowering young people, college students, and women in communities to spearhead the restoration of our environment through tree planting. 

Mission Statement
To empower and mobilise communities, especially women in rural areas, to actively participate in tree-planting initiatives. We aim to restore and preserve the environment, enhance food production, improve health, and secure livelihoods through sustainable tree-planting practices.

properties.name: Safeguarding Tomorrow : Aerobic Agroforestry's Path to Sustainable Climate Action
properties.description:
Humanity, and the planet that we have the privilege to call home, is facing no shortage of problems. Climate change. Biodiversity loss. Food insecurity. Any one of these issues alone threatens life. Unfortunately, much like buses, they have come along all at once.
There is one thing that lies at the crossroads of all of our problems; Agriculture. At Aerobic we know the impact of climate change is causing, for us we must connect the lines between climate change, water scarcity, and food security. To achieve this, we initiated a programme called “Tree the Solution” The idea is to provide 500,000 tree/fruit seedlings which will be planted and fostered by the communities and schools especially area experiencing the brunt of the climate crisis like flood, erosion, water shortage, herder/farmer clashes and desertification. 
The goal will be achieved through the implementation of the following objectives:
(i) To sensitise the farming community about the linkages between food security and climate change.
(ii) To promote adoption of climate smart farming practices (regenerative agroforestry). 
(iii) To ensure availability of seedlings in commercial quantities for farmers.
(iv) Creation and maintenance of jobs, improvement in average income for families with low incomes especially women and young people.
(v) To take urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts, end poverty in all its forms, achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls, sustainably manage forests, combat desertification, halt and reverse land degradation, halt biodiversity loss.

proj_GBLXtbJ4Zpxhe7jTdkwFP2Z7.description: With 100 years of experience working with communities around the world, the International Tree Foundation has developed a community-centred approach that builds on local knowledge to increase environmental sustainability and enhance wellbeing. Our holistic approach is rooted in four key elements: education, environment, livelihoods, and capacity building. We have supported communities to grow over 5 million trees in the last ten years. This programme is working in partnership with communities in Africa to restore and protect forests and degraded landscapes, improve fragile ecosystems and transform livelihoods through planting trees. Planting trees will improve communities’ access to these vital resources and protects ancient woodlands against deforestation. Through the planting of trees on farms, known as agro-forestry, smallholder farmers will improve soil fertility and water quality which in turn increases agricultural productivity.

proj_APxvAapPEARZBTWB3fBMYCtl.description:
Planting fruit trees in the reserved areas of Handeni District's public schools in Tanzania is a wonderful initiative for several reasons. Firstly, it will providea sustainable source of nutritious fruits for the students. This can greatly enhance their diet and overall health, as fruits are rich in vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants.

Secondly, planting fruit trees can serve as an educational tool for the students. They willa sustainable source of nutritious food for the students. Fruit trees such as mango, avocado, and orange can thrive in the local climate and soil conditions, ensuring a bountiful harvest. This will not only improve the students' diets but also contribute to their overall health and well-being.

In addition to the nutritional benefits, planting fruit trees in school areas will also serve as an educational tool. Students can learn about the importance of trees, the process of planting and caring for them, and the value of environmental conservation. It will instill a sense of responsibility towards nature and foster a connection with the environment.

Furthermore, the presence of fruit trees will create a beautiful and inviting atmosphere within the school premises. Green and lush surroundings will uplift the overall aesthetics and provide a peaceful environment for students to learn and play.

To make this initiative a success, it is crucial to involve the students, teachers, and community members. The school administration can organize tree planting events and workshops to educate everyone about the benefits and proper care of fruit trees. Local agricultural experts can also provide guidance on the appropriate tree species and cultivation techniques.

By planting fruit trees in the reserved areas of public schools in Handeni District, Tanzania, we can nourish the minds and bodies of our students while creating a greener and more sustainable future.

proj_h3Yx0ZOVm11bac9cqUAhRHoC.description:
The Lower Rio Grande Valley (LRGV) is the fertile delta for the Rio Grande River, combining climate, vegetation and wildlife to create an ecosystem that supports a diversity of wildlife and plants, including threatened and endangered species and creates one of America’s biodiversity hotspots. The ecosystem’s future depends on thornforests, which have been so aggressively cleared for agriculture and development that less than 10 percent of the original forest remains. Since 1997, American Forests has supported the planting of more than 2 million trees over 4,266 acres in the region. American Forests has partnered with Salesforce to reforest the La Sal del Rey tract of the South Texas Refuge Complex by planting 20,000 trees in the Fall of 2020 and Spring of 2021. This tract was identified as one of the highest priorities primarily due to its importance to connecting corridors for the endangered ocelot.

Final Update: We planted the majority of these trees at the Sal del Rey tract in spring 2020 with help from an Americorps crew. La Sal del Rey is a recently acquired sorghum field that is valuable to restore given its proximity to intact thornforest parcels and the Laguna Atascosa Wildlife Refuge, which has a breeding ocelot population. Shortly after planting, we received a record-breaking 10-14 inches of rain and after only four months the seedlings were already growing out of their protective tubes – something we’ve never seen before. The plantings were guided by our Drought Resiliency Strategy, and our program has since grown to include seed collection and restoring land outside of federal refuges.

proj_cVpKWdkq5nM31NfQ5Yn9pXMY.description:
More than 90% of Madagascar's original forests have been destroyed, displacing entire animal species and limiting the Malagasy's ability to farm and live on the land. With financial support from Salesforce, Eden Reforestation Projects is producing, planting, and protecting 2 million trees in Ankarafantsika National Park and 8 million mangrove trees in the Betsiboka River Estuary. Between both sites, the project will employ 200+ full-time and seasonal workers who receive a fair wage to produce and plant trees, patrol, and fight forest fires.


The Betsiboka River's estuaries were once surrounded by mangrove forests that created various habitats for unique plant and animal species.   Local Malagasy people relied on the fish and shellfish living in these ecosystems for sustainable food sources. Unfortunately, nearly a century of logging of these mangroves has resulted in massive deforestation, and exceptionally high erosion rates as the mangroves' deep root systems are vital for stabilizing the coastline and reducing erosion. With the mangroves' loss, bright red soil from the hillsides washes into the streams and rivers that lead to the coast. The sediment is filling and clogging the coastal waterways, with devastating consequences for animal life and local villagers' livelihoods.


Through our partnership with Salesforce, Eden Reforestation Projects will hire local people to plant 8 million trees at the Nosy Lageur site. The planting team will work to restore their environment while lifting the local community out of extreme poverty.

proj_35JZ2XEV2TOaq7mvQCmr1UPC.description:
Nepal is a diverse nation with magnificent snowcapped mountains to the north and hot tropical planes to the south and contains dramatic and varied landscapes and spectacular wildlife. Chitwan National Park alone hosts more than 700 species of wildlife, including leopards and the elusive Bengal tiger. It is also home to various cultures united by their close relationship with nature that has remained insulated from much of the socioeconomic development enjoyed in urban regions yet subject to far greater environmental hazards, perpetuating high inequality levels. Eden began its Nepal Reforestation Project in 2014 to help improve local livelihoods and restore forests in areas of critical importance. The planting sites are located around Community Forests from the mountainous regions to the lowland alluvial plains and around Chitwan National Park to develop a buffer zone around this national biodiversity treasure. 

Pokhara Site Description

In 2019 Eden launched a new reforestation site in the Kaski District in the City of Pokhara in Central Nepal. The project consists of several planting sites within the city limits covering approximately 300 hectares. The project aims to support local communities and bring back the forest in this scenic high-elevation city that is the gateway to the Great Himalaya Range. 
The Kaski District occupies 2017 sq Km, of which 41% is covered with forest, and harbors the richest biodiversity in Nepal. The elevation ranges from 450m (1,476 ft) to the towering Himalayan Mountains reaching 8,091m (26,545 ft). It is the region with one of the highest precipitation rates in the country (about 3350 mm/year) and a seasonal climate with summer temperatures averaging between 25 and 35 °C and winter temperatures ranging from - 2 to 15 °C.  
Pokhara hosts a population of 402,995 and is the second-largest city in terms of population in Nepal after Kathmandu. It is a major tourist destination for domestic and international tourists, mainly for adventure tourism and mountaineers seeking to explore the Great Himalaya Range. It is also known as the 'City of Lakes' because of the nine lakes found in its valley. These lakes and their abundant wetlands have recognized internationally because they host to a wide variety of globally threatened migratory birds and mammals.

proj_D9BS3eY1Y9yxdR5vZ45MXw1b.description:
THE AREA
The Taunus is a mountain range in the center of Germany, located north of Frankfurt. 

THE CHALLENGE
As in many other areas, heat, storm damage and the bark beetle have caused some terrible damage to the Taunus forests in the past years. More than a million trees have been lost and need to be replaced by new ones able to cope with the changing climatic conditions.
The biggest challenge, however, is the necessary change of awareness for the many roles of the forest beyond the function as timber provider.

THE ANSWER
The WaldLiebe is an officially recognized nonprofit organization (“Gemeinnütziger Verein”) and meets these challenges as a holistic multidimensional project for the future of our native forest.
It is absolutely neutral regarding politics, religion and special interest groups and led by an elected board.
It works very closely with the local authorities representing the community as owner of the forest but remains strictly independent of any influence on its decision making.

WaldLiebe is based on the close integration of its members, individual citizens, associations, schools & daycare centers, businesses and the Neu-Anspach city administration for a common goal.
It organizes many different activities like tree planting and protection, establishing a new tree nursery unique to the region, renaturation of water sources, an art hiking trail, tree sculptures, bee trees and other activities to provide active help and protection for the forest and to increase awareness for the many different functions of the forest.
The project continues to develop dynamically and has developed into an integration point for the local population.
Activities are led by forest and marketing professionals and supported by scientific advisors.
proj_D9BS3eY1Y9yxdR5vZ45MXw1b.longTermPlan: In Anbetracht der Natur des Waldschutzes und der Zeit, die Bäume brauchen, um zu wachsen, wurde WaldLiebe als ein Projekt mit einer Laufzeit von mindestens 50 Jahren konzipiert und eingerichtet. Langfristige Projekte zur Sicherung eines nachhaltigen Erfolgs sind: - Wiederaufforstung und Umgestaltung des Waldes zu einem nachhaltigen Wald für zukünftige klimatische Bedingungen. - Wissenschaftliche Projekte in Zusammenarbeit mit Universitäten, lokalen Experten, Praktikanten und Studenten. - Projekte zur Wasserrückhaltung und -bewirtschaftung im Wald - Begleitende Veranstaltungen und Aktivitäten, um die Integration zu fördern und das Bewusstsein für den Wald zu stärken
proj_D9BS3eY1Y9yxdR5vZ45MXw1b.mainChallenge: Das Projekt ist sehr gut organisiert und findet in den Medien große Beachtung. Es ist sehr schnell gewachsen und genießt einen hohen Bekanntheitsgrad. Die größte Herausforderung besteht darin, finanzielle Unterstützung zu erhalten, und wir hoffen, dass Plant for the planet einige Spenden sammeln wird, um die Bepflanzungsinitiative zu beschleunigen.

proj_ElCfC9yOt8MhROUL4El5dWcc.description:
The Daintree lowland rainforest in far north Queensland of Australia is a global biodiversity hotspot and is oldest continually surviving rainforests on Earth. Estimated to have existed continuously for ~110 million years. The greater Daintree rainforest is home to plant diversity unparalleled in Australia. As you walk through the Daintree you will see ferns and flowers representing every stage of plant and flower evolution. 

Deforestation for rural residential development and cattle farming has severely fragmented this ancient ecosystem leaving gaps in the rainforest canopy and damaging essential habitat for endangered species. 

We are in partnership with Jabalbina Yalanji Aboriginal Corporation who represent the Indigenous people of the Daintree and surrounding areas. We partner with them to plant trees and to support the interests of the Indigenous people of this area. 

The site, in the middle of the Daintree was deforested for animal agriculture (cattle). The site is now no longer used for agriculture and is ready for reforestation. Reforesting this site will return it to rainforest. When the site is reforested and maintained the area can be included into National Parks for protection. 

Reforestation in the Daintree is geared towards closing up gaps in the canopy, expanding existing habitat, and providing additional food and habitat for the Endangered Southern Cassowary - the iconic large bird of the Daintree.

proj_Sg6hjdf9X9lXmITqfE6pAZFs.description:
The Green Schools Program  (GSP) being implemented  by Nyasemi Self Help Group in Sironga Community  in Nyamira County,Kenya  is an on-going project  initiative  whose objective  is to promote massive  trees planting  and environmental  conservation  awareness   in schools and communities. 
Through the Green  Schools Program (GSP),we will  address  the challenges  associated with  environmental  degradation  which includes: The use of unsuitable  farming  methods by local farmers ,  negative  effects of  climate change , poor solid wastes  management, soil erosion,inadequate  hygiene and  sanitation  facilities,negative  cultural  practices  which  hinders the conservation of the ecosystems ,deforestation,poor physical planning  especially  in urban  areas and prevalence of  invasive species  in our environment. 
We have prioritized targeting  schools  and communities  around them  and helping  them address:Health,water,sanitation,environmental  awareness and trees planting  issues.  We have put more emphasis  on planting  multipurpose  tree species  especially  fruit trees and  those with medicinal and ornamental  values as well as trees which  provides shades.
Under the Green  Schools Program  (GSP), we have already:  Planted over 30 000 indigenous  tree species  in 16 different  schools  locally and around the  communities, assisted 3 schools to improve their  hygiene and  sanitation  infrastructure ,planted over 1500 shade trees, planted 360 fruit trees of different  types  in schools,200 different  types of ornamental  trees  in the community and  trees for firewood.
Also, as sources of  income  for the youths and women , we have established  tree nurseries  in schools  and communities. Training  on environmental  awareness and  conservation  is also being  intensified  alongside  the promotion of  trees  planting  via our Green  Schools Program  in schools and  communities locally. 
As an organisation,we continue to  appreciate  the support  we have received  from different  stakeholders  both locally and  globally to  make  our program a success. More support is  still needed  and most welcome   to enable us reach our goal of planting  over 1000000 in the next 2-5 years period. 
You can choose to donate cash (euros 0.27 to purchase  a seedling 🌱)  or donate a live seedling  if you are near our project site.We will appreciate your   contribution for nature restoration!

proj_A3EqDd17uZ6TwSxz43j8Z71B.description:
Rural population of Uganda depends on natural forest resources for basic subsistence needs for example, over 99% of the national energy demand is met from wood fuels. Large volumes of poles and timber are also used for construction, furniture making and other manufactures. 
Characteristically, the productivity of Uganda’s natural forests is low and has all along been known to be unable to satisfy demand of the population. Hence a deliberate policy of tree planting was promulgated way back in the 1940s. 
The tree planting project will be carried out in vulnerable and natural resource-constrained communities of Rukoki sub-county, Bulembia Division, and Nyakabingo parish in Kasese district, Uganda. Various tree species are proposed to be planted and among others are fruit trees and agro forestry trees while some are proposed to be put on bare hills like pine, spruce, cedar, and many other native tree species where crops cannot be nurtured. The proposed tree species to be planted in the proposed geographical area shall be over 1000000 trees of different tree species either nurtured by local communities from nursery beds or bought from external sources with the theme of GREENING AND CONSERVING FOR THE FUTURE 
The project shall majorly be implemented in 4 vulnerable communities of Nyakabingo, Bulembia, Kabughabugha and Kibonderya and is to benefit over 300 households from each village thus targeting 1500 households all together involving five (5) school communities and five (5) church communities from the above communities mainly focusing on greening and restoring at least 40% of the degraded bare hills adjacent to mount Rwenzori National Park that are associated with serious soil erosion, landslides, drought and other local areas that have mainly been affected with climate change effects
In here, 4 to 6 woodlots are projected to be the initial long term output with other associated ecological benefits. The objective of the project is to increase tree cover in vulnerable and resource-constrained communities due to climate change and this will help rural communities drive towards achieving two sustainable development goals (SDGs) No.13 and No. 15, thus to say *taking urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts* and protecting, restoring and promoting sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems, sustainably manage forests and combat desertification.

properties.description:
Rural population of Uganda depends on natural forest resources for basic subsistence needs for example, over 99% of the national energy demand is met from wood fuels. Large volumes of poles and timber are also used for construction, furniture making and other manufactures. 
Characteristically, the productivity of Uganda’s natural forests is low and has all along been known to be unable to satisfy demand of the population. Hence a deliberate policy of tree planting was promulgated way back in the 1940s.
During data, information collection and the subsequent stakeholder consultations, participants overwhelmingly identified the problem of land and forest degradation as a principal factor causing poverty. This project is a response to this environmental complex problem and aims at empowering the vulnerable communities to produce planting materials of tree species of their choice and grow them to meet demands for forest products and services that would enhance their livelihood other than destroying natural forests. 
Reference (Climate change, Uganda National Adaptation Programmes of Action,pg 52, 2nd paragraph).
The tree planting project will be carried out in vulnerable and natural resource-constrained communities of Rukoki sub-county, Bulembia Division, and Nyakabingo parish in Kasese district, Uganda. Various tree species are proposed to be planted and among others are fruit trees and agro forestry trees while some are proposed to be put on bare hills like pine, spruce, cedar, and many other native tree species where crops cannot be nurtured. The proposed tree species to be planted in the proposed geographical area shall be over 250,000 seedlings of different tree species either nurtured by local communities from nursery beds or bought from external sources with the theme of GREENING AND CONSERVING FOR THE FUTURE 
The project shall majorly be implemented in 5 vulnerable communities of Nyakabingo, Bulembia, Kabughabugha, Kibolhu and Kibonderya and is to benefit over 300 households from each village thus targeting 1500 households all together involving five (5) school communities and five (5) church communities from the above communities mainly focusing on greening and restoring at least 40% of the degraded bare hills adjacent to mount Rwenzori National Park that are associated with serious soil erosion, landslides, drought and other local areas that have mainly been affected with climate change effects. Different stakeholders shall be involved and some are natural resource constrained rural communities who are the primary users of the biodiversity, implementing Rwenzori Rural Health Service Community staff, local government at district level and local leaders. The project is estimated to last for a period of five years.
In here, 4 to 6 woodlots are projected to be the initial long term output with other associated ecological benefits. The objective of the project is to increase tree cover in vulnerable and resource-constrained communities due to climate change and this will help rural communities drive towards achieving two sustainable development goals (SDGs) No.13 and No. 15, thus to say *taking urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts* and protecting, restoring and promoting sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems, sustainably manage forests and combat desertification.
To achieve this, various activities will be involved and among others are sensitization and training, baseline surveys to identify constrains to tree growing in target communities, develop and promote growing of suitable high value trees, promote community involvement in planning, monitoring and evaluation, promote energy saving technologies and alternative energy sources, promote marketing and develop seedling production, field tours, community trainings and setting up demonstrations at local levels.
 Summarily, it is observed that the drivers to climate change were being caused by human activities and socio economic conditions in which people live which lead to tree felling reducing the green cover, draining wetlands for cultivation, and poor farming practices and these need to be reduced through re-greening the landscapes that are affected. As a result, this will increase various opportunities in exploiting planted tree species for alternative resources for poverty alleviation.

proj_XZfs0Uc9SDdnO1ZzIyni55cs.description:
TROFACO is a Denmark-based non-profit climate action enterprise planting trees in Cambodia and Uganda. The project was started by development consultants with decades of experience in community development and agroforestry. 

In Minziiro TROFACO works with a strong, visionary group of organised farmers called Kigazi Tukwatirewamu Forest Group. They own a huge area of rolling hills that used to be filled with trees, but are now barren due to deforestation. Last year alone they planted 30,000 trees!

The forest group decides which species of trees to plant, and they also decide where they are planted. As they have a say in the project, they are invested in it, and therefore take particular care of the trees. 

The project is based on a contract with the community, co-signed by local authorities and by our NGO partner. Our NGO partner visits the site frequently in order to talk to community and check the trees. TROFACO will visit at least once per year and take documentation pictures. These pictures will be uploaded to our website with GPS coordinates. 30% percent of the amount donated to this project will be set aside in a separate fund that will distribute the funds to the forest group over the next 20 years. 

So, we are proud to provide real benefits to the community and surviving trees for the climate and our globe.

proj_WpxQ3gwHsnHjf27bU54X0zbO.description:
Planting trees in Flanders (Belgium) with Natuurpunt	

Who is Natuurpunt?
Natuurpunt is a Flemish NGO dedicated to nature conservation for more than half a century. We specialise in creating and managing nature reserves. We manage 26.000 ha of nature in Flanders at this moment. To do this we can count on several professional field teams and on many thousands of volunteers, who make out the very heart of our organisation. We organise courses, field trips, walks; we study nature and gather scientific information; we give nature a voice when talking to local and national politicians and other organisations.
We have gathered a lot of experience in what we do. The government and even the European Commission see us as a reliable partner. They grant us subsidies and projects.
123.000 families are member of our organization and pay an annual contribution to support our work. 

Urgency
Forests everywhere in the world are having a difficult time. Flanders is the less wooded region in Europe. Only 11% of our region is wooded. The existing woods are getting smaller and less biodiverse.
That is a problem because woods can play an important part in tackling climate change. They capture carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, retain water and regulate temperature. 
That is why Natuurpunt has made the commitment to create 700 ha of woods in Flanders by 2024. That means 1.750.000 trees! Half of it will be planted, the other half will be natural regeneration.

Quality forests
We do not want the plant trees, but woods. A wood is ecosystem with a diversity of plants and animals. We choose the right trees and plants for the right soils. That is where our knowhow on ecology comes in handy. We choose plants that are typical for our region, not exotic plants. Our woods are open for everybody to enjoy them for walking, cycling, sporting, soft recreation, …

Planting trees
In order to realise our goals we have set up a Fund ‘Woods for everyone.’ In that fund we collect donations and contributions from individuals and companies or organisations. With those financial means and the government grants we can buy terrains and plant trees. We always try to own the land on which we plant so we can guarantee that the new wood will always stay a wood. We also take care of the wood in the year following the planting. 
We ask for the necessary authorisations, we order the correct trees and then we organise a planting day. We invite people to come and help us with the planting: neighbours, volunteers, donors, schools, youth organisations, companies, …

proj_8sONCwHESNzSLdPGiFmQE8Bk.description: According to the IUCN Red List of threatened species, as of 2020 one third of all lemur species, a type of primate found only in Madagascar, are critically endangered. The driving force behind lemur population declines is habitat loss and fragmentation. Planet Madagascar’s forest regeneration project focuses on increasing lemur habitat connectivity by cultivating and planting new trees between forest fragments to create corridors. We hire and train local community members to build and manage nurseries and plant seedlings. Our forest restoration project also serves to empower local women in the community by supporting community members in creating a women's cooperative called Tontolo Maitso. We purchase many of our seeds from this cooperative, and the women are engaged in nursery work. Community members benefit via a salary-based program, and we have trained 107 community members on forest restoration planting techniques thus far. In the long-term, we aim to fill 2,500 ha of deforested land, connecting forest fragments. To date, we have planted over 60,000 trees with an initial average survival rate of over 91%. However, because of the nature of planting tropical dry forest within hot/dry environments we expect survivorship in the medium and longer term to be much lower. Thus, it is imperative that we plant as many trees as possible. For our project, it costs approximately $2.50 USD to plant one tree. This price considers all costs for running our reforestation project, including employee salaries, organizational overhead, nursery and planting supplies, equipment maintenance, travel, and capacity building. Our restoration project has created the beginnings of a conservation economy, which empowers both women and men in the communities where we work.

proj_sgFVCzkFf9b0HMqxRAoI38Lp.description: London Borough of Tower Hamlets is one of the most densely populated areas of London. At the time of the 2011 Census, 69% of the ward population were black & minority ethnic groups (BME). Bromley South has very few open spaces and parks, and the importance of improving Furze Green cannot be underestimated. Furze Green, which is already surrounded on all sides by multi-story residential properties, will also see the construction of a new primary school, two new housing developments, and the extension of a secondary school. This project looks to improve the visual amenity for Furze Green, create a healthier and happier climate, increase canopy cover and biodiversity as well as use of the park by residents. The project includes consultation of local residents on the planting of 250 whips in an urban micro-forest whilst engaging 5 local school groups in the planting of the trees. These trees will complement other planting that Trees for Cities has done, be well maintained and be a valuable resource for an increasingly densely populated area. Salesforce employees in the area will also be engaged in planting the trees.

This project restores and protects 640 hectares of highly degraded mangrove forest within Kilifi County in Kenya. With the help of project partners COBEC (Community Based Environmental Conservation) and the local community, SeaTrees will support the planting of over 775,000 mangrove trees at our new project site in Kenya.

- 40% of jobs are held by women

- Increased access to healthcare and food

- Provides training to the local villagers who will manage mangrove nurseries

- Protection of local communities from storm surges and sea-level rise

proj_Rn1A8KSeZmsxekhCL1jyKLcM.description:
Ancient rainforest, waterfalls, crystal clear crater lakes, and home to Tree Kangaroos and Cassowaries. When you explore the Atherton Tablelands you notice that between lush rainforest patches lies long stretches of paddocks and grazing land. In the past 200 years there has been extensive clearing of the lowlands transforming the area from dense rainforest to savannah, fragmented remnants of rainforest, and expanses of agricultural land for animal production. 

Currently the amount of native vegetation remaining in the Atherton Tablelands is 41–49 per cent of its former size. The majority of this is broken up into small fragments, disconnected from one another and creating challenges for wildlife to pass between fragments.

A key aim of this project is to expand wildlife corridors for connectivity between forest fragments. Connectivity includes the implementation of wildlife corridors of trees that connect fragmented forest. Animals use these wildlife corridors as crossing bare paddocks or through urban areas is highly risky. Connectivity provides access to new and varied habitat and improves the genetic dispersal and variation in previously isolated populations.

proj_rcvxw70YfVmPJiVnhw37iy9n.description:
The Corridors for Life project simultaneously addresses CLIMATE change, support local COMMUNITIES and conserve BIODIVERSITY. Carefully designed, the project aims at: a) restoring large areas in private lands to promote connectivity between forest fragments and protected areas in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest; b) promoting the occupation of the restored and connected areas by the local fauna; c) promoting the change in land use practices of small and largescale farmers in rural fragmented areas; d) improving small farmers’ livelihoods and; e) providing investors a return in the form of high-quality carbon offsets.

Nature-based solutions projects are an essential part of the required strategy to address climate change. They constitute sustainable and economically viable alternative, often more cost effective in the long term than technology investments or the construction and maintenance of infrastructures (IUCN, 2020). Nature-based solutions involve three types of actions, which may be combined at regional and local level: 1) preserving the integrity and good ecological status of ecosystems; 2) improving sustainable management of ecosystems used by human activities; 3) restoring degraded ecosystems or creating ecosystems.

Plant for the Forest donations are strategic in helping IPÊ to continue and consolidating conservation strategies that represent Nature Based Solutions (NBS) within a “productive landscapes” for large landowner’s and sustainable livelihood alternatives for small settlers in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest. Tree planting will lead to replication of good practices and policies, complying with the Brazilian National Forest Code and biodiversity conservation. This project fits with IPÊ’s integrated action model, developed through years of experience, that combines research, environmental education, habitat restoration, community involvement with sustainable development, landscape conservation and policymaking. Also, is in line with IPÊs mission that is to “develop and disseminate innovative models for biodiversity conservation that promote socio-economic benefits through science, education and sustainable business”.

proj_VjRLsu9uBdGlCuvdB7VUaMeH.degradationCause: Severe infestation by invasive alien plants – over 25% of the area is invaded; over 50 species of invasive plants have been found. Also, arguably, eucalyptus plantations using too much water. Little maintenance of plantation areas.
proj_VjRLsu9uBdGlCuvdB7VUaMeH.description:
We work in a degraded remnant of eastern mistbelt forest, an endangered vegetation type, in KwaZulu-Natal – an area that falls into the Maputaland-Pondoland-Albany Biodiversity Hotspot. 
Ferncliffe is still home to large mammals and a rich variety of birds and invertebrates. It is severely infested with alien vegetation, including creepers, which are killing even large canopy trees. The project aims to steadily thin and remove alien vegetation, and plant indigenous trees (10 or more different species specific to the area) to aid restoration and increase biodiversity. Clear-cutting invasives is not undertaken as shade is vital as a temporary canopy for young trees. Constant follow-up is required to keep the invasives under control. We try to plant older saplings, and water and protect them from browsers until established. We are the “Slow Food” equivalent of restoration projects: very much on site, committed to change over time! This is very labour-intensive, but unemployment is over 34% in South Africa, and we want to create decent work opportunities that pay more than minimum wage. This, as well as the older trees planted to up the survival rate and all that alien clearing, makes our trees a little more expensive. We also enable natural regeneration and rewilding in cleared areas, and work with other local organisations to advocate for the long-term protection and conservation of the forest. We are developing a nursery, and in the interim support local, independent nurseries that grow the plants we require. In the future, we aim to grow medicinal plants used for traditional medicine to help reduce pressure on sensitive areas such as Ferncliffe.

proj_zlEj4pfcjaux7XVOH2gUvUXU.description:
The Leuser Ecosystem (LE) in Sumatra spans across Aceh province and North Sumatra province. In Aceh, The LE covers an area of 2.2 million hectares that stretches across 13 districts of the province. This ecosystem is teeming with biodiversity and natural resources. Unfortunately, it is also facing numerous threats of exploitation and inappropriate development that could destroy the ecosystem services that support life and livelihood. In most cases, women and indigenous groups become some of the most marginalized, vulnerable, and worst affected groups that bear the biggest brunt of development inequality. Yet, despite multitude of problems and systemic discrimination, women in local communities have organically engaged in efforts to protect Leuser and the ecosystems that serve as life-support for them and their families. This project supports their movement at the grassroot level in protecting their land.

Key components of the project include: 
●	Assist the community in identifying and mapping their ecological threat and biodiversity
●	Engage stakeholders to strengthen women existing initiatives to protect and manage their land
●	Forum Group Discussion using River of Life and Feminist Participatory Action Research (FPAR) method to design conservation efforts based on local-wisdom and community characteristics
●	Assist the establishment of local community group that focuses on the protection of the ecosystem
●	Assist in the establishment of community patrol team
●	Support the local community in developing economic alternatives to forest encroachment that instead align with conservation efforts.
In designing this project, we utilize the strategic approach laid out by the joint and collaborative work plan developed amongst multiple NGO working in Leuser. This strategic plan is based on the principle of ecological justice with recognition of the local context in its application.

proj_2DvPGB3vj6HiPRjer3hqYYst.description:
The Guanacas Reserve is home to key species such as the puma, oncilla and ocelot, more than 150 bird species, 130 species of orchids, as well as endangered species such as Magnolias, the Antioquia Brush-Finch and the Antioquia Chocolate Frog among many others.
We aim to restore the habitat and natural dynamics of our wildlife by planting native trees in strategic sites within the Guanacas Reserve to promote connectivity between patches of forests that were isolated by agricultural and livestock practices.
Our rangers are people from the community who lead the whole planting process, they collect the seeds of native trees in the forest patches and propagate them in nurseries, then they plant the seedlings and apply organic fertilizer. Two maintenances are carried out during the year in order to reduce competition with herbaceous plants and promote growth.
We seek to restore harmony in man's relationship with nature, so we promote planting days with people from the community and visitors from nearby urban areas in order to generate environmental awareness and education.
¡Help us protect the forest and its inhabitants!

proj_EZQ1nnevs6MoIjIzjlAFjU6M.description: The goal of this project is to support long-term and large-scale conservation of selected Albertine rift (government, community, and private) forests through a public-private partnership for forest protection and management. JGI proposes protection of existing standing forests as of 2021 by enabling local communities, Private Forest Owners' Associations (PFOAs); and National Forest Authority rangers to monitor, report and facilitate law enforcement to protect forests in Budongo, Wambaya, Bugoma, and Kagombe Central Forest Reserves (CFRs) and on private and community lands in Budongo-Bugoma Corridor (BBC).  JGI recently facilitated the formation of Private Forest Owners' Associations (PFOAs); supported forest owners in surveying and registering their land; facilitated the assignment of forest management rights; trained and equipped the forest owners in sustainable forestvmanagement practices; as well as trained and equipped forest owners and NFA rangers with the tools and skills to monitor forests using mobile technologie and near-real time forest loss alerts derived from satellite imagery. The proposed project will expand this existing capacity to advance forest protection and law enforcement by local community and NFA rangers and managers. The project proposes the implementation of the following main strategies: 1.        Strengthen forest monitoring and law enforcement; and 2.        Creating a multi-stakeholder forum for planning and implementing landscape-scale activities promoting forest ecosystem conservation.  These project strategies will address the threats that contribute to forest degradation and will focus on forest clearing for agriculture and unsustainable harvesting. In dealing with these threats, the project will also address underlying problems such as increased demand for forest products (i.e., poles, timber, for construction, charcoal production; firewood for domestic use) through establishing alternatives and incentives as safety nets for the demand of forest products.

metadata.benefits: The global environmental benefits expected to accrue from the interventions to protect the Albertine Rift include: 1) Ensuring that unique species and habitats of the Albertine Rift forests are preserved; 2) Conserving an exceptionally biodiversity-rich region of Africa, with one of the highest animal and plant diversity of the continent; 3) Conserve highly endangered species relying on Albertine Rift forests for their survival; 4) Preserving forest connectivity within the northern corridor that is essential for keystone species dispersing to and from other key protected areas; and 5) Contribute to mitigating effects of climate change, through enhanced carbon sequestration.
metadata.motivation: The significant biodiversity values of the Albertine Rift Forests (high diversity and exceptionally high endemism) have been highlighted in many global and national environmental planning documents in this past decade. Globally, the Albertine Rift is acknowledged as a major center of diversity and endemism for many taxa. It ranks first out of the 119 distinct terrestrial eco-regions of continental Africa in terms of endemic species of birds, mammals, reptiles, and amphibians, and second in terms of globally threatened species. Over 50% of birds, 39% of mammals, 19% of amphibians, and 14% of reptiles and plants of mainland Africa occur in this region[1]. Accordingly, the Albertine Rift forests are recognized among the World's top 200 ecosystems of extreme global importance for biodiversity conservation. They have many values of global significance including: 1. Hosting many endemic species, across all taxa, several of which are rare;  2. A high species diversity of plants and animals;  3. A wide cultural diversity of human –forest interactions; and 4. Acting as carbon sinks and regulating climate conditions
metadata.longTermPlan: Improving the management of private forest lands, decreasing the demand for trees in national forests, long-term conservation planning, and building capacity for monitoring tree cover in the landscape and law enforcement will substantively improve the long-term protection of forest cover in the project landscape
metadata.mainChallenge: Currently, these forests face a host of threats that are leading to further fragmentation, conversion, and degradation. The primary drivers are tree clearance for farming, timber, and fuel/wood. In biodiversity terms, these forests are relic patches of a once continuous forest cover in western Uganda. According to the Ministry of Water and Environment (2016), the increasing impact of settlement, cultivation, logging, and fire has led to an estimated drop of 24% forest cover of the total land area of Uganda in 1990 to 9% in 2015. In terms of acreage a total of 3.05 million hectares were lost in a span of 25 years. The biggest loss of forest cover is from the privately-owned category where 88% of healthy Tropical High Forests (THFs), 80% of degraded THFs, and 79% of woodlands were lost between 1990 and 2015[1].  While gazettement of forests does reduce encroachment and conversion, the continued conversion of unreserved forest patches to other land uses is further increasing fragmentation and increasing pressure on the reserved forest.    Protection of the relic forests is a priority for the conservation of biodiversity in the Albertine Rift, and in meeting of the objectives of the National Forestry Authority, i.e. "An integrated forest sector that achieves sustainable increases in economic, social and environmental benefits from forests and trees by all the people of Uganda, especially the poor and vulnerable".

proj_qJifVeiquX8oPPdXbT7DdiJO.description:
GreenAgain Madagascar is restoring damaged rainforest reserves in Madagascar. Our approach to restoration is specific to the ecology of this region. We are scientists conducting experiments to find the most successful methods of reforestation, working with communities every step of the way. Our team of staff are local farmers dedicated to long-term commitment in assisting the recovery of an ecosystem. 
Ambodihazomamy is the location of one site where GreenAgain Madagascar has trained and employed several members of the community to plant native trees locally on privately owned land.  The original forest on this land was lost mainly to agriculture and charcoal production. The community is gaining collective interest in restoring it. After gaining the skills and knowledge while training at our EcoSchool, staff are now independently constructing a nursery of native trees and office for data analysis.
proj_qJifVeiquX8oPPdXbT7DdiJO.mainChallenge: Invasive species outcompete the natives and strip the soil of nutrients. These non-Malagasy trees grow fast and decompose slowly which alters the soil and leaves it unfavorable to native species. Their dried leaves cover forest floors, encouraging fires to spread rapidly across the land.

proj_D4vq9sQe6HCxhRFv6qJpdKpq.description:
One of the most pressing issues in modern times is climate change, or the amount of carbon in the atmosphere contributing to global warming.

And through decades of chemical-industrial farming, our soil is completely deprived of carbon, which is one of the main ingredients of a healthy and sustainable soil.

Experts calculate that the soil can absorb more than 10 times as much carbon dioxide as oceans, forests and plants combined. If we treat it right. And this is our vision.

Our community organization is based in Surin (Isaan), one of the poorest regions of Thailand, where agriculture is the backbone of society. 

There are thousands of small family farms, incentivized by government subsidies,  chemical companies and banks to grow monoculture, mostly rice. 

Through modern organic agroforestry, or regenerative no-till farming, we offer locals an alternative to chemical-industrial farming.

Our modern fruit plantations, ones certified with organic- and fair-trade labels, will provide farmers with additional income. 

We do not, however, encourage or incentivize farmers to discontinue rice farming,  which of course provides an important service to society.  And we will never plant our trees on 100% of an individual's land, to ensure that rice production is not interrupted.

Our organization not only donate trees to farmers, but we also help with soil regeneration, and provide techniques and procedures to increase yield. 

As a agricultural cooperative, we act as the intermediary or wholesaler to ensure farmers receive a fair price for their products. 

We also envision to open a small market in our village, providing our partners with the opportunity to sell their fruits directly to customers within our region.

proj_5mla3wsSbiceybDkUrKF1Wef.description:
Deforestation has long been an issue for Madagascar as it is one of the world's top biodiversity conservation priorities because of its high concentration of endemic species and extreme rates of habitat loss. In the coastal zone, mangrove deforestation results in destabilizing the coastline and increasing coastal communities' vulnerability to storms and other weather events that are becoming more frequent and intense as a result of human-induced climate change. In upland dry deciduous forests, deforestation threatens one of the world's rarest and most diverse forest systems. In response to the large-scale loss of mangroves and upland forests in Madagascar, Eden initiated the Madagascar Reforestation Project in 2007 and has now successfully planted over 200 million mangroves and dry deciduous trees. Eden Reforestation Projects works collaboratively with many different communities with full support from national, local and tribal governments to reforest large areas of mangrove and dry deciduous forests and the coast and inland areas. Eden will provide training and financial support to the local community to collect mangrove propagules and strategically plant millions of trees in coastal mangrove systems and upland dry deciduous forests that have been heavily degraded or deforested.

Akalamboro Site Description

This restoration area is located on a lowland mangrove forest along the Akalamboro Estuary surrounding the Akalamboro community in northwest Madagascar. The northern edge of this estuary is part of the
Baie de Baly National Park. Before starting the project, the mangrove forests found in this area were severely impacted by deforestation and forest degradation from charcoal production and wood collection for cooking, construction, and other purposes. This mangrove forest is important because it is a deep-water canal that meets up with an extensive, freshwater river system. This makes it a vital nursery for numerous fish species, abundant Nile crocodile (Crocodylus
niloticus), and multiple bird species, including the endangered Madagascar sacred ibis (Threskiornis bernieri). It provides habitat for the critically-endangered giant sawfish (Pristis pristis), once prolific in these estuaries. The mangrove forest runs adjacent to a fragmented dry deciduous forest with many healthy patches. The grey mouse lemur (Microcebus murinus) is commonly seen at night and during the day. Van der Decken’s sifakas (Propithecus deckenii) are regularly seen jumping through the mangrove and dry deciduous forests.

We initially collected general donations within a single project for different countries, and now we have separated our projects into one project for each nation!

Eden will provide training and financial support to the local community to collect mangrove propagules and strategically plant millions of trees in coastal mangrove systems and upland dry deciduous forests that have been heavily degraded or deforested.

Antsanitia Mangrove Site Description

This is a vital mangrove estuary that needs long-term protection and restoration. The project site is located along the northwest coast of Madagascar, 15 miles north of the regional capital of Mahajanga. 

The project area has a deep-water mangrove estuary that opens to the sea surrounded by large mangrove forest swaths. It is abundant in giant barracuda, mangrove snapper, jacks, trevally, grouper, stingrays, and other fish varieties. It is also an essential fishery for shrimp, crab, and shellfish and provides habitat to various birdlife.  

Charcoal producers and tree poachers have targeted the mangrove channel and forest beyond. Over the last ten years, these threats have had a tremendous impact on the mangrove forest, and it is dwindling quickly. 

Both the government and local Malagasy communities are opposed to the charcoal production and illegal wood harvesting and support the long-term conservation and restoration of these sites. Eden's initial reforestation activities empower the community to protect what is left of the old-growth and while reforesting areas where mangroves have been lost.

proj_StWEs2TGZFPf1WgfT6IJQoLC.description: Over 80% of Kenya’s mangrove forests have disappeared. If conserved and restored, mangroves provide a highly productive natural carbon sink, storing up to 4 times more carbon than a tropical rainforest. They also protect coastal communities from storm surges and provide a vital habitat for fish. Working with two local community groups, the project is restoring the mangroves and creating bee-keeping programs so the communities can sell the lucrative mangrove honey, which is medicinal and in high demand. The community group manages the mangrove nurseries before they begin planting, using 3 species of mangroves (Rhizophora mucronata, Ceriops tagal, Avicennia marina) which are well-adapted to the local environment and chosen because of their high survival rates.

proj_iS4tktbXYmiwI2vq2iqWbViX.description:
A Tiny Paradise: A Fruit Tree Garden and safe clean water for one village.

For a donation of 295€ (here: please select exactly 1 "trees") you finance the installation of a Wells for Zoë - pump in a village and the planting of 10 indigenous or typical fruit trees surrounding the well.

A Tiny Paradise: Fruits and water for children without "lunch money" on their way to school.

A Tiny Paradise: Women often walk miles and miles for clean water and carry heavy buckets back to their homes, several times a day. Reducing these walkways while additionally increasing the water safety opens opportunities to start a business and thereby this donation is also a push for gender equality.

We provide safe clean water for about 700,000 Malawians in rural areas since 2005 and nearly 2000 pumps are already GPS-mapped (maps.wellsforzoe.org).
All pump donors can share a phrase which will be inscribed into a ceramic tile at the pump, e.g. Happy Birthday dear Papa. If you wish to do so, please forward your donation confirmation for this donation to info@wellsforzoe.org and send us a message which phrase you would like us to inscribe (4-6 words, space is limited on a tile).

After the installation (normally takes 14-21 days) and the planting of the trees you will receive an email with a link to your pump (see here for an example: https://wellsforzoe.org/pump-installation/2526/).

Please make sure to also send us a message even if you don't want to inscribe a message as we have otherwise no means of contacting you due to data-protection-regulations.

This is also great as a birthday-gift for people who already have more than they could possibly need...

proj_vNIY8JgkxRtWu6K1S6kuK7Qa.description:
The Caribbean Tree Planting Project (CTPP) aims to plant one (1) million trees across at least ten (10) countries/territories in the Caribbean between January 2020 and June 2021. Through international, regional and national collaboration, the CTPP will not only ensure that trees are planted, but will also encourage public engagement in other activities centered around climate action. Components of the project will include encouraging farmers to engage in climate-smart agriculture and commissioning campaigns targeted towards the general public and behavioural change into making more climate-conscious decisions. 
The project is a youth-led initiative to mobilize partnerships across the private, public, and philanthropic sectors in order to achieve the UN's Sustainable Development Goals. More specifically, activities will address SDGs 13 - Climate Action & 15 - Life on Land. The three (3) core objectives of the project are:
1.	To plant at least one (1) million trees and engage the general public in related climate actions across at least 10 Caribbean countries;
2.	Promote Caribbean Youth and Caribbean Diaspora activism around climate change;
3.	Highlight the significance of multi-stakeholder partnerships and collaborative actions, especially among philanthropists, required to accelerate achievement of SDGs.
The CTPP is coordinated by the Caribbean Philanthropic Alliance in collaboration with several individuals and organizations including the Clinton Global Initiative (CGI), the Trees That Feed Foundation (TTF), Jamaica Diaspora Taskforce Action Network (JDTAN), Jamaica Institute of Environmental Professionals (JIEP), International Telecommunication Union (ITU), Caribbean Girls Hack, Media Institute of the Caribbean, CARICOM Youth Ambassadors, Sandals Foundation, Grace Kennedy Foundation and LASCO Chin Foundation. 
With the latest collaboration of the Smallholder Farmers Alliance, together with Timberland and other sponsors, and their commitment to plant 25 million trees in Haiti over five (5) years, it is expected that the CTPP will exceed its projected one (1) million target by 2021.
proj_vNIY8JgkxRtWu6K1S6kuK7Qa.name: Caribbean Tree Planting Project  (CTPP)

proj_QU4TNMgPdBqH7Y1wikSQ3Cd4.description:
Western Australia is recognised internationally as a global biodiversity hotspot with rich flora & fauna and unique species. Unfortunately there is an extreme level of threat in the form of historical land clearing for agriculture and ongoing land degradation. Land degradation impacts biodiversity, landscape functionality and ultimately, food production in Western Australia. It has also caused disastrous impacts on the Aboriginal Noongar community. This community was once removed from country, breaking a 65,000+ years of cultural identity and cultural connection to country which supplied food, shelter, clothing and medicines. 

Through this project, you are supporting the people of the Noongar community that have become active land managers. Commonland works in partnership with the Noongar land managers and Greening Australia. In 2008, the first plantings included Sandalwood, host species and biodiverse planting (to stabilize extreme erosion) on 170 hectares. From 2014 to 2018, biodiverse restoration took place on 300 hectares. In 2020, there is potential to plant 160.000 trees! Help us achieve this goal and restore country in Western Australia.
