proj_mD2EAJmhfgm3gsux56izjdGA.description:
This project includes the plantation of 85000 trees for Irula Tribes in Tamil Nadu, India. The Irular tribes, also known as Adivasis or Indigenous people, are some of the earliest settlers in the Indian subcontinent and have made contributions to its culture, history, heritage, and ecosystem. Unfortunately, they have become refugees in their own land and victims of dominant cultural hegemony, human rights violations and development displacement. The Irular tribes are semi-nomadic and settled as a landless and voiceless community in this region. Irulas are an aboriginal ethnic group and they mainly inhabit the parts of Nilgiri mountains and coastal plains in southern India. They are classified as a 'Scheduled tribe', and their population is estimated to being about 189,621 in Tamil Nadu.

Traditionally, the main occupation of the Irulars has been snake and rat-catching. They also work as labourers in the fields of landlords during the sowing and harvesting seasons or in the rice mills. However, after the implementation of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, capturing snakes was prohibited in India. This has led the Irular families to permanently perform labour works, where they kept as bonded labour for long periods with inconsistent pay and low access to sufficient food.

Even though the irular's population is high in the identified project area, they are considered backward in terms of economic and educational advancement. The plantation project aims at engaging the irular communities in implementing on-ground activities which in turn will create job opportunities for the locals. An additional source of income will support their vulnerable economy while also bringing multi-faceted ecological advantages like enhanced carbon sequestration potential, improved greenery and wildlife habitats, increased food, fuel, fruits and flowers, and improved groundwater level.

proj_7gmlF7Q8aL65V7j7AG9NW8Yy.description:
This project represents a socially and technologically based climate corridor project in south-eastern Costa Rica. It will connect Highland forest, Lowland Rainforest, Mangrove wetlands and Coral reef and sea grasses.

In total One Tree Planted will be supporting the planting of 348,000 trees in the following areas:

-Highland forest : Talamanca Mountain Range in the AmistOsa Biological Corridor (San Vito area)

-Lowland rainforest: Riparian areas within the corridor connecting La Amistad International Peace Park, Piedras Blancas National Park, and Corcovado National Park.

-Mangrove: Terraba Sierpe National Wetlands.

Conserving such elevation gradients can also provide the best opportunity to provide local and regional micro climate refugia (areas for species to survive outside of their regular distributions) – such features will be critical for  the survival of species in a rapidly shifting climate. This is especially important as Southern Costa Rica arguably hosts the two most important sites for conservation in Central America: the Osa Peninsula (home to approximately half of the country’s 500,000 species) located on the Pacific coast and La Amistad National Park, the largest remaining forest in central America encompassed within the rugged Talamanca mountain range.
proj_7gmlF7Q8aL65V7j7AG9NW8Yy.longTermPlan: Create 2 biological corridors connecting the Amistad National Park and the coastal ecosystem of the Osa region.

proj_LbegUSF08Keuw0gMR5SdK3vu.description:
The Bulindi Chimpanzee & Community Project (BCCP) is a grassroots conservation initiative dedicated to conserving critically threatened wild chimpanzees and promoting environmental conservation throughout the 1000 km2 mosaic landscape between the Budongo and Bugoma Forest Reserves in western Uganda. This region is known as the ‘Budongo-Bugoma corridor’ (BBC) and is recognized by the IUCN as a ‘Chimpanzee Conservation Unit’, owing to its 300+ chimpanzees living on private land. Since the 1990s, most unprotected forest throughout BBC was cleared by landowners for farming, negatively impacting climate, water and biodiversity, including the endangered chimpanzees.
BCCP’s mission is to:
(i) Conserve wild chimpanzees living in unprotected habitat in the BBC, and restore and enrich habitats for chimpanzees and other wildlife;
(i) Support local residents to develop livelihood alternatives to deforestation and increase their capacity to engage in environmental conservation, replant forests, and accommodate chimpanzees in their environment.
Since 2017, BCCP has raised over 4.5 million trees in our tree nurseries for planting by over 3000 landowners in 300+ villages. Our experienced and qualified team or foresters and agriculturalists provide training to farmers, and carry out land checks, evaluation and long-term follow up. 
Our goal for 2022-2025 is to raise 3,750,000 seedlings to ensure 3 million surviving trees (target: 75% survival), comprising 3 kinds of seedlings: 2,500,000 indigenous forest species for restoration, enrichment, and shade in agroforestry; 625,000 fast-growing species for woodlots, providing residents with an alternative wood source (reducing dependence on natural forest for energy, construction and timber sales, allowing natural regeneration); and 625,000 high-quality coffee as an environmentally-friendly alternative livelihood, further enhancing local capacity for conservation.

properties.description: This project aims to significantly reduce threats via restoration and conservation of chimpanzee habitat in key areas in the Hoima corridor, with development of long-term alternatives to deforestation. It directly addresses root causes: need for alternative livelihoods and wood for cooking and timber. Enrichment planting: indigenous fruit/timber trees. This planting programme complements our other project activities such as daily long-term monitoring of chimpanzees within the corridor. The Bulindi Chimpanzee & Community Project is tax deductible in Uganda!

proj_zD0ka2pSTr202yEj6SQFAzxF.degradationCause: Charcoal burning, lumbering and seasonal bush burning
proj_zD0ka2pSTr202yEj6SQFAzxF.description:
The restoration of the burnt Tarawe forest reserve in Handeni District, Tanzania is a crucial undertaking. After the devastating fire that swept through the area,efforts are being made to restore the forest to its former glory. The burnt Tarawe forest reserve was home to a diverse range of plant and animal species, and its destruction had a severe impact on the local ecosystem.

In order to restore the forestefforts have been made to bring life back to the Tarawe forest reserve. The first step in the restoration process is to assess the extent of the damage and identify the areas that require immediate attention.

Local communities, along with government and non-governmental organizations, have come together to replant trees and restore the ecosystem. They have organized tree planting campaigns, involving community members of all ages, to ensure that the forest reserve regains its lush greenery.

Additionally, measures are being taken to prevent future wildfires, such as creating firebreaks and educating the local population about the importance of fire safety and prevention. This includes teaching them about controlled burning practices and the dangers of uncontrolled fires.

The restoration efforts also focus on habitat restoration for wildlife that may have been affected by the fire. This involves creating suitable environments for animals to thrive, such as installing nesting boxes and setting up feeding stations.

The restoration of the burnt Tarawe forest reserve in Handeni District is a long-term commitment, requiring ongoing monitoring and maintenance. However, with the dedication of the local communities and the support of organizations, it is possible to rejuvenate this vital ecosystem and protect it for future generations.

proj_R4CZdfML0w5D46JUdTh3qNgU.description:
The Mangkutub-Project is a joint reforestation project of BOS Schweiz and the BOS Foundation restoring 50 ha (with a potential up to 971 ha) of burned valuable peatland in Central-Kalimantan, Indonesia. 

The expected climate effect is huge because tropical peatland stores up to 20 times more carbon than non-peat mineral soils. In addition, the rainforests of Borneo, Indonesia belongs to the most biodiverse forests of the world. The Mawas area even sustains one of the largest remaining orangutan populations with an estimated 2550 orangutans inhabiting the forest!

The main focus of the Mawas Program is the protection of wild orangutan habitat and forest restoration by involving the local communities. This includes - apart from the reforestation - the blocking of drainage-canals, the protection from wildfires and the creation of sustainable livelihoods for the local communities. 

The main goal of the project is to ensure the sustainable management of the Mawas area as a peatland orangutan habitat with high conservation value, together with the local communities and other stakeholders as well as the provision of environmental and economic benefits for the surrounding community.

The price for 1 tree (7.65 CHF) includes 1.) the collection of seeds in the area, 2.) the production of the seedling itself (in project-owned tree nurseries), 3.) the planting of the seedling and 4.) 5 years of care (including the removal of seedlings that die) by local communities.

Donations to BOS Schweiz are tax deductible in Switzerland and elsewhere (depending on your tax system)!

proj_nua2hRfsSaBgf3rSG151u9hD.degradationCause: Clearing of forests and wetlands for cattle rearing
proj_nua2hRfsSaBgf3rSG151u9hD.description: For over four years, FBC and its allies have been building capacity and supporting the local fishermen community of Barbacoas with a  tree nursery and forest restoration. The aim is to provide a source of income through nature conservation to improve their livelihoods. In 2020, FBC expanded its El Silencio Natural Reserve to a former cattle ranching area that neighbors the community. The aim of this project is to raise funds for the community to provide tree seedlings and pay for labor to restore cattle pastures in two areas: 1) the border of the main stream in the area in order to improve habitat for water and terrestrial animals, and where the community can carry out community-based ecotourism; and 2) the basin of a deep well where the community pumps out their household water through a solar system that our foundation supported building in 2019. Restoring the forest cover of the basin would ensure water provision for the future and improve the community's resilience to climate change.
proj_nua2hRfsSaBgf3rSG151u9hD.mainChallenge: Our main focus for 2021-2022 is to use active reforestation to make vital wildlife corridors and use passive restoration to reach up to 13,000 trees planted.

proj_1y4M0K04UnCHkUc3u1W31ZDJ.description:
The 5MTrees initiative’s goal is to plant 5 million trees before the year 2030, this program also involves the removal of Alien Invasive vegetation. This program will help towards achieving South Africa’s AFR100 and Global Sustainable goals commitments.

The 5MTrees project is defined by its threefold nature of the following sequential objectives:
- The removal of alien invasive vegetation 
- The planting of indigenous vegetation to increase tree and bush cover 
- The care and maintenance of the planted vegetation in its vulnerable growth period.
This approach type has enabled LLB to zone in on Land Degradation Neutrality(LDN) and Forest Landscape Restoration (FLR) activities. The 5MTrees is more than just planting trees, as illustrated by the relationships of SDG 15 as central to achieving the other number of goals and sub goals of other SDG’s. Goal 15 promotes sustainable use of land, smart and resilient agriculture and efficient use of resources. Our project brings in to play other key interventions such as food security and
climate action, all in the pursuit of resilient communities in our vulnerable areas.

proj_qHXqiZND9hSkmVWZTRJD2uzi.degradationCause: Urban green infrastructure is unequally distributed across income and race geographies in South Africa, and Thembisa is no exception. Spatial inequalities are mirrored in both public and private green space. Green space inequity has been maintained and entrenched since Apartheid.
proj_qHXqiZND9hSkmVWZTRJD2uzi.description: Through this project, our planting partner will collaborate with 10  schools in Johannesburg to establish 10 indigenous urban forests at the schools. We aim to provide learners, educators and community members with the knowledge and practical horticulture skills required to plan, establish, maintain and extend urban greening . The programme also encourages ecological awareness, environmental responsibility and economic empowerment for the school, community and cultivates future green leaders. The core of the project is to establish a centralized, school-based tree nursery that will grow trees for the 10 schools. Partnering organizations will mentor the students, from teaching them to identify plants, passing on horticultural skills and assisting with urban forest, to general exposure in the horticultural industry.

metadata.motivation: This project aims to address the multiple needs of the youth's environmental needs which enable them to access opportunities for employment, income generation, horticultural skills development and personal development while contributing to the reconstruction of their green spaces in Johannesburg.
metadata.mainChallenge: Setting up tree production nurseries that grow indigenous trees creates jobs and entrepreneurial opportunities for communities, especially among youth. As Johannesburg is the largest emitter of fossil fuels on the continent, this project is critical to the health and wellbeing of the community.

proj_nNyQoc7XC4hxrJlJLyvr4j6Z.description:
Often eclipsed by the better-known forests of the Amazon Basin, the Atlantic Forest is an equally important part of Brazil’s heritage, Rio’s source of clean water, and the planet’s biodiversity. Notably ranking among the world’s great forests, the Atlantic Forest of Brazil harbors exceptional numbers of plant and animal species.

Sixty percent of Brazil’s endangered species are found in the Atlantic Forest. In total, there are 24,000 species of plants, mammals, birds, and amphibians, and reptiles, of which 9,500 species exist nowhere else on earth. Importantly, there are also countless more unknown to science.

What remains of the once great Atlantic Forest of Brazil is a patchwork of remnants that are the last refuge for some of the greatest wealth of biodiversity on the planet.  As the forest continues to dwindle, the increasingly stranded species have been called “the living dead” by Brazilian conservationist Antonio Rossano Mendes Ponte.

Over time, this wide-scale deforestation, Brazil’s Atlantic Forest has already lost a great deal. In fact, barely five percent of the original forest cover remains today.  Consequently, this tropical forest, its rich biodiversity, and its ecosystem services are among the most imperiled on the planet. 

We are working with local partners to restore this important place for biodiversity and the local community.

proj_LZ3573Pl6ZGjsusKr9F8ZkVi.description:
In the dry summer of 2018, embers from a coal locomotive drifted into a cluster of pine trees near the mountain town of Durango, Colorado, and ignited one of the largest fires in state history. The 416 Fire burned 54,000 acres in the San Juan National Forest, killing multiple ‘Champion Trees’ and scorching the Hermosa Creek watershed – home to a rare strain of Colorado River cutthroat trout. American Forests and Salesforce are working with the US Forest Service to replant 300 acres around the beloved Hermosa Creek campground and trailhead, in areas where the fire burned so hot that it killed all adult, seed bearing trees. This part of the forest is perfect for re-growing record-breaking trees because of the area’s fertile soil, moist air and protection from hot, dry weather.

Final update: We approach fire scar restoration holistically, and in the 416 that meant coordinating large-scale front country plantings completed by professional crews and community volunteers, more focused plantings in the headwaters with the Southwest Conservation Corps and Forest Service hydrology team, protecting natural springs with fencing, as well as post-fire regeneration research with the local university.

proj_Ly4lVzw50r6hJtocv74al9Ps.description: Doñana Natural Park is one of Spain's most emblematic biodiversity hot spots and one of the most important protected natural areas in Europe. A crucial hub for migratory birds travelling between Africa and Europe and the last refuge for numerous endangered species. In 2017 a fire caused vast damage to almost 10.000 ha of forest  lands. Over several project phases Plant-for-the-Planet is restoring affected areas in collaboration with local authorities to help the flora and fauna recover. The first project phase aims to restore 431ha with 65.000 new trees until the end of 2021. Doñana Reforestation is part of the project „One Million Trees for Andalusia. One Billion Trees for the Planet“. Further your contributions in our project in Doñana also support the empowerment of children, the development of the App and our worldwide campaign "Stop talking. Start planting."

proj_pli2A70F18ZrgXVB6Vz6cfYF.description:
We Ecopower International Initiative aim to put an immediate stop to the consumption of precious wood as a fuel source which is a major contributing factor for the decline of our rain forests and together socially and economically empower and liberate our indigenous populations.

We solicit and empower rural indigenous communities by way of planting trees such as endangered tropical varieties together with Castor Trees, the seeds of which are used to produce vegetable oil that is then transformed into renewable clean energy in the form of nontoxic bio-combustibles.

Rural Indigenous communities and individual families can then make their own clean renewable non-toxic energy that is reliant on the regenerative restoration and reforestation of our rain forests. The excess production generates an income that is devised via sustainable means, enabling these communities to build schools, hospitals and other social structures along with economic independence. 
The Bosawas Biosphere Reserve is one of the largest contiguous forest in Latin America. It is a rich landscape with 21 different ecosystem types and is home to 13% of known species worldwide. There are numerous rare and endangered animals like Jaguars, Giant Anteaters, Baird’s Tapir, and more than 200,000 species of insect. The reserve stretches across the Nicaraguan-Honduran border and is an integral part of the Mesoamerican Biological corridor – which connects 8 countries and provides free movement for biodiversity.

Intercropping castor bean with food production makes efficient use of land resources and acting as pioneer trees, castor grows fast and plays a vital role in providing protection during the establishment of indigenous tropical trees. Castor pioneer trees stabilize soil, improve soil aeration, prevent erosion provide organic matter/nutrients, give canopy and shade, which enables understory plants to become established.
So by empowering communities, tackling energy poverty and alleviating food insecurity, it becomes possible to kick-start the reforestation of the Bosawas reserve while laying the groundwork for a local, independent and alternative energy industry.
We would like to restore the Biosphere Bosawas back to 100% health, starting with the first 5% in 2021 and over the next 20 years restore over 600,000 hectares of destroyed rain forest with both Castor and Tropical Indigenous trees. In 2041, established the indigenous trees will be on their way to a long healthy secure life that should see the next 200 years green and alive for future generations to thrive and all natures species to endure in prevention to extinction.
Trees are the source of life. Establishing indigenous tree species will attract and retain rain clouds, produce oxygen, capture carbon monoxide and draw carbon into the soil. Reforested areas prevent soil erosion while securing water reserves and maintaining water quality. A healthy and cared-for environment will retain natural biodiversity and sustain many life forms.
Landscape restoration based on castor bean production provides biofuel an independent local energy industry. As well as the potential for marketing biofuel, bioenergy and biodegradable consumable products to an international market. This creates regenerative jobs around regenerative living.
Castor bean & intercropped food
Converting degraded land within 6 months Castor will kick start the growth for the first 5 years to allow tropical and indigenous trees to take off, thereafter the tropical trees will supersede in height and surpass the castor trees creating a micro climate and regenerating the biosphere using intelligent regenerative reforestation as our basis.

proj_kNhq21LXs0CTOm0LeU1lDZs9.degradationCause: -Until 20th century, intensive charcoal extraction wiped out 80% of the woodland vegetation . -In the 1950s, reforestation with Pinus halepensis was carried out by the public administration, causing great damage to biodiversity. -In 1978 these pine reforestations burned down and regenerated again.
proj_kNhq21LXs0CTOm0LeU1lDZs9.description:
The forests of Andalusia, Spain, are deeply degraded. 
Sierra Lujar has been punished by coal mining, then by pine monoculture reforestations and finally by a series of fires that have considerably diminished its biodiversity.

The association Semillistas works on the ecological restoration of this forest by means of methodologies of imitation of nature. We use various seed technologies (priming, pelleting and mycorrhizae) to make it possible to sow seeds directly in the forest.

As we say: "Nature doesn't plant trees, it sows seeds".

These techniques are much more respectful and economical than planting trees. In southern Spain it is difficult to use tree planting techniques with species other than pine. And these are a management problem and cause very recurrent fires. 
We need to recover the Mediterranean ecosystems with all their diversity of species. 
Our Sierra Lujar project this year will plant 20 species of trees, shrubs, bushes and lianas, as well as various types of mycorrhizal spores.  

The project will establish 20,000 plants in the winter of 2020, for which we will sow around 200,000 seeds.

We want to restore this mountain range to its former splendor.
We want the richness of its diversity to encourage the return of the shepherds.
We want to fully restore the sierra, which means introducing 4000000 trees and shrubs.

One of the great tasks in Spain is to solve the error of pine monocultures in forest areas. This, in addition to causing fires, makes traditional forms of livestock farming impossible. Livestock and Mediterranean forests are closely linked, and there is an urgent need to recover this form of forest management in rural areas.

That is why the basis of our plantations is the holm oak. The fruit of this tree, the acorn, provides food for countless wildlife, as well as for herds of goats. It also creates the conditions for the development of other plant species and mycorrhizal fungi.

If you want to know more about our project and our sowing methodology, you can stay informed by subscribing to our mailing list:

http://eepurl.com/iokamM

Thank you for your collaboration in greening the Mediterranean.
proj_kNhq21LXs0CTOm0LeU1lDZs9.longTermPlan: With the methodology that we use, the tree and shrub seeds sown do not need maintenance or watering. Therefore, no additional resources are needed for their maintenance. The trees and shrubs will carry on their grow without any human support.
proj_kNhq21LXs0CTOm0LeU1lDZs9.mainChallenge: The main challenge, without a doubt, is the climatological situation we are confronting. Our ecosystem is undergoing an accelerated process of desertification. And the uncertain conditions of rainfall and water stress make it a great challenge to carry out successful regenerations.

proj_hQTZQFNzPP2G7x66a5Vct20i.description: The Green Caravan is a programme that was launched by APN in 2003, with the aim to increase the national green cover and reverse the effects of rapid urban sprawl that has resulted in high rates of desertification. The Green Caravan primarily targets vulnerable small-holder farmers across Jordan who are at the core of the Jordanian food basket, but have fallen victim to poor economic and political conditions and a neglected agricultural sector. It seeks to reinvigorate the farming culture in Jordan, and revive the connection of local communities with their land, particularly in an effort to prevent selling off or losing fertile agricultural land to larger institutions.

One tree for charcoal is $50 for a family. So trees are cut down to make lives better. Less rain means less farming crops, so more trees are cut. 1 mature tree is $200!
proj_8SXvAl8ptT4sVwCboopW6ZEE.description:
Much of the rainforest in Haiti has been cut down over the last 50 years. Here’s how our project is restoring the forest by empowering local communities.

Our agronomist visits villages requesting reforestation and presents the importance of trees/forest to communities at churches and schools, such as:

1. Where and how to plant each kind of tree
2. What trees provide to the ecosystem and to the people… he talks a lot about bringing back the songs of birds pulling people heart strings
3. How trees build the water table and hold soil for crops
Composting
4. Companion planting with crops, shade grown crops etc.

Much of the rainforest in Haiti has been cut down over the last 50 years. Here’s how our project is restoring the forest by empowering local communities.

Our agronomist visits villages requesting reforestation and presents the importance of trees/forest to communities at churches and schools, such as:

1. Where and how to plant each kind of tree
2. What trees provide to the ecosystem and to the people… he talks a lot about bringing back the songs of birds pulling people heart strings

Composting
4. Companion planting with crops, shade grown crops etc.

proj_adZmtfmLtRDGYtTmfVyrJDNA.description:
Jeji Restoration is a tree planting initiative that works closely with indigenous communities and internally displaced people affected by war and environmental conflicts to restore degraded landscapes by planting trees as a means of livelihood development. 

Jeji Restoration was initiated to restore land through intensive afforestation strategies in agricultural and forest contexts. Its first aim is to  restore a pilot area of 500ha of indigenous lands by encouraging farmers to adopt farmer-managed natural regeneration of trees, adaptive multi paddock grazing systems, and the  planting of trees. 

While it is important that frontline communities plant trees to restore their degraded landscapes, it is also critical to engage individuals who as a result of war, climate or other forms of instability have lost their homes and livelihoods. 

The project will plant 250,000 trees which will restore 500 hectare at an average density of 500 trees per hectare. This will also provide 1,000 people (at 2 people per hectare) with income, food and shelter, 70% of which are women previously affected by war and/or environmental conflicts.

The project involves displaced people affected by war and environmental conflicts and not only members of a given community because of the significant amount of climate induced migration in Northern Nigeria that is driven by climate risks and insecurity.

proj_PWNssUQw5JmqqSWZyEZ3yvyF.description:
The Araguaia Biodiversity Corridor in Brazil, will be connecting two of the world’s most vital ecosystems: the Amazon rainforest and the Cerrado savanna.

By planting native trees on a massive scale: restoring 1 million hectares by planting 1.7 billion native trees, we will bring back biodiversity and directly fight the climate crisis.

We know we set ourselves an extremely ambitious goal. That is why we proceed in well-planned steps to complete this 30-year mission. We are now operating in our 5th planting season, completing the first million native trees by 2024. The coming years we will scale-up towards 10 million native trees, restoring 6000 hectares by 2028.

We are currently focussed in the region of Santana do Araguaia (Pará Sate) and Caseara (Tocantins), but as we complete the 2600 km corridor we will move north or south alongside the corridor. 

JOIN OUR COMMUNITY AND BECOME PART OF ONE OF THE LARGEST REFORESTATION PROJECTS ON EARTH!

proj_xg4KhtMod9t1eL4gL8yDRx70.description:
Burundi is experiencing an alarming deterioration of its environment due to significant demographic pressure in a country where most of the population lives off agriculture.                                                                                                                                       This results in overexploitation of land, soil degradation, destruction of protected areas and deforestation. 
Wood is the main source of domestic energy with 96.6% of the overall energy balance, and 77% of charcoal is consumed by the urban population. The Burundian research conducted a reflection on this phenomenon estimate the consumption at 104,718 tons of charcoal for the urban population alone. This consumption, especially by the population of Gitega and Bujumbura, leads to an annual loss of 3,505 to 4,673 ha of forest cover, i.e. annually between 5,236 to 6,980 ha if we extrapolate these figures to the entire urban population of the Burundi. At this rate, Burundi's forest cover, estimated at 171,625 ha, could disappear in 25 to 33 years. (Http://akeza.net/au-burundi-les-foretspourrait-disparaitre-dici-25-a -33-years-because-of-charcoal-consumption/) 
With a view to sustainably preserving the environment, sectoral policies (environmental code, land code, water code, etc.) as well as national action plans for adaptation to climate change have been developed by national authorities. However, the country's environmental situation remains critical and alarming, especially since the vast majority of young people have not yet been won over by the spirit of protection and preservation of the environment. 
For most young people, climate change sounds like a western and distant problem, although its effects are already being disastrously felt, notably with the rising waters of Lake Tanganyika and the Rusizi which has disrupted life in the area of Gatumba (2020) with displaced populations, houses submerged under water, etc. On the other hand, the floods in Gatunguru (north of Bujumbura) which have plagued the country on numerous occasions over the past 3 years. Coming from the mountains overlooking the city, the rain waters, descend the slopes without obstacles (the mountains are deforested), carrying large stones and mud in their path. 
These issues are garnering both national and attention. Greening Burundi, being among organizations which are mobilizing for the protection of the environment, has already taken actions in this direction. These themes are therefore the subject of this offer, which aims to help strengthen environmental protection, the fight against climate change but also the fight against the spread of Covid-19. As part of this proposal, we will organize activities aimed at raising awareness on a large scale as well as a practical involvement of farmers, young people, schooled in particular (tree planting, waste sorting, recycling, awareness sessions). 
Climate change is underway and we have suffered consequences.                                                                                                Indeed, following the deforestation of forests, our soil becomes gradually infertile.                                                        As a result, the agricultural sector, which brings a lot of Burundians to live, is seriously damaged and production is almost unsatisfactory.                                                                                                                                  Poverty is lodged in households, diseases directly linked to malnutrition burst and the country becomes the first loser. Faced with these scourges, we felt challenged as young Burundian to contribute to reforestation in order to protect the environment. 
Agriculture is the main economic activity in Burundi.  It occupies more than 90% of the active population and provides 50% of the GDP. A majority of Burundians live on small-scale food crops (maize, sorghum, beans, tubers) that are grown on small farms with very low yields due to intense soil erosion and climate change.                                                                                                               In addition, the clearing of new lands causes the rapid decline of the forest, which covers only 5.6% of the country's area against 50% in 1990. There is therefore a serious problem of environmental protection. 
In addition, Burundi has been greatly affected by deforestation, through the intensive felling of trees so that farmers can meet their basic needs. This has serious consequences for the environment and agriculture, increasing the poverty of the region.  
Thus, as evidenced by these environmental indicators in BURUNDI, Greening BURUNDI was motivated and convinced to fight against these scourges by setting up tree nurseries in order to increase the forest cover by planting a large number of trees and involve community in tree planting that. Since 2019, large number trees have been planted on some mountains. 
The reforestation of Burundi via the Greening Burundi Project is a goal and expect to plant 50,000,000 trees by 2040.

proj_Oac7zpiTJE0intexvrbrNxnm.description:
The Apuí Agroforestry Coffee project is an initiative created by IDESAM in 2012 in an effort to counter the rate of deforestation in the municipality through strengthening the production chain of “agroecological coffee.”The planting of native trees combined with coffee is a sustainable alternative for income generation to contain deforestation in the municipality.

Apuí is a Brazilian municipality located in the southern region of Amazonas State, along the banks of the Trans-Amazon Highway (BR-230) – the deforestation belt of the state. The city is the second municipality with the highest deforestation rate in the state and the eighth in Brazil, mainly due to the ever-expanding livestock production, where vast areas of forest are destroyed and transformed into environmentally and socially unsustainable pastures.

To mitigate the deforestation pressure, our project promotes the intercropping of coffee trees as the agricultural species and forest species of economic and food interest. Plantations that were previously planted with coffee monoculture are combined with indigenous trees such as ipê, andiroba, jatobá, among others, and are gradually transforming the landscape of the municipality. 

The Apuí Agroforestry project has contributed to the reforestation of 33 hectares of land in the Amazonas State and increased productivity and diversification of products from local producers. The intercropping of coffee plants with native forest provides shading for the coffee plantations, which reduces exposure from the region’s intense sunshine and changes the local microclimate. These conditions help to retain moisture and to gradually build the fertility of the soil which also help to enrich the quality of the coffee and increase its productivity. Besides, native species can also be exploited economically due to the value of their products.

With this kind of approach, the planting of trees is not only restoring degraded areas, but also providing an economical alternative for local producers, who can increase their income generation while also being involved with the forest conservation. 

Idesam is not tax deductible and cannot issue donation receipts!

proj_7MLbI0nE3Fpme6CR20qulQFZ.description:
Community greening and trees growth initiative is a tree planting initiative that targets public schools, church grounds and Government trust lands for tree planting; the driving force behind these initiative is to plant trees in degraded places and restore them to their original form and in the process, contribute to the conservation of the local environment and in our small ways, contribute to carbon reduction in the atmosphere which brings global warming. Apart from helping fight the adverse effects of climate change, some of the trees planted will be a source of fruits, food, medicine, shades, firewood and timbers for the local community. The trees will also regulate the water cycle and facilitate  farming activities, promote ecosystem balance and  also contribute to the prevention of soil erosion.
Since inception of the project, we have managed to plant 3000 trees in various places locally including local schools, community land and churches. Our objective is to plant 240,000 trees in two years time and  over 800,000 to 1,500,000 trees in 6 to 10 years time.
We are currently focusing on planting trees mainly in schools and public lands with big land sizes unlike before, where we were targeting  mainly schools regardless of the land size. The reason for doing this is to maximize the impact of our trees planting through the economies of scale (large planting area is more economical compared to a small area).
As an organization, we are planting indigenous trees/species best suited in our area sourced from the local tree nurseries and suppliers.
Training on better environmental management is being done from time to time targeting  both local farmers, teachers and students in schools.
Going forward, we intend to intensify both trees planting and awareness campaigns activities on environment conservation activities and also  support as many farmers as possible, to establish more local tree nurseries to promote tree planting activities.
Also, we will support schools through students volunteers and teachers to initiate the program of planting trees especially shade trees, fruits trees and trees that beautifies the schools compound while helping to conserve the environment.
Initially, during our trees planting efforts, we had challenges sourcing tree seedlings. Pricing per seedling was pegged at Euros 2-3  to cater for the cost of buying, transporting, planting and caring for the tree; something that hindered the sourcing of more seedlings for planting and thus slowing down the planting process to reach our target of planting 240,000 trees. Another challenge that we faced was the limited awareness of local people on the need to plant indigenous trees instead of  planting exotic trees. Massive sensitization through community awareness has been done and the concept of planting local trees species has been embraced.
In our bid to mobilize the locals and schools to plant more trees, we have identified local sources of indigenous trees/seedlings who sells a seedling at a very reasonable rate( euro 0.25). Increased sensitization  on the importance  of planting  trees, increased  establishment  of tree nurseries  locally and individuals,organisations  and more people  volunteering  to plant more trees  and save our planet  have contributed  dramatically to  the cost of acquisition of a seedling  in our area.Our organisation wants to bring you on board by supporting  our trees planting initiative.

proj_4Xde51IgWMaMaUtEJdTP0Uzc.description:
The reforestation-project is one crucial component of a community-led holistic approach within the Green Heart Project (GHP), which Love for Life undertakes together with its local partner Amisacho Restauración and local communities of the Northeastern Amazon region of Ecuador. The main objectives of the GHP is i.) restoring the local Amazon Ecosystem; ii.) restoring the health of the communities; iii.) empowering communities through capacity-building and environmental education. 
The Green Heart Project is carried out in the heart of the Sucumbios and Orellana provinces of the northeastern Amazon of Ecuador, where published studies suggest that the exceptionally high population of human cancer rates in the region correlate directly to environmental pollution from perilous petroleum extraction, mining, and unsustainable agriculture methods. One of the largest oil disasters in South America left behind deforestation, severe contamination, and led to displacement of Indigenous people and their health deterioration. 
However, an important community-led movement has been forming in the upper headwaters of the Ecuadorian Amazon towards environmental and social reparations as well as self-determination. 
Since 2006, Amisacho Restauración, our local partner, has been dedicated to conservation and restoration of a jungle area isolated from the encroaching cities and deforestation practices by developing an environmental research station and training facility focused on reforestation, preservation, investigation, and education. Together with our partner, we recognize that survival of trees and environments as a whole depend on the ecological literacy and accompaniment of community members and small-holder farmers. We therefore provide not merely seedlings and a tree nursery, but grounded environmental education and capacity-building on reforestation, preservation as well as alternative methods for soil regeneration and sustainable agriculture. Together with our local partner, as well as Indigenous and local communities we will ensure that trees are maintained and monitored, therefore being able to achieve a tree survival rate of 80-90%. By caring for trees and bushes that sequester atmospheric carbon, regenerate soil ecology, provide nutrient-rich harvest, restore Amazonian habitats, we also support diverse local income streams. Amisacho Restuaración collaborates with farmers – especially women farmers – schools, municipalities, as well as with the self-founded environmental committee of the Union of affected people by the severe oil contamination (UDAPT). 
With the Green Heart Project, we provide necessary tools and skills to regenerate the health of the ecosystem and the local communities. High tree survival rates depend on the regeneration of soil ecology as well as the sustained participation of local communities and their long-term protection. In addition to planting trees, the planting-project also focuses on planting crops, cultivating mushrooms and creating habitats for the human population but also for wildlife and biodiversity protection. These habitats include natural buffer zones to protect streams, prevent soil erosion and filter water. LFL and Amisacho Restauración – with further public and private stakeholders – are engaged in co-creating a biological corridor that acts as air filter around urban & industrial contamination areas and connects biodiversity between Amazonian animals and species that are threatened with extinction.

Love for Life e.V. is tax deductible in Germany!

proj_AHwkOumVTbskpZORMfJoqgQ8.description:
The Haiti Reforestation Project restores tree cover by planting agroforestry systems that protect watersheds and improve food security. The project equips local farmers with the training, tools and trees needed to design their plots, grow, and care for their own trees, and increase the food production and biodiversity of their farms. In addition, starting in 2020, Eden will be rolling out a large-scale mangrove restoration initiative. 
In Haiti, Eden Reforestation Projects works to change the approach to growing food by introducing agroforestry systems containing a diversity of fruit and nut trees combined with those that provide timber, fuelwood, and habitat values. The program includes training local farmers to effectively cultivate land in highland regions that respond poorly to intensive agriculture and are best suited for agroforestry applications. By doing so, the Haiti Reforestation Project helps stabilize the land, increases soil fertility, and increases food production that can be sold domestically and internationally to increase household income while bringing back the natural ecological function to a highly degraded landscape.

Belanger Site Description

Eden's reforestation program in northern Haiti is located where the Noir and Massif du Nord Mountain ranges meet the Artibonite Plains of Gonaives. This is a neotropical, dry area with sparse tree cover and rugged topography.  From the 17th to the 19th century, most of the forests were cleared for logging, grazing, and agriculture. As a result, this area has been heavily impacted, and without active reforestation supports limited wildlife. The population of Gonaives is roughly 300,000.  This area suffers from extremely high rates of deforestation, drought, and poverty. 
Eden's agroforestry program is bringing this area back to life. We serve over one hundred eighty smallholder farmer families in five localities and distribute tens of thousands of seedlings annually. Eden offers farmer training, extension services, and distributes fruit trees to help locals reforest their farm plots.  Our project is creating habitat to help increase biodiversity, restore healthy soil to slow down erosion and improve food security. Eden Reforestation Projects employees partners with local farmers to plant agroforestry trees such as orange (Citrus sinensis), moringa (Moringa oleifera), mango (Mangifera indica), and cocoa (Theobroma cacao) to expand and diversify food production and improve food security for the local population.

properties.description: Plant trees | Save lives. Eden Reforestation projects reduces extreme poverty and restores healthy forests by employing local villagers to plant millions of trees every year. Learn more about the work being done and how you can help. At Eden Reforestation Projects we have a holistic approach to reforestation and ecological restoration. • Our national leaders partner with villages that are committed to restoring their forests. • We then hire and train local villagers to plant new trees. • They plant native tree species. • The villages protect their new forests because they have a vested interest in them. • Top tier seedling survival rate – over 80%. Even higher when natural generation is factored in. VILLAGES MANAGE OUR NURSERIES & PLANTING SITES: We start by hiring the local villagers to plant trees. This gives them a consistent income so they can provide for their families again. As the reforestation effort goes on, healthy forests begin to emerge, and the negative effects of deforestation begin to disappear. Since we began over 250 million trees have been planted around the world in Ethiopia, Madagascar, Nepal, Haiti, Indonesia, Mozambique. Eden Reforestation Projects is tax deductible in the US!

proj_7jHqc0ZfHVrPWkO70TJGL9pI.description:
Rocciaviva sits on 73 hectares of hilly land and is nestled in a valley located close to the rustic town of Salandra (Italy).
While the northern slopes of the hills are covered by the remaining of the ancient oak forests that gave the name to this region (Lucania = from the Latin word 'lucus', 'sacred wood'), the Southern slopes have been severely over-exploited over the centuries due to intensive agriculture and animal grazing. The agricultural exploitation degraded the soil and turned this area into barren land. The soil is left uncovered and exposed to the elements and, year after year, the summer heat and the sun are further deteriorating it. These once forest-covered and biodiverse lands are now turning into a desert where the land doesn't have the capacity to capture and store any water. 

At Rocciaviva, our group of motivated volunteers is working to prepare the land with the appropriate earthworks that will create a home for the little saplings. This will initiate perpetual land transformation with the aim of bringing the lush forest cover and biodiversity.

In addition to bringing back vegetation cover, we also aim at restoring three nearby lakes to further improve plant, insect, and animal biodiversity.

Join us and help us restore this barren region to the lush, green, biodiverse 'land of sacred woods' that it used to be centuries ago!
You can also join us as a volunteer - come plant with us! (more details here: https://www.ecosystemrestorationcommunities.org/community/rocciaviva-italy/).

proj_0A74ghLQsx842038zk8fEQC9.description:
This project, in partnership with the U.S. Forest Service and Salesforce, on the Willamette National Forest in Oregon, will reforest 670 acres of land heavily impacted by the 2017 Whitewater Fire in the North Santium Watershed, a primary tributary of the Willamette River.  A seedling mix of ~130,000 native conifers, including Douglas fir, noble fir, Ponderosa pine, white pine, and western hemlock, will be planted at irregular spacing to mimic natural regeneration. 

Planting sites are located on the NE quadrant of the Forest, which borders the Warm Springs Reservation, home to the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs. These lands and resources are subject to and managed in part for subsistence rights retained by Treaty Tribes including the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs and Confederated Tribes of Grande Ronde. 
 
A primary goal of this post-fire reforestation project is watershed restoration, as it is an important as a water source for proximate communities and for wildlife habitat, including Endangered Species Act (ESA) listed endangered spring chinook salmon and threatened winter steelhead trout. The watershed provides high-quality drinking water to communities, including Salem and Corvallis.

A secondary goal of the project is to restore visual quality. Outdoor recreation is an important economic driver in the area, providing an abundance of recreational opportunities including hiking, fishing, and camping. 

This project is part of the 50 Million for Our Forests Campaign, which was publicly launched on Earth Day 2018, with a goal to raise funds to plant 50 million native trees on our National Forests by Earth Day 2023. Every dollar donated is matched with two dollars from the U.S. Government. Through our tree-planting program, we plant native trees in priority areas in need of reforestation as a result of natural disturbance, i.e. wildfire (80%), landslides, hurricanes, wind storms. Over one million acres of our National Forests are in need of reforestation. Our goal is to have all projects completed by 2025.

We work with the U.S. Forest Service to plant trees. Trees we plant are sourced from six Forest Service tree nurseries where native tree seedlings are grown for planting on National Forests. These trees are grown from locally sourced seeds, and the nurseries serve as research centers for the agency to develop disease-resistant strains of trees.  
Seedlings are planted only when conditions are optimal, using the best available science, and monitored post planting, ensuring the highest possible survival rate.

proj_s0Dt9sivTkYLAptM2OfJSleb.degradationCause: Hauptursache ist die Trockenheit tlw. in Verbindung mit sehr hohen Temperaturen und in Folge dessen geschwächte und geschädigte Bäume ohne ausreichende Abwehrkraft gegen Insekten (Borkenkäfer) und Pilzbefall (Dyplodia).
proj_s0Dt9sivTkYLAptM2OfJSleb.description: The state of our forests is becoming increasingly critical. Climate change and monocultures are endangering our livelihoods in the long term. With our campaigns, we want to provide information and raise awareness for the forest and the environment. Our Spessart is the largest contiguous area of mixed deciduous forests in Germany and we want to keep it that way. The tree species suitable for adapting the forests to climate change should be ecologically and economically well integrated or integrable into our forests. This means that both native and alternative tree species can be used. The focus here is particularly on close relatives of native species from the European-Asian contact area. In particular, the origin of the propagation material is of decisive importance for adaptability and successful cultivation. (Excerpt from the Bavarian Forestry Administration's guideline for the selection of tree species in climate change) In practical implementation, the priority is to strengthen rare native species. The following were selected from the range of rare native tree species: Sweet chestnut, field maple, slippery elm, cherry, small-leaved lime, wild pear, Norway maple, yew, hazel, copper beech and hornbeam. The first planting campaign took place in Mainaschaff on October 30, 2021, marking the start of a great collaboration. Our next goal is now 300,000 new trees for our Spessart, Aschaffenburg, Alzenau, Mainaschaff and the surrounding area. Our biggest partner is Salesforce, together we want to plant 1 million trees in Germany by 2030 - you can find more information here: https://www.salesforce.com/de/blog/vanessa-weber-stiftung-partnerschaft/

proj_32MovMetcmr05uGEouJN0HpM.description:
This project is a community-based conservation and restoration initiative in Kenya, East Africa. The organizer works to coordinate efforts to conserve and restore the Kijabe Forest, the incredibly special forest along the eastern wall of the Great Rift Valley. The forest is small but mighty, producing water, creating soil stability, and other ecosystem services for more than 200,000 people. The organizer works to Protect this forest by working directly to conserve biodiversity and restore areas that were previously degraded. They also work with farmers in the adjacent areas to provide access to markets for non-timber forest products, alternative energies, and other livelihood diversification opportunities. 

Their restoration approach is primarily centered on two methods: fostering natural regeneration, and enrichment planting. They complete reforestation at a density of roughly 1500 stems per hectare of indigenous species, using a combination of emergent colonizers, and slower-growing, climax species.

proj_kcFeNrstIRmgN9FhHkEIfctV.description:
The Luanshya district is Zambia's most densely populated region and as a result its forests have been disappearing. Through a holistic approach that integrates livelihood development with ecological restoration, WeForest supports farmers to restore the native Miombo woodlands that are disappearing from the region. By employing assisted natural regeneration of Miombo woodlots (plots of native woodland on farms) and introducing economic activities such as bioenergy and honey production, local communities can restore their forests. The farmer population benefits from diversified jobs, higher incomes and new skills. The project establishes market linkages between small-scale farmers and local private sector companies. In addition, this project looks to aid farmers in obtaining ownership of land in order to secure the sustainability and longevity of the conservation and livelihood outcomes.

WeForest is tax deductible in the Netherlands! TGE is possible in several European countries.

proj_3cXBgeoedy3kuAtzsVC9cqy7.description:
The project is based in Nakuru and Bomet Counties that lie in the South Rift valley region in Kenya. These counties lie within the Mau Forests ecosystem that once covered large areas of both counties. The area lies within the tropical subtropical moist broad leafed forests biome and thus is marked by tropical montane forests. The two counties form important water catchment areas. Bomet County is the source of major rivers that flow to Lake Victoria while the project areas within Nakuru County are an important source of water for Lake Baringo and Lake Nakuru. The two counties have however experienced serious degradation over the years that affected local biodiversity, climatic conditions, hydrological functions, and even community livelihoods and economic activities. This degradation mainly occurred through deforestation as people cleared land for agricultural production and subsistence through unsustainable utilization of forest products. The increase in population and hence pressure on the natural resource base and land also led to negative effects including land fragmentation that aggravated degradation. The degradation and climate change through increased temperatures, reduced rainfalls, erratic rainfall patterns, increased evapotranspiration, and reduced infiltration rates, and increased population pressure and land degradation has impacted the availability and thus access to water resources. This includes effects on river streamflow’s and underground water levels.
Youth for change has been addressing this problem through repair of water infrastructure. This has mainly entailed the rehabilitation of boreholes previously sunk in the area through repair of the damaged hand pumps and other systems. However, the group realized that to address the water problem there is a need to address challenges facing the water sources through forest landscape restoration. This will entail rehabilitation of the watersheds through planting of trees in schools. The project thus target to plant 100,000 fruits and native tree seedlings in 100 schools (50 in Bomet and 50 in Nakuru) that also are target by the boreholes rehabilitation activities. The project will also support the establishment of tree nurseries in the target schools and establish and strengthen the schools environmental clubs. It also engage in awareness and capacity building on forest restoration especially through training, sensitization, and establishment of demo sites for practical learning. The projects will are designed and planned through community involvement, and the communities will also be actively involved in implementation and monitoring and evaluation of the project. It is expected that the project will contribute to improvement of the landscapes water catchment functions and water security, climate change mitigation and adaptation, improved food and nutritional security, improved awareness and knowledge and skills on forest restoration, create committed environmental stewards, and develop networks and communities of practice on forest landscape restoration, among other outcomes.

proj_3aQZi1SCNWqqmM8duObtYchF.description: ReForest Now is working to reforest cleared land that once made up Australia's largest patch of subtropical rainforest - the "Big Scrub" in northern New South Wales. 99.6% of this dense, biodiverse rainforest was cleared by early European settlers and it is now classified as a critically endangered ecological community under federal legislation. Our team does everything from seed collection, nursery, tree planting, tree maintenance and bush regeneration (removing invasive weeds). With your donations to this project, we can help bring back this magnificent forest.

proj_7OA3iSjhVGSngkNPXTvkSfHU.description:
This restauration project is critical to the communities and forests surrounding Santa Rita Coapan.  In the ejido of Coapan the people depend on their environment for much of their livelihood.  Their land is under stress from increased severity of the dry season and increases in population.  This project will restore many hectares of natural forests which will provide habitat for many animals, ensure that underground water reserves continue to be replenished and minimize soil erosion.  

The mesquite trees that we plant will also support the natural local ecosystem by providing nectar to local bees in support of honey production.  

Also, the ejido is continuing to attract ecotourism to the area and a vibrant healthy forest is important to that.  The desert surrounding this community is full of much unique flora and fauna such as cactus and as such it does attract ecotourism.  The community is keen to protect and restore this area to continue to attract visitors.

The trees will be planted by members of Donate a Tree to the World, volunteers and members of the ejido of Santa Maria Coapan.

The project involves and aids significantly the people of Santa Maria Coapan.  It includes an education program that will help give them tools and understanding so they can live more sustainably and successfully with their environment.  The people of this community will do most of the planting with our guidance.
proj_7OA3iSjhVGSngkNPXTvkSfHU.longTermPlan: We will be restoring other plots surrounding Santa Maria Coapan in the years to come. Although a lot is dependent on the results of what we plant this year, we could plant a total of 100 thousand trees (13 different species) over the course of the next several years.
proj_7OA3iSjhVGSngkNPXTvkSfHU.mainChallenge: The main challenge we have is to make sure we water the saplings during the dry season and to make sure no goats are allowed to pasture in the area.

proj_DbGBDHbePvTCUgndUcvrJodr.description:
The region of the TANDA located in the EAST zone of Ivory Coast is a region that undergoes every day the effects of climate change. The population, having little information on the behavior to adopt in the face of this global scourge accuses most often the State which, at its level is sometimes limited in its actions. It is the responsibility of NGOs to look at it and provide a lasting solution to mitigate the effects of climate change. The contribution of the NGO PAGE VERTE will be one of the biggest support that the NGOs that fight in Côte d'Ivoire in the field of the Environment try to put at the disposal of the populations. Raising the awareness of more than 30,000 people to the protection of the environment in this area and also planting 50,000 trees will be a saving action for the population as this will prevent the advance of dessert and will also produce a mild climate in reforested sites.
The general objective of the project is to develop actions aimed at Reforestation and Environmental Education in the northern area of Côte d'Ivoire, specifically in the region of TANDA.
In other words:
·       Environmental Education in Elementary and Secondary Schools in the communities of the region of TANDA,
·         Raising awareness among charcoal producers and farmers on slaughter illicit trees for the production of charcoal and agriculture in the pitches with slopes,
·         Construction of the plant production center and activities of reforestation in the Communities
This is, from the start of the project, to involve all the customary leaders, religious, civil, youth associations and any other group that exists in the area and is likely to be affected directly or indirectly by said project.
This involvement must be done by raising awareness in order to understand the merits of the project and to get every helping hand possible.

proj_7WNIZ3c4U66QRlRsR6m5z57s.description:
The main milestone of this project is the biodegradable system that we have developed, which allows not only to avoid the use of many plastics but also to generate added value to local communities. 

For years one of the main challenges in reforestation projects was the tons of plastics used. We have developed, tested, and validated a system that avoids the use of plastics and generates a sustainable source of income for the nearby local communities with the manufacturing of the biodegradable pots.

Our three pillars are:

- Ecosystems: The project is located in an area that has suffered 95% deforestation in recent years. There are two families of chimpanzees struggling because they do not have enough space and food, which forces them to have to go out to eat in the nearby plantations, generating conflicts with the locals. The project consists of recovering these degraded areas and creating forest corridors.
- Waste: The hundreds of thousands of plastic bags used for planting have always seemed a bit contradictory to us. We have found a solution that is simple but yet very effective. By using the dry banana leaves to make an organic bag. With this, we not only avoid generating all that plastic waste, but we also generate income in local communities. 
- People: An environmental recovery project cannot be understood without integrating people and looking for alternative ways so that they can earn a living from protecting nature. These sources include both the labor to plant the trees, guide tourists and scientists to see the chimpanzees and the manufacturing of the pots. Thanks to the manufacture of these pots we are employing women at risk of exclusion. Currently, the project generates sustenance for 1,500 families.

proj_vkncX8GWeV8t0FWItQyhJA2b.description:
This project, 9000 trees of which will be planted through our partnership with Salesforce and the U.S. Forest Service, is on the Lassen National Forest in California. The Eiler fire decimated once thriving true mix conifer stands of Ponderosa pines, Jeffery pines, Incense Cedars along Douglas Firs and Sugars Pines. 100 acres will be planted here. 

This project is part of the 50 Million for Our Forests Campaign, which was publicly launched on Earth Day 2018, with a goal to raise funds to plant 50 million native trees on our National Forests by Earth Day 2023. Every dollar donated is matched with two dollars from the U.S. Government. Through our tree-planting program, we plant native trees in priority areas in need of reforestation as a result of natural disturbance, i.e. wildfire (80%), landslides, hurricanes, wind storms. Over one million acres of our National Forests are in need of reforestation. Our goal is to have all projects completed by 2025.

We work with the U.S. Forest Service to plant trees. Trees we plant are sourced from six Forest Service tree nurseries where native tree seedlings are grown for planting on National Forests. These trees are grown from locally sourced seeds, and the nurseries serve as research centers for the agency to develop disease-resistant strains of trees.  
Seedlings are planted only when conditions are optimal, using the best available science, and monitored post planting, ensuring the highest possible survival rate.

proj_WmTavt6uBSBC0DYIPMFiuuM0.description:
This location is located in Kebumen Regency, Central Java Province, Indonesia. It is part of the Serayu and Opak river basin. From year to year, the push for changes in land use increases, especially in the agricultural sector, which results in massive land clearing. The challenge of daily income sources and profit orientation is one of the good potentials and obstacles we face.
We approach the community to carry out planting activities using an agroforestry system and use the Multi-Purpose Tree Species Timber Tree Conservation Pattern as well as several developments in accordance with the culture and expectations of the community who participate in our planting program. The plants in our program consist of production plants or fruit plants that have economic potential and ecological benefits that have been taken into account with the characteristics of the planting location. So that the output of planting activities received by the people who take part in our program will have a win-win solution impact economically and socially.

proj_S4D42YfYdfWTMAPYt2xzrnCL.description: Acción Andina is a long-term forest restoration and protection initaitive, currently involving 16 local implementing organizations and upwards of 40,000 people in its activities. A key component of Acción Andina is our pan-Andean forest protection plan, where we have already prioritized the most critical sites for Polylepis forest conservation across the Andes. This plan will guide restoration priorities in the coming decade, as well as help us identify the grassroots leaders and on-the-ground implementing organizations we need to support to reach our long-term goal of protecting and restoring one million hectares of high Andean, native forest ecosystems. It will also enable us to produce the ambitious, multi-year projections, plans, and budgets needed to unlock major funding resources that can sustain Acción Andina.

metadata.motivation: High Andes forests contribute to climate change resilience, particularly water and land security, as well as provide community and biodiversity benefits. No other habitat is proportionally more important for all that it influences below, yet the conservation of these forests have been largely overlooked.
metadata.longTermPlan: Acción Andina’s prime objective is to establish fully-functioning high Andean forest ecosystems in strategic landscapes across the Andes. Ongoing protection of remaining forests is essential to achieving this objective.
metadata.mainChallenge: Deforestation is one of the gravest threats to life on Earth, a driving force of global climate change, water scarcity, loss of community livelihoods, and the decline of species diversity.
metadata.actions: Protecting standing forests through the creation of legally protected areas is a process that takes approximately three years. The status of the protected area is renewed every two years. Once approved, protection measures include patrols of the area by hired guards, provision of alternative forest products or more efficient products (such as efficient cookstoves) to communities, training of guards and community members in the importance of protecting the area, and maintenance of needed vehicles and equipment for fire control and monitoring.

proj_CfACz11uytfqP3Dqao8BL39f.description:
Established in 1979 and formerly known as the Men of the Trees (WA) our mission is categorised under 4 pillars:

- ENVIRONMENT - To restore degraded land, support biodiversity, and encourage the growth of healthy tree canopies in both urban and rural settings. 
- COMMUNITY - Our mission is to bring people together to grow, plant, establish and maintain trees to achieve a healthy, and bio diverse environment. 
- CORPORATE - Individuals, communities, business and government are provided opportunities to financially support ecological restoration across WA to improve the health and sustainability of the land and grow biodiversity 
- SPIRIT - We are directed by a vision of a world in which all people recognise the value of trees and forests 

We are an organisation who are able to mobilise thousands of people across the state to focus on revegetation of WA's ancient lands, reducing the impact of climate change. Importantly we reconnect people (especially those in urban areas) with nature, and inspire a love and respect of the natural environment. 

In Western Australia the botanical diversity is incredibly high. Botanically it is in the top 10 most diverse places on the planet. But it is threatened by land clearing for agriculture, housing and recreation that can bring weed invasions, animal road deaths, habitat destruction, species extinction and climate change.

The cost per tree: €3.1 is comprised of the following:

Pre-Planting Activities
- Land acquisition/negotiation with landholder,
- Site preparation including weed & pest control, species selection, reticulation installation.
- Preparation of planting event which includes up to 160 volunteers

Planting Day
- Setting up at the planting site 
- Induction of volunteers for Occupational Safety & Health
- Training volunteers in planting procedures
- Catering
- Quality control of planting
- Packing up the tree planting activity

Post Planting Activities
- monitoring and maintaining the site for 3 years.

proj_LNkzAs25ssXd259RE2uh6vDj.description: "One student One tree and conservation Education" is a campaign launched by Loliondo Actions for Green Earth early this year 2020 with the aim of planting 50,000 trees in Ngorongoro district in Tanzania which is very close to Serengeti National park whereby every student in Ngorongoro is given a tree to plant and taking care of it, This planting trees campaign is going hand in hand with educating youths( students) on sustainable use of natural resources and environmental conservation and protection since as the matter of fact the youths are our tomorrow leaders and citizens hence imparting the conservation spirit to them is helping in saving mother Earth. This campaign aims at preparing students to take part in environmental conservation and become good conservationists but also for those who will become leaders will carry this agenda in their future leadership. proj_DlbJv5ybKOprfqt8rEMwMxN7.description:
Uganda is suffering from the rapid loss of its rainforests and is already feeling the negative effects of climate change. The reason for this is a rapidly growing population and its need for arable land and firewood.
 
The good news is that Uganda offers ideal conditions for reforestation. As part of our country program entitled "Lasting Solutions," we are taking advantage of this. We are working with many smallholder farmers and local organizations. In our so-called agroforestry approach, native tree species are planted on the same area as food crops such as beans and peanuts. Besides the future income from the wood, the smallholders can harvest them after a short time and sell them on markets. 

Through your support, seedlings can be raised in our nurseries every year, which are distributed free of charge to smallholders during the planting season. 

In so-called Farmer Field Schools, the experiences and knowledge of the smallholders are supplemented with expert forestry knowledge. In the courses, participants learn basic concepts and techniques of agroforestry and apply them practically through workshops in nature.
 
Together we can create sustainable solutions!

proj_A6VGUK6pWC3KdDLxxXiskQzW.description:
In 2015 Rainforest Rescue was approached by land-owner Annie Shoenberger to return fifteen hectares of old sugarcane fields back to thriving Daintree lowland rainforest. In 2016 and 2017 with the help of many individuals, organisations and businesses, we cultivated and started planting trees and revived a wetland area to draw in wildlife. Between 2018 and 2019 tens of thousands of trees were planted at NightWings to repair this damaged land.
Today over tens of thousands of seedlings are growing and calling this land home. By project’s end, these seedlings will be flourishing between the lowland Daintree to the upland Rainforest and beyond to the coast.

proj_s8STPZmf9dWfyd60ZVrRTc0M.description:
Ausgangssituation
Das südbrasilianische Klima ist mit seinen langen Sommern und hohen jährlichen Niederschlägen bestens für eine hochproduktive Landwirtschaft geeignet. Neben der industriellen Produktion, erzeugen brasilianische Kleinbauern dabei rund 70% der täglichen Lebensmittel des Landes. Allerdings wird auch ein Großteil der weltweit eingesetzten Agrotoxine in Brasilien verwendet. In den letzten Jahren hat sich nicht nur der ökologische Lebensmittelanbau ohne Chemie, sondern auch die Agroforsttechnik in Brasilien weit verbreitet. Trotz des generell wirtschaftlich besser entwickelten Südes des Landes, gibt es nur wenige Bauern, die dieses innovative Konzept von kombinierter Waldwirtschaft und Feldfruchtanbau nutzen.

Projektziele und -umsetzung
Die Regionalgruppe in Araranguá hat sich angesichts dieser Sitation mit diesem Projekt zum Ziel gesetzt, dieses Konzept lokalen Kleinbauern näher zu bringen. Dazu soll ein Agroforstsystem (AFS) entwickelt und auf einer Pilotfarm angepflanzt werden. Das technische Projekt und Fact-Sheet sollen dabei als Vorlage für weitere Projekte im globalen Süden dienen. Neben der Anpflanzung werden Kleinbauern in einem Workshop die Vorteile von AFS vorgestellt und die Pilotfarm als Demonstrationsfläche genutzt. Neben den technischen und praktischen Grundlagen von AFSs beinhaltet der Workshop auch einen Teil über Online-Vermarktungsstrategien der Produkte sowie die Nutzung von Sozialen Netzwerken. Um für die regionale Kleinbauerngruppe weitere Einkommensmöglichkeiten sowie Bildungschancen zu eröffnen, wird ein bestehender Stall zu einem Mehrzweckworkshop ausgebaut, der eine Saatgutbank, Baumschule sowie Platz für weitere Veranstaltungen und Präsentationen dienen soll.

Internationale Zusammenarbeit
Das Vorhaben wird in Zusammenarbeit mit lokalen und deutschen Partnern durchgeführt: In Brasilien ist die Bundesuniversität von Santa Catarina (UFSC) in Araranguá ein tragendes Element und beheimatet die brasilianische Regionalgruppe. Weiterer wichtiger Projektpartner ist das brasilianische Biobauern-Netzwerk "EcoVida", was die Verbindung zu den lokalen Kleinbauern und Experten herstellt. Von deutscher Seite erhält das Projekt technische Unterstützung von der Fachhochschule für Forstwirtschaft in Rottenburg am Neckar (HFR), die über langjährige Erfahrung mit Forschungsprojekten im Bereich Forstwirtschaft und Regionalmanagement in beiden Ländern verfügt.

proj_26OP7JiC5mapekmJ4OahxzD8.description:
ITF was formed in Kenya in 1922 when Richard St Barbe Baker and Chief Josiah Njonjo formed ‘Watu wa Miti’ – the People of the Trees. This became the society of the Men of the Trees, a worldwide organisation that promoted forest conservation and tree planting on a huge scale. 

Today ITF’s Sustainable Community Forestry (SCF) Programme continues that vision, and is aimed at supporting small, grassroots projects in local communities in Sub-Saharan Africa. These initiatives are aimed at planting trees, restoring forests, education and improving livelihoods.

All these projects are designed by the community, and for the community. They are run by small, local organisations that embedded in the communities they aim to help. All our SCF projects are small-scale and aim to get to the heart of local issue, be it food insecurity, soil erosion, or water conservation.

Plant for the Planet is helping us to continue funding an existing project in Masaka, Uganda – an area damaged by extensive farming and deforestation. 

This project aims to:
      -	Train teachers and children in 27 Primary Schools to raise seedlings and plant valued indigenous trees. 
      -	Planting 84,000 indigenous trees in schools and neighbouring farms will help the nutrition of local children and parents alike.
      -	The tree nurseries in the schools can provide a convenient and affordable source of tree seedlings for the community members to plant on their own land. These children are encouraged to take trees home to their parents who in turn will be able to create their own sources of wood and fuel without further exploiting local natural forests.

proj_js644aJ4g1UWa3EhxwkzCMi9.description:
Final Update: This project marks the latest in the year that the Hoosier National Forest has ever completed a prescribed burn. This spring was unusually wet, which made it difficult to find a window of weather with the right burning conditions. But the right conditions occurred on March 28th, April 17th, and May 13th. 

Young oaks are rare across the Midwest due to intense grazing by deer, and competition from trees species like maple and beech that have spread due to fire suppression. The young oaks in this project will resprout from deep, well-established root systems shortly after the fire and grow quickly with abundant light and resources.
